description: Read-only analysis snapshot of the retrieval bank used by the current construction package; not qualified SFT targets. Skill text is unchanged. Runtime and source metadata omitted.

skills.title: Stop Once Recent Commits Are Visible
skills.principle: On GitLab’s Commits page, recent commits appear in reverse chronological order with the newest entries at the top. Once the commit list and newest commit messages are visible, the viewing task is complete. Report completion and stop instead of scrolling, clicking unrelated author/avatar elements, or opening commit details.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view recent commits and the GitLab Commits page already shows the project’s commit list, especially with the newest dated entries and commit messages visible.

skills.title: Stop After Commits Page Loads
skills.principle: Once the GitLab commits page visibly lists commit messages, authors, and dates for the target repository, treat the task as complete. Report completion and terminate instead of issuing no-op actions or retrying navigation with stale element IDs.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view recent commits and the current GitLab page is the repository’s Commits view with a visible commit list.

skills.title: Inspect README Sections Directly
skills.principle: When a GitLab project README is already present in the accessibility tree, locate the task-relevant heading (such as “Used by”) and extract its list items and links directly. Verify the complete list is visible in the current observation, then report the results and stop without unnecessary scrolling or no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab tasks asking about README-documented users, applications, support, or other sections when the README content and relevant heading already appear in the accessibility tree.

skills.title: Read GitLab Starrers Directly
skills.principle: On a GitLab project’s Starrers page, treat the visible user entries as the answer. Read every listed display name and username, including the current user, and report them once the starrers count and list are visible. Do not click numeric counts or navigate to profiles unless the task explicitly requires additional user details.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked who uses, follows, or starred a GitLab project and the project’s Starrers page visibly lists users with a total count and usernames.

skills.title: Create and Verify a GitLab Issue
skills.principle:
1. Open the target project’s Issues page and select “New issue.”
2. Fill the required title and Description fields, leaving optional settings unchanged unless requested.
3. Select the standard “Issue” type if the type menu is opened, then click “Create issue.”
4. Confirm the resulting page shows “Issue created,” the entered title, and description before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to add an issue to a GitLab project and the project’s Issues navigation and creation form are accessible.

skills.title: Use Project-Specific Merge Requests
skills.principle: From a GitLab project page, select the project sidebar's “Merge requests” link rather than the global dashboard link. On the resulting page, read the “Open” count to determine pending requests, then report the relevant status counts and stop once verified.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to check pending or open merge requests for a specific GitLab project and the project page is already open. Verify the destination is the project’s merge requests page before reporting counts.

skills.title: Follow Expanded Merge Requests Menu
skills.principle:
1. Click the GitLab navigation entry labeled “Merge requests” to expand its submenu.
2. Select the relevant child view, such as “Assigned to you” or “Review requests for you,” rather than waiting on the expanded menu.
3. Confirm navigation by checking the URL and that the main area shows merge-request results or an empty-state message.
skills.when_to_apply: When GitLab’s “Merge requests” navigation entry expands a submenu but the page remains on the dashboard and the requested merge-request list is not yet visible.

skills.title: Open GitLab Project Commit History
skills.principle:
1. On a GitLab project overview, locate the repository summary link labeled with the commit count or open Repository > Commits.
2. Activate it to navigate to the branch commit-history page.
3. Confirm the page shows the commits list, branch context, and chronological entries before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view a GitLab project's commits and the project overview exposes a commit-count link or Repository > Commits navigation. Verify the resulting page is the commit history before stopping.

skills.title: Stop After Reaching Commit History
skills.principle: Once the project’s Commits page is displayed and shows the commit list, treat the task as complete. Confirm the page identifies the target project and branch, then report completion and terminate instead of opening individual commits or repeatedly returning to the list.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to check or view a GitLab project’s commit history and the Commits page visibly lists commits for the relevant project and branch.

skills.title: Extract Roadmap Items from README
skills.principle:
1. On a GitLab project page, locate the README's “Roadmap” heading using the accessibility tree or page text.
2. Inspect the nested list beneath the relevant category, such as “Editors,” and collect each listed item.
3. Report the items as planned future support, preserving their displayed names, then stop once the list is verified.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when a GitLab task asks what features, integrations, or editor support are planned and the project README is rendered on the repository page.

skills.title: Verify Link Context Before Clicking
skills.principle: Use the link’s accessible name and surrounding heading to confirm it matches the requested topic before clicking. When labels repeat, choose the instance inside the relevant feature section, then verify the resulting page title and content. If navigation lands on an unrelated repository file or page, backtrack and select the correct contextual link instead of treating it as completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When researching GitLab roadmaps or feature plans through pages containing repeated labels such as “Learn more,” especially after opening drawers or dynamic menus.

skills.title: Use Project Navigation for Snippets
skills.principle: From the target GitLab project page, inspect the Project navigation sidebar and select the link labeled “Snippets.” Confirm completion when the page heading reads “Code snippets” and the breadcrumbs include the project and “Snippets”; then stop and report success.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to visit a repository or project’s Snippets page and the project page is available. Use the sidebar’s semantic “Snippets” link rather than guessing a URL or selecting unrelated repository controls.

skills.title: Stop After Verifying Merge Requests
skills.principle: Once GitLab shows the Merge requests page and its results, inspect the visible state immediately. Confirm pending items using the Open count or listed merge requests, then report completion and terminate instead of repeating no-op waits.
skills.when_to_apply: When navigating GitLab dashboard or project merge requests, after the URL and accessibility tree show the Merge requests heading, state tabs, or result list.

skills.title: Use Direct URL Fallback
skills.principle: When a visible GitLab navigation link repeatedly fails to activate, use its observed destination URL directly with navigation. Verify success by checking the page title, URL, and expected content (for example, a commits list). Once the target page is confirmed, report completion and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab repository tasks when the relevant navigation entry is visible but clicks produce empty-action errors, no page change, or an unrelated menu; the destination URL must be observable in the accessibility tree.

skills.title: Use GitLab’s Commits Navigation
skills.principle: From the target GitLab project, use the visible Repository → Commits link or its observed href, rather than stale accessibility IDs. Verify the destination by checking the page title contains “Commits” and a chronological commit list is displayed, then stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view a GitLab repository’s commit history and the project page or repository navigation is visible; especially after a stale element ID fails or the page remains unchanged.

skills.title: Verify Directory Navigation Before Stopping
skills.principle: In GitLab’s repository file browser, locate the target directory by its visible name, activate its link, then verify the breadcrumb, URL path, and resulting file table show that directory. Once confirmed, report completion and stop without unnecessary navigation.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to open or navigate to a repository directory and the current page displays a GitLab file listing with the target directory visible.

skills.title: Stop After Reaching Target Directory
skills.principle: When the requested repository directory is visible and its breadcrumb confirms the target path, treat navigation as complete. Report completion and terminate instead of opening individual files or repeatedly returning to the directory.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab tasks asking to navigate to a repository directory, once the directory listing and matching breadcrumb are visible.

skills.title: Use Fresh Accessibility Targets
skills.principle: After each page observation, identify the target project by its currently exposed link name or role, then invoke a syntactically valid click using that exact current target. Do not reuse stale bids, combine labels with unrelated URLs, or retry an element after a not-found error; re-scan the latest accessibility tree and select the matching project link before continuing.
skills.when_to_apply: When navigating GitLab project lists with BrowserGym and a click returns an empty-action or element-not-found error, especially when accessibility-tree identifiers may have changed.

skills.title: Navigate GitLab Repository Directories
skills.principle:
1. Open the relevant GitLab project and select Repository.
2. Follow directory links by matching their visible names, using breadcrumbs to confirm the current path.
3. When the target directory appears, open it and verify its contents in the files table.
4. Optionally open a representative file, then return via the breadcrumb and report the observed items.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to browse a named directory in a GitLab project, especially when the directory is nested and the repository root does not expose it directly.

skills.title: Revalidate Repository Navigation Targets
skills.principle: After each GitLab directory navigation, reread the current accessibility tree and use the visible directory link matching the intended path. Confirm the breadcrumb or URL changed to that directory before inspecting contents. Never reuse stale element IDs or infer that files are absent after landing in a different directory; recover by returning to the intended parent and selecting the correct link.
skills.when_to_apply: When browsing GitLab repository trees, especially after a click, navigation error, or page update changes accessibility-tree element IDs. Verify the current path before reporting directory contents or file absence.

skills.title: Stop After Navigation Is Confirmed
skills.principle: After selecting the target GitLab project-navigation entry, verify that the URL, page title, or breadcrumb reflects the requested section. Once confirmed, report completion and terminate; do not repeat clicks or issue actions against stale accessibility-tree node IDs.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when navigating GitLab project sidebar sections, especially after a click changes the URL or page title to the requested destination.

skills.title: Refresh Locators After Click Errors
skills.principle: After an element lookup fails, re-read the current accessibility tree and select a newly observed target locator. Match the project link by its accessible name or URL, not a stale bid or unrelated letter/avatar link. Use GitLab’s “Filter by name” field when the project list is large, then click the freshly observed project link and verify the URL or page heading changed.
skills.when_to_apply: When navigating GitLab project lists or any dynamic page, especially after a click reports that an element or bid cannot be found.

skills.title: Verify GitLab Star State
skills.principle: On a GitLab repository page, inspect the star toggle by its accessible label. Click “Star” when the repository is unstarred; if it already reads “Unstar,” leave it unchanged. Confirm completion when the control reads “Unstar,” then report success and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to star or bookmark a GitLab repository and the repository page exposes a “Star”/“Unstar” toggle. Use the post-click label to verify the desired starred state.

skills.title: Interpret GitLab Star State Correctly
skills.principle: On a GitLab project page, treat the button label as the current state: “Star” means unstarred and requires one click; “Unstar” means already starred and requires no click. After clicking “Star,” verify the label changes to “Unstar,” then stop to avoid toggling the setting back.
skills.when_to_apply: When bookmarking a GitLab repository, inspect the project action button before acting. Use the visible label, not assumptions or stale observations, and stop once “Unstar” confirms the repository is starred.

skills.title: Verify Fork Form State Before Retrying
skills.principle:
1. Open the repository’s “Fork” action and select the intended namespace.
2. Preserve the generated valid project slug; change the project name only when the interface reports a collision or validation issue.
3. Submit only when “Fork project” is enabled, then verify redirect to the new project or a success notice.
4. If an error leaves the form disabled, reload or reopen the fork form and retry instead of clicking disabled controls or guessing field formats.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when forking a GitLab project and submission fails, the form remains on the fork page, or the “Fork project” control is disabled after an error.

skills.title: Verify Fork Completion
skills.principle: After selecting GitLab’s “Fork,” inspect the refreshed page and URL before reporting success. If the repository page remains visible and “Fork” still points to the fork-creation route, open it and complete the fork form. Confirm completion by observing the new fork project or a success state, then stop.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when forking a GitLab repository and the initial “Fork” click does not visibly navigate, open a form, or change the repository’s fork state.

skills.title: Retrieve GitLab Clone URLs
skills.principle: Open the repository’s “Clone” control and inspect the expanded options. Capture both “Clone with SSH” and “Clone with HTTP” URLs. If GitLab warns that SSH requires an added profile key, recommend HTTP/HTTPS as the immediately usable option while still reporting SSH and its prerequisite.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab repository page is open and the task requires cloning locally or providing clone commands. Use the visible Clone menu and check any SSH authentication warning before choosing a method.

skills.title: Complete GitLab Clone After Finding URL
skills.principle:
1. Open the project’s “Clone” menu and choose “Clone with SSH” or “Clone with HTTP.”
2. Read or copy the corresponding repository clone URL using its “Copy URL” control.
3. Run `git clone <copied-url>` in the local shell, then verify the repository directory exists and contains Git metadata.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab project page displays clone options and the task requires cloning locally; finding or focusing the URL is only preparation, not completion.

skills.title: Find Topic Sections in GitLab READMEs
skills.principle: Use the repository page’s rendered README as the primary source. Locate the heading matching the requested topic, scroll until its complete section is visible, and extract only explicitly stated claims plus relevant screenshots or links. Summarize the evidence and note when implementation details are absent.
skills.when_to_apply: When answering questions about a GitLab repository’s documented feature or support, especially when the README is rendered inline and the target topic appears in a lower section.

skills.title: Stop After Sufficient Evidence
skills.principle: Once the relevant README section directly answers the question, summarize only the supported facts and terminate. Do not repeat the message, issue no-op actions, or explore unrelated repository folders unless the user explicitly requests implementation details or the evidence is genuinely insufficient.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab README visibly contains the requested topic and you have sent a grounded summary, especially when further navigation would only duplicate evidence.

skills.title: Use Project-Scoped GitLab Code Search
skills.principle:
1. Open GitLab’s “Search GitLab” control and enter the exact target value, such as a hexadecimal color code.
2. Select the suggestion scoped to the current project, not “all GitLab.”
3. Verify the results page shows the query, project filter, and code-result count, then inspect matching files and lines.
4. For another value, clear the search field, enter the new query, click “Search,” and verify the updated results.
skills.when_to_apply: When locating exact strings in a GitLab repository and the project is already open. Use this when results must be restricted to repository code rather than global GitLab content.

skills.title: Scope Searches to Repository Code
skills.principle: Use the requested color codes exactly; do not invent sample values. Open the target project’s Repository search (or set the GitLab search Project scope), submit each code, and verify results are code/file matches. If global results show only issues or projects, refine the scope instead of opening unrelated records.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to find values inside a GitLab repository and the initial search surface is global or returns mixed result types. The target project and exact requested values must be known.

skills.title: Read Roadmap From Project README
skills.principle: On a GitLab project page, inspect the rendered README content for a heading matching the requested topic, such as “Roadmap.” Extract the relevant nested list items and report them, distinguishing planned entries from unrelated sections. Verify the heading and items are visibly present before responding.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to find planned features, future support, or roadmap details in a GitLab repository whose project page renders its README.

skills.title: Extract Lists From README Sections
skills.principle: On a GitLab project page, inspect the rendered README for a semantic heading matching the requested category, such as “Used by.” Read every list item beneath that heading, preserving the displayed names, and stop once the list ends before the next section. Report the collected items directly; scrolling is only needed if the accessibility tree does not expose the section.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when answering questions about projects, users, applications, or other entities documented in a repository README and the rendered page exposes semantic headings and lists.

skills.title: Inspect Visible Content Before Scrolling
skills.principle: After opening a GitLab project, inspect the current accessibility tree for the requested heading, such as “Used by,” and its associated links. If the target section is already present, extract the listed names and URLs immediately. Scroll only when the target is absent, and verify each scroll changes the observed page state.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when researching project README content in GitLab, especially when the accessibility tree already exposes headings, lists, or links relevant to the question.

skills.title: Use GitLab’s SSH Key Shortcut
skills.principle: When GitLab warns that SSH access is unavailable, activate the alert’s “Add SSH key” link to open User Settings → SSH Keys. The form requires a real public key in “Key” and a descriptive “Title”; “Add key” remains disabled until required inputs are provided.
skills.when_to_apply: Apply when a GitLab project page displays the SSH access warning and an “Add SSH key” link, especially when the user has not yet configured profile SSH credentials.

skills.title: Open SSH Keys Settings Directly
skills.principle:
1. From the GitLab profile menu, choose “Edit profile” to enter User Settings.
2. In the settings sidebar, click the visible “SSH Keys” navigation entry; do not keep scrolling the Profile form, because it is a separate page.
3. On the SSH Keys page, enter the key and title, submit the add-key form, and verify the new key appears in the keys list.
skills.when_to_apply: When adding an SSH key in GitLab and the User Settings sidebar visibly contains “SSH Keys.” The prerequisite is reaching User Settings; the SSH-key form is on that dedicated navigation page, not the Profile form.

skills.title: Explore All Security Configuration Tabs
skills.principle:
1. Open the project’s “Security & Compliance” navigation entry and verify the “Security Configuration” page.
2. Inspect the initially selected “Security testing” tab, then select “Compliance” and “Vulnerability Management” in sequence.
3. After each selection, verify the tab is selected and read its tabpanel for enabled features, plan restrictions, and relevant alerts.
4. Summarize findings only after all tabs have been inspected.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to explore GitLab project security configuration options and the page presents multiple tabs such as Security testing, Compliance, and Vulnerability Management.

skills.title: Stop After Configuration Is Visible
skills.principle: Open the project’s “Security & Compliance” navigation entry and verify that the “Security Configuration” page displays its configuration options. If the task only asks to view or explore them, stop after this confirmation—or after selecting the specifically requested tab—instead of opening help links or repeatedly scrolling.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab tasks asking to view Security & Compliance configuration options, when the configuration page or requested tab is visibly loaded and its relevant headings or settings are present.

skills.title: Create GitLab Wiki Documentation
skills.principle:
1. Open the project’s “Wiki” navigation entry.
2. If the wiki is empty, select “Create your first page”; otherwise use “New page.”
3. Enter a meaningful title and Markdown documentation in the “Content” field, then click “Create page.”
4. Confirm the resulting page displays the content and a “Wiki page was successfully created” message before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to browse or create GitLab project documentation and the project’s Wiki is accessible, especially when the Wiki page shows an empty-state prompt or a New page control.

skills.title: Verify Wiki Navigation Before Continuing
skills.principle: Use the current accessibility tree to activate the project’s “Wiki” link or navigate to its observed destination. Confirm the page title, URL, and Wiki content are present. Once the Wiki homepage is confirmed, report completion and stop; do not click stale element IDs or pursue unrelated headings, profiles, or projects.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to browse a GitLab project’s Wiki and the Wiki page is reachable. Apply especially after navigation changes the accessibility tree or when the task is satisfied by opening the Wiki homepage.

skills.title: Open GitLab Project Storage Quotas
skills.principle:
1. On the project overview, select the visible project storage usage link.
2. On the Usage Quotas page, select the "Storage" tab.
3. Confirm the Storage tab is active, such as by the storage-specific page state or URL fragment, then report completion.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab tasks asking to view a project's storage usage or quotas, when the project overview exposes a storage usage link or Usage Quotas is available in Settings.

skills.title: Verify Storage Details Before Finishing
skills.principle: After opening GitLab Usage Quotas, select the Storage tab once and inspect the resulting page. Confirm that storage usage or quota metrics are actually visible; a URL hash or selected tab alone is insufficient. If content is absent, inspect the page state or navigate through Settings > Usage Quotas rather than repeatedly clicking the same tab.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when viewing a GitLab project’s storage usage and quotas, especially when the Storage tab appears selected but the accessibility tree shows no storage metrics.

skills.title: Filter GitLab Issues by Open State
skills.principle:
1. From the GitLab dashboard, select the navigation entry labeled “Issues.”
2. On the Issues page, activate the “Open” state link showing its count.
3. Confirm the resulting page indicates the opened state and displays the issue list or matching count, then report completion and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view open GitLab issues and the dashboard provides an Issues navigation link plus state tabs such as “Open,” “Closed,” and “All.”

skills.title: Use Valid Accessibility References
skills.principle: When clicking from an accessibility tree, pass a valid current element reference or target the element by its accessible role and name. Do not emit unevaluated expressions such as `" + str(bid) + "`, which are treated as literal IDs and fail. If the page’s direct link is known, navigate to it instead and verify the resulting URL and visible state.
skills.when_to_apply: Use this on BrowserGym or GitLab pages when an action reports that an element bid cannot be found, especially after the accessibility tree has changed or the requested destination URL is already observable.

skills.title: Create Branch from GitLab Branches Page
skills.principle:
1. Open Repository, then Branches, and select “New branch” instead of using the branch selector’s revision search.
2. Enter the desired branch name and confirm “Create from” is the intended source branch, such as “main.”
3. Click “Create branch” once enabled.
4. Verify GitLab redirects to the new branch’s Files page and the branch selector displays the new name.
skills.when_to_apply: When creating a GitLab project branch from an existing branch, especially after the repository branch selector only offers revision search and reports no matching results.

skills.title: Refresh Locators After Form Changes
skills.principle: After any form action that changes the page, re-read the accessibility tree and locate the current control by role and label. For branch creation, target the current “Branch name” textbox, enter a unique name, keep “Create from” set to the requested base branch, submit, and verify the new branch appears in the branch list.
skills.when_to_apply: When creating a GitLab branch after clearing, submitting, or receiving validation feedback, especially when accessibility-tree IDs may have changed or stale IDs resolve to non-editable elements.

skills.title: Verify GitLab Pipeline Status
skills.principle: Open the project's GitLab "CI/CD" section and select the pipelines view. Use the "All" tab count to determine the total, then inspect each row's status and stage indicators. Report the total, latest run timing, failed or successful stages, and whether any successful runs are visible. Once the status is confirmed and reported, stop.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to check a GitLab project's CI/CD or pipeline status and the project navigation exposes a "CI/CD" entry with a pipelines list.

skills.title: Stop After Reading Pipeline Status
skills.principle: Once GitLab’s Pipelines page or a pipeline detail page visibly shows the build status, extract the status and relevant failed stages/jobs, report it, and terminate. Do not repeatedly click the same status link or issue no-op actions after the requested information is already displayed.
skills.when_to_apply: When checking a project’s CI/CD build status and the current accessibility tree already shows a pipeline status, pipeline detail heading, or stage/job outcomes.

skills.title: Navigate GitLab Repository Directories
skills.principle:
1. Inspect the repository file table and identify the target directory by its visible name and link role.
2. Activate that directory link.
3. Confirm completion from the updated breadcrumb, URL path, and directory listing, then report the visible contents and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to open a directory in a GitLab repository and the repository root or current directory visibly lists the target folder.

skills.title: Inspect All Repository Image Examples
skills.principle:
1. From the GitLab repository tree, open the directory named in the request.
2. Enumerate every image file listed there and open each file through its link.
3. Use the breadcrumb to return to the directory between files, tracking which examples were viewed.
4. After the complete listing has been checked, report the filenames and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab tasks asking you to inspect all visual examples in a repository directory, once the repository tree and target directory are accessible.

skills.title: Refresh Accessibility Targets After Navigation
skills.principle: After every navigation, reread the accessibility tree and select controls by their current role and label, not IDs from an earlier page. Verify the resulting URL or heading before continuing; if it is not the intended project section, recover immediately and choose the correct sidebar link.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when exploring GitLab projects after search or back navigation, especially when accessibility IDs may have changed and you must reach Issues, Wiki, Repository, or documentation pages.

skills.title: Save GitLab Visibility Changes
skills.principle:
1. Open the project’s Settings and expand “Visibility, project features, permissions.”
2. Change “Project visibility” using the parent combobox; use select_option for native dropdowns rather than clicking hidden option elements.
3. Click the section’s “Save changes” button.
4. Confirm the success alert and verify the combobox shows the requested visibility.
skills.when_to_apply: When changing a GitLab project’s visibility or access permissions, with sufficient project settings privileges and the General Settings page available.

skills.title: Change GitLab Project Visibility
skills.principle:
1. Open the target project and select Settings > General.
2. Expand “Visibility, project features, permissions.”
3. Set “Project visibility” to the requested level, then select “Save changes.”
4. Confirm the success alert appears and the visibility control shows the new value before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When changing a GitLab project’s visibility or related access permissions, with sufficient project permissions and the target project already identified.

skills.title: Report Pipeline Status From Table
skills.principle: On GitLab’s CI/CD > Pipelines page, read the status directly from the pipeline table, including labels such as “In progress,” “stuck,” and stage states. Report the observed status and stop once it answers the request. Open a pipeline or stage only when details are explicitly needed, using its actual link and verifying that navigation occurred.
skills.when_to_apply: When checking a repository’s CI/CD status and the Pipelines page already displays status labels in its table. Avoid extra clicks when the requested status is visible.

skills.title: Navigate Directly When Element Lookup Fails
skills.principle: When a repository item is visibly listed but text-based clicking repeatedly fails, use its observed destination URL directly with navigation. Then verify the address, breadcrumb, and directory table show the requested path before stopping.
skills.when_to_apply: Use this in GitLab repository browsing when the target directory appears in the accessibility tree, but clicking its label produces element-not-found or stale bid errors.

skills.title: Verify Merge Closure Timestamp
skills.principle:
1. Open the project’s “Merge requests” page and select the “Merged” state.
2. Identify the most recent merged request using its ordering and timestamps.
3. Open that request and report the explicit “Merged by” or “closed” timestamp, not merely its created or updated time.
4. Confirm the detail page visibly shows the status and exact date, time, and timezone before responding.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked when a project’s latest merge request was closed or merged, and the project’s GitLab merge-request list provides state filters and request detail pages.

skills.title: Use Current Project Navigation Controls
skills.principle: In GitLab, select the project’s actual link or its project-specific “Merge requests” control from the current accessibility tree, not a parent list item or copied URL. After each navigation, verify the page URL or heading changed to the target project before searching statuses. If it remains on the dashboard, reacquire fresh element bids and retry.
skills.when_to_apply: When locating issues, merge requests, or other records within a GitLab project, especially after a click produces no navigation or the accessibility tree still shows the dashboard.

skills.title: Inspect GitLab To-Do List
skills.principle: Open the global “To-Do List” navigation entry, then verify the “To Do” count and read each listed item’s title, project, actor, and status. Report the pending tasks and available actions without selecting “Mark as done” unless explicitly requested.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to check pending GitLab tasks and the global navigation exposes a “To-Do List” link or count. Confirm the destination shows the pending-task list before reporting.

skills.title: Stop After Confirming Issues Page
skills.principle: Once the project Issues page loads, verify the Open tab is selected and the issue list is visible. Report completion immediately and terminate instead of repeating no-op actions or waiting for additional observations.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view a GitLab project's open issues and the project navigation's Issues link has loaded a page showing an Open tab and visible issue entries.

skills.title: Stop After Opening Project Issues
skills.principle: Navigate directly to the target project's project-navigation “Issues” entry, then select or verify the “Open” tab. Confirm the page shows the project's open-issue list and stop; do not open individual issues or return repeatedly unless the task explicitly requests issue details.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view a project's open issues and the project page or project navigation is available. Completion is indicated by the project Issues page displaying the selected Open tab and issue list.

skills.title: Navigate GitLab Help Documentation
skills.principle:
1. Locate the global navigation entry labeled “Help” and activate it.
2. If it expands a menu instead of navigating, choose the nested “Help” link.
3. Confirm the destination by checking the page URL and visible documentation headings such as “GitLab Docs” or “Use GitLab,” then stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to access GitLab documentation from a project or dashboard page, especially when the global “Help” control opens a submenu rather than navigating directly.

skills.title: Re-identify Elements After Navigation
skills.principle: After each page change, use the newest accessibility tree to locate controls by their current label and role. Verify the breadcrumb or page title shows the intended directory before continuing. Never reuse element IDs from an earlier page; if navigation lands elsewhere, recover using the visible breadcrumb or repository listing.
skills.when_to_apply: When browsing GitLab repository trees, especially after opening a file or directory and returning to a parent path. Required whenever element IDs may have changed or the observed URL/path differs from the intended destination.

skills.title: Navigate to GitLab Analytics
skills.principle: Select the project’s “Analytics” navigation entry, then verify the destination by checking for the “Value Stream Analytics” heading and metric sections such as “Key metrics” or “DORA metrics.” Report completion even when metrics display dashes or an insufficient-data message.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to visit a GitLab project’s Analytics page and the project sidebar exposes an “Analytics” entry. Stop after the analytics heading and metric content are visible.

skills.title: Terminate After Analytics Verification
skills.principle: Click the project’s “Analytics” navigation entry, then verify the destination by its “Value Stream Analytics” heading or URL. Once the target page is loaded, report completion and terminate immediately instead of issuing repeated no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to visit a GitLab project’s Analytics page and the accessibility tree confirms the Value Stream Analytics heading or destination URL after navigation.

skills.title: Navigate Repository Directories Semantically
skills.principle:
1. Inspect the repository’s directory table and identify candidate folders by their names and commit descriptions.
2. Open likely folders, then use the breadcrumb or parent control to return when contents do not match the requested artifact.
3. Continue until the target directory is visible; verify its path and listed files.
4. Report the confirmed contents and stop once the requested directory is being viewed.
skills.when_to_apply: When locating a named folder or file set in a GitLab repository, especially when the root listing contains multiple similarly plausible directories.

skills.title: Submit Global Search Suggestions
skills.principle: Use the accessible global "Search GitLab" searchbox, not a nearby heading or stale element ID. Enter the target term, then select the matching suggestion such as "<term> all GitLab" or press Enter to submit. Verify that the resulting search page lists the target project or directory before navigating further.
skills.when_to_apply: When locating a project, directory, or file across GitLab and the global searchbox displays a suggestion or live result after entering the target term.

skills.title: Systematically Explore GitLab Repository Directories
skills.principle:
1. Start from the repository file listing and open the likely parent directory for the requested artifact type.
2. Select the subdirectory whose visible name and commit context match the request.
3. Inspect each listed file, using breadcrumbs to return to the directory between files.
4. Summarize all relevant files and distinguishing properties only after the directory listing and contents have been checked.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to explore a GitLab repository directory and report its files or themes; first ensure the repository tree is visible, then verify each relevant file from the directory listing.

skills.title: Use Current Accessibility Targets
skills.principle: After every navigation, re-read the latest accessibility tree and act only on element identifiers present in that observation. Match the requested directory or file by its displayed role and name, then click its current link target; never reuse textual names as bids or stale targets. If the target is not listed, use repository search or Find file instead of guessing directories.
skills.when_to_apply: When browsing GitLab repository files through BrowserGym, especially after a page transition or failed click, when accessibility-tree bids may have changed or the requested path is not visible.

skills.title: Use Project-Specific Issues Navigation
skills.principle: From a GitLab project page, choose the project sidebar's “Issues” link rather than the global Issues navigation. Confirm completion when the page title, URL path, or breadcrumb identifies the project’s Issues page and the issue list or management controls are visible.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view or manage issues for the current GitLab project, especially when both global and project-specific “Issues” links appear in the accessibility tree.

skills.title: Stop After Confirming Issues Page
skills.principle: Click the GitLab navigation entry labeled “Issues,” then verify the destination by checking the page heading and visible issue filters or lists. Once the “Issues” page is confirmed, report completion and terminate instead of opening an issue, editing content, or performing unrelated exploratory actions.
skills.when_to_apply: When the task only asks you to navigate to GitLab’s Issues page and the resulting accessibility tree shows an “Issues” heading with issue-state filters or listings.

skills.title: Navigate GitLab Issues to Boards
skills.principle: From a GitLab project page, open the project’s “Issues” navigation entry. When its submenu appears, select “Boards.” Confirm completion by checking that the “Issue Boards” page loads and displays issues in kanban columns such as Open and Closed. Report the visible board state and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to view a GitLab project’s issues in a kanban-style board, starting from the project overview or another project page where the Issues navigation is available.

skills.title: Terminate After Board Confirmation
skills.principle: In GitLab, open the project’s Issues section, select the nested “Boards” entry, and verify the board page shows issue columns such as Open or Closed. Once this state is visible, report completion and terminate immediately rather than issuing repeated no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to view a project’s issues in kanban form and the accessibility tree shows the “Boards” navigation entry or a board page with issue-status columns.

skills.title: Navigate GitLab Milestones
skills.principle:
1. Open the project’s Issues section to reveal its submenu.
2. Select the “Milestones” navigation entry.
3. Inspect the page for milestone rows or an empty-state message, then report the observed roadmap status.
4. Stop after confirming the page state; mention “New milestone” only as an available option when the list is empty.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to check a GitLab project’s roadmap or milestones, and the project page provides an Issues navigation entry with a Milestones submenu.

skills.title: Use the Issues Milestones Submenu
skills.principle:
1. Expand the project’s Issues navigation entry and inspect its submenu for “Milestones.”
2. Select “Milestones” directly rather than exploring unrelated sections such as Project information or CI/CD.
3. Confirm the Milestones page by its heading or empty-state message; once displayed, report completion and stop without unnecessary scrolling or waiting.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view a GitLab project’s milestones and the main sidebar lacks a visible Milestones link, first expand Issues and use its nested Milestones entry.

skills.title: Navigate GitLab Analytics Views
skills.principle: Use the project navigation sidebar to select “Analytics.” If its submenu is expanded, choose the requested view such as “Value stream,” “CI/CD,” or “Repository.” Confirm completion by checking the resulting page heading and analytics URL.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to open a GitLab project’s Analytics page or a specific analytics view, provided the project navigation sidebar is visible.

skills.title: Stop After Confirming Analytics
skills.principle: Once the project’s Analytics page is visibly loaded, verify its heading and statistics area, then report completion and terminate. Do not repeat no-op actions after the goal is already achieved.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when navigating GitLab project pages to Analytics succeeds and the observation shows the Analytics heading, metrics, or an empty-data message.

skills.title: Navigate GitLab Deployments Reliably
skills.principle: In a GitLab project, select the project-navigation link labeled “Deployments,” then verify the destination by checking for the “Environments” page title, breadcrumb, or environment-management controls. Once the Environments page is visible, report completion and stop; do not navigate further unless the requested task specifies another Deployments subsection.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to open a GitLab project’s Deployments area or manage environments, especially when the sidebar exposes Deployments with Environments as its active or nested destination.

skills.title: Stop After Reaching Deployments
skills.principle: Click the project navigation entry labeled “Deployments,” then verify the resulting page or breadcrumb shows the Deployments/Environments section. Once the requested destination is confirmed, report completion and terminate instead of opening review-app dialogs, creating environments, or changing settings.
skills.when_to_apply: When the task only asks you to navigate to GitLab’s Deployments section and the page visibly shows “Environments” or the Deployments breadcrumb after navigation.

skills.title: Stop After Reaching Target Directory
skills.principle: Once the repository breadcrumb and page heading confirm the requested directory is open, report completion immediately and terminate. Do not add repeated no-op actions or explore extra files unless the task explicitly requests reviewing their contents.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab repository-navigation tasks when the target directory is visibly listed in the breadcrumb, URL, and file table, confirming navigation succeeded.

skills.title: Identify Root Directories from GitLab Table
skills.principle: On a GitLab repository’s Files page, inspect the root file table and collect entries represented as directories, using their names rather than commit metadata. Exclude files such as README or LICENSE, then report the complete directory list once all visible root rows have been checked.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to list repository directories and the GitLab Files page is already open at the target branch or path, with the root contents exposed in an accessibility tree or table.

skills.title: Filter Repository Entries by Link Type
skills.principle: Inspect the repository files table directly and collect names from the Name-column links. Treat links leading to directory/tree views as directories; exclude file/blob links and adjacent commit-message cells. Use the complete accessibility tree when all rows are already present, then report the collected names and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When listing directories from a GitLab repository tree and the accessibility tree exposes the files table, especially when directory and file rows are mixed with commit metadata.

skills.title: Navigate Directly to Project Issues
skills.principle: From a GitLab repository page, use the project navigation sidebar’s “Issues” link rather than the global Issues entry. Confirm the destination by checking the repository-specific Issues page and its issue tabs or list, then report completion and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to open a repository’s Issues section and the GitLab project sidebar is visible. Verify the page belongs to the target repository before finishing.

skills.title: Use Valid Element References
skills.principle: When selecting a repository section, use the accessibility tree’s current element reference directly; do not construct or concatenate reference expressions inside the click argument. If clicking fails because the reference is invalid, navigate using the observed section URL, then verify the page title and URL show the requested section and terminate.
skills.when_to_apply: Use this on GitLab repository navigation tasks when the target link is visible in the accessibility tree or its destination URL is observable, especially after a click reports an invalid element reference.

skills.title: Open GitLab Project Pipelines
skills.principle: From the repository page, select the project navigation entry labeled “CI/CD,” then verify the resulting page is titled “Pipelines” and displays pipeline rows or pipeline controls. Once the pipelines page is confirmed, report completion without taking additional actions.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to access a GitLab repository’s CI/CD pipelines and the repository page is already open with project navigation visible.

skills.title: Stop After Confirming Pipelines
skills.principle: In GitLab, select the project’s “CI/CD” navigation entry, then verify the page shows “Pipelines” and the pipeline list or controls. Once this destination is visibly confirmed, report completion and terminate instead of issuing repeated no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to access a repository’s CI/CD pipelines and the GitLab page visibly shows the Pipelines breadcrumb, title, tabs, or pipeline table.

skills.title: Create Directories Through Repository Files
skills.principle:
1. Open the target repository’s Repository > Files view, not Settings or Branches.
2. Use the visible “Add to tree” control and select “New directory.”
3. Enter the required directory name; retain or edit the commit message and target branch as needed.
4. Wait until “Create directory” is enabled, submit it, and verify the new directory or resulting commit appears in the repository tree.
skills.when_to_apply: When creating a directory in a GitLab repository and the repository Files view exposes an “Add to tree” menu. The directory name is required before submission.

skills.title: Create a Commit Through GitLab New File
skills.principle:
1. From the repository Files view, open the “Add to tree” menu and select “New file.”
2. Enter a filename and content; confirm the commit message and target branch are populated.
3. Click “Commit changes.”
4. Verify the resulting file page shows “The file has been successfully created” and commit details before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to add a commit to a GitLab repository and the Files view is available, especially when creating a new file is an acceptable change.

skills.title: Complete the GitLab New File Commit
skills.principle: After opening GitLab’s “New file” page, stop retrying navigation. Use the current accessibility tree to fill the “File name,” editor content, “Commit message,” and target branch fields, then activate “Commit changes.” Verify that the repository page or commit confirmation shows the new commit before finishing.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab repository task requires adding a commit and the “New file” form is visible. Use freshly observed element references, especially after navigation, and proceed through the form instead of re-clicking stale repository controls.

skills.title: Copy Latest GitLab Commit SHA
skills.principle: On a GitLab repository’s Files page, identify the latest commit shown near the repository header and activate the accessible “Copy commit SHA” button. Once the button is activated, treat the SHA as copied, report completion, and stop without unnecessary actions.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to copy the latest commit SHA and the repository Files page visibly shows the current branch’s latest commit with a “Copy commit SHA” control.

skills.title: Verify Repository Navigation Before Continuing
skills.principle: Use the currently observed repository-name link, not a stale or guessed element ID. After clicking, verify that the URL and page heading show the target repository. Only then locate the repository’s commits control and copy the first/latest commit SHA; if the page did not change, recover by reopening the target link rather than continuing with unrelated navigation.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab project list contains the target repository and subsequent actions depend on entering its project page. Confirm navigation succeeded before using project-specific controls.

skills.title: Read README Support Sections
skills.principle: On a GitLab repository page, open the project’s README.md and locate the relevant heading, such as “Support” or “Libraries.” Extract the top-level list items under that heading, excluding nested plugin or feature entries, then report the listed libraries exactly as shown.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked which libraries, frameworks, or tools a GitLab project supports and the repository contains an accessible README.md with organized headings and lists.

skills.title: Use Visible README Content Directly
skills.principle: When the README is rendered inline, read the accessibility tree’s headings and lists instead of clicking text labels that may lack actionable element bids. Extract the requested entries from the visible section, verify they answer the question, then report the result and terminate without unnecessary clicks or scrolling.
skills.when_to_apply: Use on GitLab project pages when README content is already visible in the accessibility tree, especially after a click fails because a displayed heading or link has no usable bid.

skills.title: Verify Section Before Claiming Completion
skills.principle: Use the visible navigation link matching the requested section and confirm the resulting URL, heading, or page content shows that section. Do not infer that a section is active merely because its link appears in the sidebar; if navigation fails, retry with a valid semantic target before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to open a GitLab dashboard section and the current accessibility tree still shows another page’s heading or URL, especially when the target link is visible but not visibly selected.

skills.title: Verify Open Count Then Stop
skills.principle: On GitLab’s project Merge requests page, use the state tabs to verify the Open count. If Open is zero, treat that as confirmation that no pending merge requests exist, report the result, and terminate. Do not inspect merged or closed requests unless the task explicitly asks for them.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to check pending merge requests and the project Merge requests page displays state tabs with an Open count.

skills.title: Inspect a GitLab Repository File
skills.principle:
1. In the repository’s Files list, locate the requested filename by its visible label.
2. Activate the file link and wait for the blob page to display its contents.
3. Read the requested fields directly from the rendered code, distinguishing absent dependency sections from keyword names.
4. Report the findings concisely, then stop once the requested information is confirmed.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab task asks for metadata or dependencies from a repository file and the repository tree visibly lists the target file.

skills.title: Read And Report Package Metadata
skills.principle: Once the GitLab file view opens, inspect the visible JSON directly. Read the `version` field and check for dependency sections, reporting their observed values or stating when they are absent. Provide the result to the user, then stop instead of issuing repeated no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab repository task asks you to check a package manifest’s version and dependencies and the manifest contents are already visible in the file view.

skills.title: Verify File Before Uploading
skills.principle: Before invoking GitLab’s file chooser, obtain a real, accessible file path and verify it exists. Use that exact path with the upload control; do not substitute guessed filenames or paths. After selection, confirm the file appears and the “Upload file” button becomes enabled, then submit the commit.
skills.when_to_apply: When uploading a repository file through GitLab’s “Add to tree” → “Upload file” dialog, especially when the task does not specify a file or the environment requires an existing local path.

skills.title: Create a GitLab Branch via Branches
skills.principle:
1. Open the project’s Repository > Branches page when the branch selector lacks a creation option.
2. Select “New branch,” enter the requested branch name, and keep or choose the correct source branch, tag, or commit.
3. Click “Create branch” after the button becomes enabled.
4. Confirm completion from the branch page, current branch selector, or success alert showing the new branch.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for creating a branch in a GitLab project when starting from repository files and the branch selector only lists existing revisions. Ensure the intended source revision is available.

skills.title: Use Repository Navigation for Branches
skills.principle: On a GitLab project page, use the observed “Repository” link or the visible branch control instead of guessing a repository URL. Open the repository tree, then use the branch selector or “Branches” page to choose the create-branch action. Enter the requested branch name, submit it, and verify the new branch appears in the branch list or selector.
skills.when_to_apply: When creating a branch in an existing GitLab project and the project page visibly provides “Repository,” a current branch selector, or a “Branches” link.

skills.title: Create a GitLab Repository Tag
skills.principle:
1. Open the repository’s Repository > Tags page and select “New tag.”
2. Enter the requested release tag name, typically using semantic-version format, and verify “Create from” points to the intended branch, tag, or commit.
3. Leave the optional Message blank unless an annotated tag is required, then select “Create tag.”
4. Confirm the resulting tag details page displays the new tag and its commit reference before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When creating a release tag in a GitLab repository and the target repository, tag name, and source branch, tag, or commit are known.

skills.title: Verify Tag Name Before Submission
skills.principle:
1. Open GitLab’s Repository → Tags and inspect existing tag names before choosing a release tag.
2. Use the exact requested release version; if it is unspecified, do not invent one from visible examples.
3. On duplicate-name errors or page rerenders, re-scan the accessibility tree and locate the current “Tag name” textbox by label before editing.
4. Submit only after the textbox shows the intended unique name, then verify the new tag appears in the Tags list.
skills.when_to_apply: When creating a GitLab tag, especially if the requested version is ambiguous, existing tags are visible, or a failed submission causes the form to rerender and accessibility references change.

skills.title: Use Project Navigation for Merge Requests
skills.principle: From a GitLab repository page, locate the project navigation entry labeled "Merge requests" and activate it. Confirm completion by checking that the page heading or breadcrumb identifies the repository's Merge requests page before reporting success.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to open a repository's Merge requests page and the current GitLab page belongs to that repository. Use the project-scoped navigation rather than the global dashboard link.

skills.title: Stop After Confirming Target Page
skills.principle: After navigation, verify the page heading, URL, and expected content match the requested destination. Once confirmed, report completion and terminate immediately; do not issue repeated no-op actions or continue interacting.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for navigation-only tasks when the target page is visibly loaded and its heading or URL plus relevant content confirm arrival.

skills.title: Open Target File from Repository Listing
skills.principle:
1. In the GitLab repository’s Files view, locate the requested filename in the file table.
2. Activate the filename link, not its commit message or metadata, to open the file page.
3. Confirm the destination identifies the requested file and that its rendered contents are visible before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to view a specific file in a GitLab repository and the repository Files page displays that filename as a link.

skills.title: Use Valid GitLab File Navigation
skills.principle:
1. Emit native BrowserGym actions directly, such as `click("element_id")`; do not embed unevaluated code like `json.dumps` in the action string.
2. From the repository page, locate the file link labeled `README.md` in the current accessibility tree and click that link.
3. Confirm completion when the page title, URL, or visible content identifies the README file, then stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view a file in a GitLab repository, especially after navigating from a project dashboard. Reinspect the current accessibility tree after each navigation because element IDs change.

skills.title: Open and Verify a GitLab Wiki
skills.principle:
1. Locate and open the requested project from the GitLab project list.
2. In the project navigation, select the “Wiki” link.
3. Confirm the Wiki page loaded by checking the breadcrumb or page title and visible Wiki content.
4. Report completion and stop once the requested page is visibly open.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab tasks asking you to check or open a project Wiki, when the target project is identifiable and the project navigation exposes a “Wiki” link.

skills.title: Reinspect After Navigation
skills.principle: After every navigation, discard old element IDs and re-read the current accessibility tree. Locate the target control by its visible label or role, activate it, and verify completion by checking the page title, URL, breadcrumb, or main heading. If the resulting state is unchanged, stop repeating the same stale action and reselect from the refreshed tree.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when navigating GitLab project sections such as Wiki, especially after a click changes pages or when the expected destination does not appear. The current accessibility tree must be available before selecting the next control.

skills.title: Open and Verify a GitLab Directory
skills.principle:
1. Open the target project and select the Repository navigation entry.
2. In the repository file table, locate and open the requested directory by its visible name.
3. Confirm the directory page using its breadcrumb and the files table listing its contents.
4. Once the directory listing is visible, report completion without opening individual files or taking unnecessary navigation actions.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view a directory in a GitLab repository and the project is accessible from the dashboard or project list.

skills.title: Report Completion After Directory Navigation
skills.principle: After selecting the target directory, verify the page title, breadcrumb, and repository file table show that directory. Once confirmed, provide a concise completion response and terminate the task rather than issuing repeated no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab repository task asks you to view a directory and the resulting page visibly shows the requested path and its contents.

skills.title: Compare Dashboard Update Times
skills.principle: On GitLab’s Projects dashboard, inspect each visible project card’s “Updated” time, compare relative or absolute timestamps chronologically, and identify the project with the newest update. Report both the project and its displayed update time once the comparison is complete.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked for the most recently updated project on a GitLab dashboard, with the Projects list and each project’s “Updated” timestamp visible.

skills.title: Read Visible Timestamps Semantically
skills.principle: Use the accessibility tree’s visible project cards and semantic time elements directly. Compare their absolute timestamps or relative ages, then select the newest. If a time shows only relative text, activate the time element to reveal its tooltip and read the absolute date. Do not use fill on static text or hard-code unstable element IDs.
skills.when_to_apply: When GitLab’s dashboard lists projects with “Updated” times and the task asks for the most recent update. Prefer visible semantic content; activate a timestamp only when its absolute date is hidden.

skills.title: Use GitLab’s Assigned Issues Navigation
skills.principle: Select the GitLab navigation link labeled “Issues,” especially when its destination visibly includes an assignee filter. Confirm completion by checking the page heading is “Issues,” the URL reflects the assignee filter, and issue counts or assigned issue cards are displayed. Then report the page is ready to view.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to open GitLab’s Issues page for the current user’s assigned issues, regardless of the starting page. Verify the destination shows the Issues heading and an assignee-filtered list.

skills.title: Emit Valid Browser Actions
skills.principle: Use the browser tool’s required action format directly, with a complete click target and parameters; do not wrap the action inside another JSON string or truncate it. After execution, verify that the URL or page heading changed to the requested destination before retrying. If the state is unchanged, switch to another supported navigation method, such as activating the visible link by its accessible label.
skills.when_to_apply: When a visible GitLab navigation link exists but the tool reports an empty or malformed action, especially after repeated failed clicks and an unchanged page state.

skills.title: Use Visible Navigation Labels
skills.principle: Identify the requested destination from the current accessibility tree by its visible label, activate that navigation link, then verify completion using the resulting page title, heading, URL, or distinctive content. Once the destination is confirmed, report completion and stop without extra actions.
skills.when_to_apply: When a task requests opening a specific GitLab page and the current page exposes a matching navigation link or menu entry with a recognizable label.

skills.title: Stop After Confirming Navigation
skills.principle: When the requested page is visibly loaded, verify its heading or URL once, then report completion and terminate. Do not issue repeated noop actions or continue interacting after the navigation goal is satisfied.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for simple navigation tasks when the accessibility tree shows the target page heading and matching destination URL after a click or direct navigation.

skills.title: Navigate Via Semantic Help Link
skills.principle: Use the accessibility tree to locate the navigation entry labeled “Help.” If it expands a menu, select the nested Help link. Confirm completion when the page URL ends in `/help` and the content shows GitLab documentation or help resources, then stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to visit GitLab’s Help page from another GitLab page, especially when the Help navigation item opens a submenu before exposing the destination link.

skills.title: Stop After Confirming Completion
skills.principle: Once the page state visibly matches the requested destination, treat the task as complete. Report completion and terminate the interaction instead of issuing repeated no-op actions or continuing to wait.
skills.when_to_apply: Apply to navigation tasks when the accessibility tree and URL confirm the requested page is loaded, such as GitLab showing the Help page and its Help heading or breadcrumb.

skills.title: Verify Project List Exhaustion
skills.principle: On a GitLab project-list page, scroll through the visible list and inspect the updated accessibility tree. Compare project entries before and after scrolling; when no new entries appear and the list has reached its end, report that there are no additional projects instead of continuing unnecessary actions.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to explore all projects and the current GitLab page already shows a project list, with scrolling available to reveal potentially additional entries.

skills.title: Paginate Until No Next Link
skills.principle: On GitLab’s Explore Projects page, inspect each page and follow the visible “Next” pagination link. Continue until the current page has no “Next” link; only then report that all projects have been explored. Do not treat reaching one Explore page or an arbitrary page number as completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to explore all GitLab projects and the Explore Projects results are paginated. Verify completion by checking that pagination no longer offers a “Next” link.

skills.title: Stop After Starred List Appears
skills.principle: Click GitLab’s “Starred” navigation entry, then verify the URL or visible project list shows starred projects. Once the starred-projects page is confirmed, report completion and terminate instead of opening a project or performing unrelated exploration.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to check out or view starred GitLab projects and the dashboard visibly contains a “Starred” navigation link or the resulting page shows the starred-project list.

skills.title: Verify Navigation Before Retrying
skills.principle: After selecting a navigation entry, inspect the updated URL, page title, and main content before acting again. If they match the requested destination, treat the task as complete—even when the page reports an empty state—and stop retrying or clicking.
skills.when_to_apply: When navigating GitLab sections such as Explore or Topics, especially after an action error or unchanged-looking interface. Confirm destination through observable URL and heading/content before retrying.

skills.title: Stop After Confirming Navigation
skills.principle: After navigation, verify the URL or a distinctive page heading matches the requested destination. Once confirmed, report completion and terminate instead of issuing repeated no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for navigation tasks when the accessibility tree shows the requested destination’s URL, heading, or distinctive content; confirmation is the prerequisite for stopping.

skills.title: Read GitLab Issue Status Counts
skills.principle: Open the target project’s Issues page and use the selected status tab’s count rather than counting listed issues. Confirm the tab is labeled “Open” and selected; report the adjacent number as the open-issue total. Stop once the status and count are visibly confirmed.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked for a GitLab project’s open-issue count and the project can be located from the project list or navigation. Use the selected “Open” tab count as the authoritative visible result.

skills.title: Complete Repository Exploration Efficiently
skills.principle:
1. Open the target GitLab project and use the Repository/Files view to inspect the root tree and README.
2. Follow only the most relevant directories or representative files needed to understand the repository’s purpose and structure.
3. After gathering sufficient evidence, summarize the explored contents and key findings.
4. Report completion and terminate instead of continuing exploratory clicks.
skills.when_to_apply: For GitLab tasks asking to explore a repository, especially when the project page already exposes its README and file tree. Stop once the requested overview is supported by visible repository evidence.

skills.title: Clear Tooltips Before Clicking
skills.principle: When a tooltip intercepts the intended repository file link, move the pointer to a neutral area or wait for the tooltip to disappear, then retry the original target. Confirm the file page opens before choosing an alternative item.
skills.when_to_apply: Use in GitLab repository listings when a click timeout reports that a visible tooltip or overlay is intercepting pointer events.

skills.title: Submit GitLab Navbar Searches
skills.principle:
1. Focus GitLab’s navbar “Search GitLab” field rather than the projects-page “Filter by name” field.
2. Fill it with the requested query.
3. Press Enter to submit the search.
4. Confirm the Search page shows the query and the relevant “Projects” results tab or count.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to search GitLab broadly for projects or other content and the dashboard contains both a global “Search GitLab” field and a local project filter.

skills.title: Stay on the Project Filter
skills.principle: Use the projects page searchbox labeled “Filter by name,” enter the requested text, and verify the URL or visible project list reflects the filter. Once filtered results appear, stop. Do not click unrelated controls such as “New project” or switch to GitLab’s global search.
skills.when_to_apply: When filtering projects on GitLab and the project-list searchbox is visible. Apply after entering the query, especially when the page already updates results or URL parameters automatically.

skills.title: Navigate GitLab Profile Menus
skills.principle:
1. From the GitLab dashboard, activate the signed-in user name or avatar in the top navigation.
2. If this opens a dropdown instead of navigating, select the menu link showing the user’s name and username.
3. Confirm completion by checking the URL and page heading identify the user profile, then report success and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view the signed-in user’s GitLab profile from the dashboard, especially when clicking the top user control opens an account dropdown rather than navigating directly.

skills.title: Choose Public Profile, Not Settings
skills.principle: When asked to view a user profile, open the username link from the account menu (the link showing the display name and handle), not “Edit profile,” “User Settings,” or the settings-sidebar “Profile” link. Confirm navigation by checking that the URL is the user’s public handle path and the page shows public profile content.
skills.when_to_apply: Use on GitLab when the account menu is open and both a public username link and profile-edit/settings links are visible; viewing differs from editing profile settings.

skills.title: Create and Verify a GitLab Group
skills.principle:
1. Open GitLab’s “Create new...” menu and choose “New group.”
2. Select “Create group,” then enter the required Group name; confirm the Group URL is populated or valid.
3. Submit with “Create group,” leaving optional personalization fields unchanged unless required.
4. Verify the destination group page shows a success alert confirming the group was created.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to create a new GitLab group and you have permission to do so. Start from a GitLab page where the “Create new...” navigation entry is available.

skills.title: Choose Group Creation, Not Project Creation
skills.principle: For a GitLab group task, navigate through the account or dashboard menu to the explicit “New group” control. Do not use “Create new...” or “Create blank project,” which opens project creation. After each navigation, verify the page heading and form labels identify group creation before entering values.
skills.when_to_apply: When the task asks to organize projects in a new GitLab group and the current page shows project listings or a “Create new project” page. Check for an explicit group-management entry before filling any form.

skills.title: Terminate After Confirming Completion
skills.principle: Once the target page is reached, verify its heading, URL or active filter, and visible content match the request. Then report completion and terminate immediately instead of repeating no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: Use after navigation tasks when the observed page clearly shows the requested destination and any required scope, such as GitLab Issues filtered to the current user.

skills.title: Activate GitLab Help Navigation
skills.principle:
1. Click the top-level “Help” control to open its menu.
2. Select the nested “Help” link, not merely the menu toggle.
3. Confirm navigation by checking the URL changes to the Help page and documentation content appears.
4. Once confirmed, stop interacting and report completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When accessing GitLab documentation from the dashboard, especially when the “Help” control expands a menu containing a separate nested “Help” link.

skills.title: Turn Repository Browsing Into Contribution
skills.principle:
1. After locating a relevant accessibility issue and its source file, stop broad exploration and inspect the concrete implementation.
2. Edit the source files, not generated output, using the repository’s Web IDE or an available contribution workflow.
3. Commit the focused change with a descriptive message and link it to the issue through a merge request or equivalent review submission.
4. Verify the resulting commit or review request is visible before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab task asks you to contribute code or accessibility improvements and you have identified both a relevant issue and the responsible source file; browsing alone is insufficient.

skills.title: Turn Repository Browsing Into Contribution
skills.principle: After locating the target GitLab repository, move from inspection to an actionable change: use the Files tree to identify a relevant source file, open it, then use “Open in Web IDE” or the file edit control to make a focused accessibility improvement. Commit the change with a descriptive message, and verify the resulting commit or changed file state before stopping.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when the task requests both viewing repository code and contributing improvements, especially after reaching the repository’s Files tree and identifying a relevant source or template file.

skills.title: Verify Open Merge Requests From Project List
skills.principle:
1. Locate the target project in GitLab’s project list and use its merge-request count/link to open the project’s Merge requests page.
2. Confirm the page shows the requested open count, such as an “Open” tab with the expected number.
3. Review the visible merge-request entries and summarize titles plus relevant statuses, including pipeline failures or merge blockers.
4. Report completion once the expected entries are displayed.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to check pending or open merge requests for a specific GitLab project, especially when the project list exposes a merge-request count link.

skills.title: Use Project-Scoped Merge Requests
skills.principle: Navigate directly to the target project's merge-request page, preferably using its visible merge-request count or project URL. Select the Open/Pending state and verify the displayed project matches the requested repository before collecting items. Do not substitute the dashboard's assignee-filtered merge requests, which may show unrelated projects and an incomplete count.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to inspect pending merge requests for a specific GitLab project, especially if the dashboard shows an assignee filter or a total different from the requested number.

skills.title: Use Observed Commit Link URLs
skills.principle: When the project page exposes a commit-count link, use its exact observed destination URL or the link’s valid accessibility target rather than guessing text or IDs. Navigate to the commits route, then verify the page title or commit list appears before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When viewing a GitLab project and the accessibility tree shows a repository commit link, especially after text-based clicks fail or resolve to ambiguous elements.

skills.title: Follow Semantic Repository Paths
skills.principle:
1. Open the project’s Repository view and inspect the root file table for likely style-related directories.
