2. If no exact CSS directory exists, choose a semantically relevant distribution or library directory based on its name and contents.
3. Open the directory and verify that the resulting file table contains stylesheet files before reporting their location and roles.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to inspect project styles in GitLab and the repository has nested or non-obvious directories; repository access and a visible file listing are required.

skills.title: Verify Repository Paths Before Editing
skills.principle: Use the repository file listing to locate the exact requested directory, confirming its name and presence before opening files. Do not infer a project or substitute a similarly named CSS file. Once the requested directory is displayed, review it and stop unless modification instructions specify a file and changes.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab task requests checking a directory but does not identify a project or file, especially when multiple projects or similarly named style files are visible.

skills.title: Follow Expanded Help Menu Links
skills.principle: When a navigation control expands a menu instead of navigating, inspect the updated accessibility tree and activate the submenu destination link. Verify that the URL or page heading changes; do not repeatedly click the parent toggle. If the submenu remains unusable, use its observed destination URL directly.
skills.when_to_apply: Use this on GitLab when clicking a top-level navigation item such as Help only expands a menu, leaving the current page unchanged and exposing a second, destination link.

skills.title: Navigate GitLab Repository Files
skills.principle:
1. Identify a likely repository from the project listing using the requested file’s domain or technology.
2. Open the repository’s “Repository” view and enter the likely directory, such as “examples.”
3. Select the exact filename from the file table and verify the file page displays its source code.
4. Report completion and stop once the requested file is visibly open.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view a specific file in GitLab and the repository is not yet open; requires using project listings and repository directory tables to locate and verify the target file.

skills.title: Search Before Browsing Projects
skills.principle: Use GitLab’s global search to locate the target project or file instead of guessing from project lists. Activate only element IDs currently present in the accessibility tree; treat displayed URLs as destinations, not click targets. After each navigation, verify the page heading or URL changed before continuing.
skills.when_to_apply: When locating a specific repository file from the GitLab dashboard, especially if many projects are listed or repeated clicks leave the page unchanged.

skills.title: Verify Admin Access Before Guessing URLs
skills.principle: Use GitLab’s visible navigation or user menu to locate an explicit “Admin Area” entry before navigating. Treat global search results for “admin” as content results, not administrative navigation. If the standard admin route returns “Page Not Found,” stop guessing subpaths, reassess permissions or instance configuration, and report that the announcements area is unavailable unless a visible route confirms it.
skills.when_to_apply: When managing site-wide GitLab settings such as announcements from a dashboard, especially when no Admin Area link appears and a guessed administrative URL returns a 404 page.

skills.title: Recover From Malformed Click Actions
skills.principle: When a visible navigation link is present but click attempts produce an empty-action error, retry with the simplest valid click targeting that link, without unnecessary arguments. Confirm success by checking the page heading and URL, then stop and report completion.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when navigating GitLab dashboards or similar pages and the intended navigation control remains visible, but the browser reports an empty or malformed action instead of changing pages.

skills.title: Stop After Confirming Target Page
skills.principle: After navigation, verify the page heading, title, or URL matches the requested destination. Once the target state is visibly confirmed, report completion and terminate immediately instead of issuing repeated no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for simple navigation tasks when the observed page clearly shows the requested destination, such as GitLab displaying the Issues heading and dashboard URL.

skills.title: Use GitLab’s Merge Requests Navigation
skills.principle: From GitLab’s dashboard, activate the “Merge requests” navigation entry. If its submenu expands, select the relevant dashboard view, such as “Assigned to you.” Confirm navigation by checking the page heading and URL for the Merge requests dashboard, then report completion and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to open GitLab’s Merge Requests dashboard from another dashboard page, especially when the navigation entry expands a submenu instead of navigating immediately.

skills.title: Use Expanded Merge Requests Navigation
skills.principle: On GitLab’s dashboard, treat the top-level “Merge requests” control as a menu toggle. Click it once to expand the submenu, then select the relevant submenu link such as “Assigned to you” or “Review requests for you.” Verify the URL and page heading change before stopping; do not repeatedly click the toggle.
skills.when_to_apply: When the GitLab dashboard remains on the Projects page after selecting “Merge requests” and the accessibility tree shows an expanded submenu containing destination links.

skills.title: Disambiguate Duplicate Assignment Entries
skills.principle: On GitLab’s To-Do List, locate the entry matching the requested merge request by title and project. If duplicates exist, distinguish assignment direction from the entry text: select the one stating another user “assigned you,” not the one stating you assigned it yourself. Report that user as the assigner, optionally including the merge request identifier.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when a GitLab To-Do List contains multiple entries for the same merge request, especially both incoming and self-assignment records.

skills.title: Follow the Assigned Merge Requests Link
skills.principle: After opening GitLab’s “Merge requests” navigation, check whether it expanded a submenu instead of navigating. Select “Assigned to you” to reach the actual assigned-MR list, then verify the page heading or URL changed before searching or scrolling.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab navigation entry expands on click and the address or main content remains unchanged, especially when locating a merge request assigned to the current user.

skills.title: Verify Pending Count Before Acting
skills.principle: Open GitLab’s To-Do List and inspect the pending-state indicator before searching for bulk actions. If “To Do” shows zero and the page displays an empty-list confirmation, the requested state is already achieved; report completion and stop. Only investigate item controls when pending items are actually present.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to complete, clear, or bulk-update GitLab to-dos, especially after navigating to the To-Do List. Use this whenever the page exposes a pending count or empty-state message.

skills.title: Find GitLab’s Oldest Completed To-Do
skills.principle:
1. Open GitLab’s “To-Do List” and select the “Done” view.
2. Read each completed item’s displayed timestamp, title, and project; compare timestamps rather than relying only on list position.
3. Report the item with the earliest completion time and include its project and timestamp.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab tasks asking for the oldest completed to-do when the account’s To-Do List is accessible and the “Done” view exposes timestamps for its entries.

skills.title: Identify the Oldest Completed To-Do
skills.principle: Open GitLab’s “Done” to-do view and compare each visible item’s full timestamp. Do not assume the first row is oldest; select the item with the earliest timestamp, typically the last row when sorted newest-first. Report its actual title and timestamp, then stop using a valid completion message.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked for the oldest completed GitLab to-do item and the “Done” view lists multiple entries with timestamps. Verify ordering and use the item title, not the tab count or status label.

skills.title: Restore a Completed GitLab To-Do
skills.principle:
1. Open the GitLab To-Do List’s “Done” view.
2. Locate the row whose issue title matches the requested target exactly.
3. Click that row’s adjacent “Add a to do” control, not another item’s restore link.
4. Open “To Do” and confirm the target issue appears in the pending list before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when restoring a completed GitLab issue or merge request to the active To-Do list. The Done view must contain the target row and its corresponding “Add a to do” control.

skills.title: Restore Done GitLab To-Dos Directly
skills.principle:
1. Open GitLab’s “To-Do List” and select “Done” to view completed items.
2. Locate the target by its visible issue title and project context.
3. Click that item’s “Add a to do” restore link, not the issue link or unrelated icon.
4. Verify it appears under “To Do” or the pending count increases.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when a GitLab issue was completed and must return to the active to-do list. The target must appear in the Done view; match its title and project before restoring.

skills.title: Filter To-Dos by Author
skills.principle:
1. Open the GitLab To-Do List and expand the “Author” filter.
2. Enter the requested author in “Search authors” and submit the search.
3. Verify the result: “No matching results” indicates no matching to-dos in the current view; otherwise, the displayed list is filtered to that author.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to show GitLab to-do items assigned by a specific person, with the To-Do List page and its Author filter available.

skills.title: Use the To-Do Author Filter Correctly
skills.principle: On GitLab’s To-Do List, use the `Author` filter for items assigned by someone. Open it, type the person’s displayed name into the `Search authors` searchbox, then click the matching author result. Do not use `select_option` on the searchbox or substitute the Issues assignee filter. Confirm the author filter is applied in the To-Do List before finishing.
skills.when_to_apply: When filtering GitLab dashboard to-dos by who created or assigned them, especially when the Author control opens a searchable custom dropdown rather than a native select.

skills.title: Sort GitLab To-Do Items by Creation
skills.principle: Open GitLab’s “To-Do List” from the dashboard, then use the creation-date sort control labeled “Last created.” Select or toggle its direction until the list is ordered from oldest to newest, and confirm the resulting sort state or item order before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab task requires ordering to-do items by creation date. Ensure the dashboard’s “To-Do List” page is open and use its visible creation-date sorting control.

skills.title: Select and Verify Oldest Created
skills.principle: On GitLab’s To-Do List, open the creation-date sort control and select “Oldest created.” Confirm completion when the control label reads “Oldest created” and the page URL reflects ascending creation order; then stop without reopening the menu or issuing repeated no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: When sorting GitLab to-do items from oldest to newest and the sort control offers distinct “Last created” and “Oldest created” options.

skills.title: Stop After Filter Confirmation
skills.principle: After selecting the Type menu’s “Merge request” option, verify completion by checking that the URL includes the type filter and the button label changes to “Merge request.” Once confirmed, report completion and terminate instead of clicking navigation or reopening the filter.
skills.when_to_apply: When filtering GitLab To-Do items by type, especially after the page refreshes and visibly shows the selected type in the filter control or URL.

skills.title: Check Both To-Do States
skills.principle: On GitLab’s To-Do List, inspect both the pending “To Do” view and the completed “Done” view, even when one count is zero. Confirm each page’s displayed empty-state message or item list, then report the verified counts and completion status.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to view all GitLab to-do items, especially when the To-Do List shows separate pending and completed tabs or count links.

skills.title: Filter To-Dos by Issue Type
skills.principle: On GitLab’s To-Do List, keep the task context there instead of opening the Issues dashboard or an individual item. Open the “Type” filter, select “Issue,” and verify the resulting list contains issue entries (for example, “Issue #…”) rather than merge requests. Treat the filtered list as complete when all displayed pending entries are issue-related.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view all to-do items related to issues and the To-Do List shows mixed item types such as merge requests and issues, with a visible “Type” filter.

skills.title: Terminate After Verifying Navigation
skills.principle: After navigation, verify the page title, URL, and main heading match the requested destination. Once confirmed, report completion and terminate immediately. If a click produces an empty-action error, issue one correctly formatted direct navigation using the observed link URL, then recheck the resulting page before stopping.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for simple GitLab navigation tasks when the destination is already visible or a navigation click fails. Prerequisite: the accessibility tree exposes the destination’s link, URL, title, or heading.

skills.title: Navigate GitLab Issues Precisely
skills.principle:
1. Use GitLab’s global search to find the target project, then select the matching project result.
2. Open the project’s “Issues” navigation entry and identify the requested issue by its number and title.
3. Open the issue, verify its status and relevant description or activity, then summarize the observed details.
4. Once the issue is checked and the summary is sent, terminate without further actions.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to inspect a specific issue in a GitLab project, especially from a dashboard or unknown starting page. Verify the project and issue identifiers before reporting completion.

skills.title: Use the Exact Issue Link
skills.principle: When the issue list visibly contains the target project and issue number, click that issue’s title link directly instead of scrolling or using global search. After navigation, verify the page heading and project/issue identifier match the requested target before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When checking a specific GitLab issue and the current accessibility tree already shows a matching project#issue entry or title link. Reinspect the current tree before acting if earlier element references may be stale.

skills.title: Use Dashboard Link for Projects
skills.principle: From another GitLab dashboard page, activate the global “Dashboard” link. Confirm completion when the resulting page has the title “Projects · Dashboard · GitLab,” a “Projects” heading, and the user’s project list; then report completion without further navigation.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to open GitLab’s Projects Dashboard from a dashboard subpage, especially when no direct “Projects Dashboard” link is visible but the global “Dashboard” link is available.

skills.title: Use Current Accessibility Targets
skills.principle: After a selector fails, re-read the current accessibility tree and use the element’s observed bid or verified href, not a guessed text selector. For GitLab navigation, activate the actual Dashboard link target, then confirm the URL or page heading changed before trying another action. Do not repeat an identical failed selector or invent a Projects control absent from the tree.
skills.when_to_apply: When navigating GitLab from a page whose accessibility tree exposes navigation links, especially after a click reports that a label or bid cannot be found.

skills.title: Explore GitLab Public Projects
skills.principle:
1. From GitLab Dashboard, open Projects, then select the “Explore” navigation entry.
2. Inspect public projects through “All,” “Most stars,” and “Trending” tabs; use “Filter by name” or visibility controls when needed.
3. Open a project listing to verify its overview, repository files, README, license, and activity statistics.
4. Report the explored views and observed project details once the Explore page and project page have loaded.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for open-ended GitLab tasks asking to explore public projects, especially when the starting page lacks a direct Explore link and project discovery should include multiple listings or one detailed project.

skills.title: Reinspect Before Each Navigation
skills.principle: After every page transition, inspect the current accessibility tree and locate the intended control by its current label, role, and surrounding context. Do not reuse element IDs from an earlier page. Before clicking, verify the target’s visible name and destination; after clicking, confirm the URL or heading reflects the intended project.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when exploring GitLab projects across list, repository, README, issue, or profile pages, especially after navigation changes the accessibility-tree IDs or when a click times out or lands on an unexpected page.

skills.title: Verify GitLab Topics Availability
skills.principle: From GitLab’s Projects dashboard, select the “Topics” navigation entry. Confirm the destination is the Topics page, then inspect its content. If it displays “There are no topics to show” and advises adding topics to projects, report that browsing is unavailable until topics exist.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to browse GitLab projects by topics and the Projects navigation exposes a “Topics” entry. Stop after verifying the page’s topic-list or empty-state message.

skills.title: Navigate and Verify Topics
skills.principle:
1. On GitLab’s Projects exploration view, select the navigation link labeled “Topics” rather than relying on the current project list.
2. Confirm the page heading or URL identifies the project Topics page; report any displayed empty-state message, then stop once the requested page is reached.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to view GitLab’s project Topics page and the Projects exploration navigation is visible, including when the page may contain no topics.

skills.title: Verify State After Submission Timeout
skills.principle: When a form submission reports a timeout, inspect the current page before retrying. If the page has navigated to the target resource and shows a success alert or resulting content, treat the operation as complete and report success; do not submit again.
skills.when_to_apply: Use after clicking a create, save, or submit control when navigation-wait timeout occurs. Verify the resulting page and explicit success message before taking further action.

skills.title: Use Visible Controls When Clicks Are Intercepted
skills.principle: When a form control’s click is blocked by an overlapping element, inspect the accessibility tree for the associated visible label or action control and activate that instead. For GitLab templates, click the visible “Use template” control associated with the chosen template rather than repeatedly clicking the hidden radio input or scrolling. Confirm the radio becomes checked or the next form appears.
skills.when_to_apply: Apply on GitLab project-creation forms when a template radio is present but click errors report that its “Use template” label or another overlay intercepts pointer events.

skills.title: Navigate GitLab Issues by Project Search
skills.principle:
1. Use the current accessibility tree to locate GitLab’s global search, then search for the target project.
2. Select the matching project result and open its project-navigation “Issues” entry.
3. Find the issue by its visible title in the issue list and open it.
4. Confirm the issue detail page title and content match the request, then report completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view a specific issue in a GitLab project, especially from an unrelated dashboard page. Re-check current accessibility labels after each navigation because element identifiers can change.

skills.title: Open Project Issues Before Searching
skills.principle:
1. From the project page, activate the observed project navigation entry labeled “Issues,” rather than scrolling the repository overview.
2. On the issues page, use its issue-specific filters or search controls to find the requested title.
3. Open the issue link whose visible title exactly matches the request and verify the issue detail page loaded.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view a specific GitLab issue and the current project page shows an “Issues” navigation link, especially when repository files and README content dominate the page.

skills.title: Verify Assigned Open Merge Requests
skills.principle: In GitLab, open the navigation’s “Merge requests” menu and select “Assigned to you.” On the resulting dashboard, use the “Open” tab or count to confirm scope, then summarize every listed merge request and visible status indicators. Report completion only after the filtered page and item count agree.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to check open merge requests assigned to the current user and GitLab navigation exposes “Merge requests,” “Assigned to you,” and an “Open” filter or count.

skills.title: Validate Actions Against Current UI
skills.principle: Use the exact supported action syntax and target the observed element by its current accessible role or label. After clicking “Merge requests,” verify that the URL or page heading changed before attempting filters. If an action returns an empty-action or parsing error, correct the command instead of repeating malformed variants or assuming navigation succeeded.
skills.when_to_apply: When navigating GitLab from an accessibility tree, especially after an action error or when the page remains unchanged. Verify navigation before filtering merge requests by assignee or status.

skills.title: Use Direct Navigation When Clicks Fail
skills.principle: When a visible GitLab navigation link is hard to activate or a click produces an empty-action error, use the link’s observed destination with a valid `goto` action. Verify the resulting page URL and title match the requested section, then stop and report completion.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab section-navigation tasks when the target link is visible but clicking it fails, the action payload is malformed, or the page remains unchanged after the click.

skills.title: Copy a GitLab project ID
skills.principle:
1. Locate the target project in the GitLab Projects list and open its project page.
2. Read the displayed “Project ID” and activate the “Copy project ID” button.
3. Confirm the project page still shows the target project and report that the ID was copied.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab tasks requesting a project ID copied to the clipboard, when the target project can be found in the Projects list and its project page exposes “Project ID” and “Copy project ID”.

skills.title: Navigate to GitLab Repository Files
skills.principle: In a GitLab project, select the project-navigation "Repository" entry. Confirm the resulting page is the repository file tree, indicated by a "Files" view, the target branch, and a table listing directories and files. Once the file listing is visible, report completion without further navigation.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to view or access a GitLab repository’s code files and the project page exposes a "Repository" navigation entry.

skills.title: Match Navigation Scope to Request
skills.principle: For a broad request to view repository code files, open GitLab’s Repository > Files view and verify the file table is visible. Do not arbitrarily open individual files or descend into directories unless the request names a specific file or requires content inspection. Stop once the requested repository listing or file content is visibly displayed.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for ambiguous GitLab repository-viewing tasks where no specific filename, directory, branch, or content is requested; the Files page or requested file must already be visibly available.

skills.title: Verify Fork Completion Before Reporting
skills.principle: After selecting GitLab’s “Fork” control, inspect the resulting repository page before stopping. Confirm the URL or project namespace belongs to the current account and that the page explicitly shows “Forked from” the source repository. Report completion only after this observable confirmation; otherwise continue checking the fork workflow.
skills.when_to_apply: When forking a GitLab repository, especially after the page navigates to a similarly named project or the action provides no explicit confirmation.

skills.title: Complete GitLab Fork Form
skills.principle:
1. From the repository, open the fork form at the project’s “Fork” workflow or its “Fork project” page.
2. Open “Select a namespace” and choose the authenticated user’s personal namespace.
3. Click “Fork project” to submit; do not stop after selecting the namespace.
4. Verify the resulting project is under the user namespace and displays “Forked from” the original repository.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab repository’s Fork link does not visibly complete the operation. Use the fork form, especially when the personal namespace must be selected before submission.

skills.title: Use Current Project Navigation
skills.principle: On a GitLab project page, locate the current accessibility-tree link labeled “CI/CD” and activate it directly. Verify the resulting URL and page heading indicate the target project’s pipelines; do not reuse stale element IDs or infer a dashboard-wide pipelines URL. If the current page is unrelated, return to the project before continuing.
skills.when_to_apply: When checking a project’s CI/CD status and the interface contains project navigation. Required: identify the target project and confirm the current accessibility tree before selecting controls.

skills.title: Use the AUTHORS File for Contributors
skills.principle: In a GitLab repository contributor lookup, inspect the repository file listing for an `AUTHORS` file, open it, and read every displayed entry. Report the names and contact details explicitly listed there, clarifying that the result reflects the file’s contents rather than all historical contributors.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked who contributes to a GitLab project and the repository root exposes an `AUTHORS` file or similarly named contributor document.

skills.title: Send Valid Final Messages
skills.principle: After reaching the correct GitLab Contributors page, send one concise user message using a directly valid `send_msg_to_user(...)` action. Avoid wrapping the action in markdown, nested JSON, or over-escaped quotes. Verify the action payload is nonempty and executes successfully, then stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When the requested repository information is visible and the agent is ready to report it, especially after a prior empty-action or parsing error.

skills.title: Use To-Do Count Navigation
skills.principle: When GitLab’s navigation shows a “To-Do List” entry with a pending-count badge, select that navigation entry. Confirm the destination heading and pending tab display the requested count and list of items, then report completion without taking additional actions.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab tasks asking to view pending to-do items when the global navigation exposes “To-Do List” and its count badge.

skills.title: Use Direct Navigation After Click Errors
skills.principle: When a visible navigation link repeatedly produces an empty-action error, use its observed destination URL with direct navigation instead of retrying. Verify the resulting page heading and requested count or state, then stop once the goal is visibly satisfied.
skills.when_to_apply: Use this for GitLab navigation tasks when the target link is present in the accessibility tree but click attempts fail, and its destination URL is observable.

skills.title: Read a GitLab Repository File
skills.principle:
1. Open the project’s Repository view and locate the requested filename in the file listing.
2. Select the filename to open its blob page, then read the rendered content and relevant headings.
3. Summarize the file’s requested information, verifying the target file is open before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab tasks asking you to read or understand a specific repository file, when the project repository and target filename are accessible.

skills.title: Summarize Visible Repository File
skills.principle: After opening the target file, verify its contents are visible in the rendered or source view. Extract the requested technical details and provide them in the final response; once the information is available, stop issuing no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab repository file has been opened and its contents are visible in the page accessibility tree, especially after a render/source toggle.

skills.title: Navigate to Infrastructure Clusters
skills.principle:
1. In the project navigation, select “Infrastructure.”
2. Confirm the resulting page is the Kubernetes clusters view by checking the page title, breadcrumb, or selected navigation entry.
3. Report the visible cluster state, such as an empty Agent tab, and stop once the requested section is displayed.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to view a GitLab project’s infrastructure or Kubernetes clusters and the project page is already open with its navigation sidebar available.

skills.title: Verify Target Page Then Stop
skills.principle: After selecting the requested GitLab navigation entry, inspect the updated accessibility tree and URL. If the target section or heading is present, treat the task as complete, report completion, and terminate instead of repeating clicks or no-op waits.
skills.when_to_apply: Use after navigating to a GitLab project section when the page URL, breadcrumb, heading, or relevant content already confirms the requested destination.

skills.title: Use GitLab’s Copy Project ID Button
skills.principle: On the target GitLab project page, locate the displayed “Project ID” and activate the adjacent “Copy project ID” button. Do not copy the URL, guess a project from the dashboard, or ask the user to copy manually; verify the clipboard-success feedback when available.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab task requires copying a project ID and the target project page is open or can be reached unambiguously. Ensure the correct project is selected before using its labeled copy control.

skills.title: Verify GitLab Release Tags
skills.principle:
1. Open the target project from the GitLab project list.
2. Expand Repository navigation and select “Tags.”
3. Confirm the Tags page loads and inspect its status text; report whether tags exist, using “Repository has no tags yet” as the empty-state confirmation.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view a GitLab repository’s release versions or tags, after identifying and opening the relevant project.

skills.title: Terminate After Confirming Tags Page
skills.principle: After navigating to the repository’s Tags page, verify the page heading or URL and visible tag/release entries. Once confirmed, report completion and terminate immediately; do not repeat noop actions, since they can prevent the task from reaching a recognized terminal state.
skills.when_to_apply: For GitLab tasks asking to view tags or release versions, after the Tags page visibly loads and lists tag entries or releases.

skills.title: Navigate GitLab Repository Directories
skills.principle:
1. Locate the target project in the GitLab project list using its visible name.
2. Open the project and use the repository file table, not unrelated navigation, to find the requested directory.
3. Open the directory and verify its breadcrumb and file listing show the requested path.
4. Once the destination and relevant contents are visible, report completion and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when a GitLab task asks you to reach a named directory inside a repository and the project must first be located from a project listing.

skills.title: Stop After Confirming Navigation
skills.principle: After clicking a repository directory, verify the URL, breadcrumb, and file table show the target path. Once confirmed, report completion and stop; do not repeat clicks using stale accessibility IDs or navigate away.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when navigating GitLab repository directories or files, especially after the page updates and accessibility-tree element IDs change.

skills.title: Navigate Nested GitLab Directories
skills.principle:
1. Start from the repository root and inspect the file listing for the likely parent directory.
2. Open the parent directory, then locate the target folder by its visible name in the accessibility tree.
3. Select the target folder and verify completion using the breadcrumb and resulting directory listing.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when locating a named directory in a GitLab repository, especially when it is nested and not visible at the repository root. Confirm each navigation step from the updated file listing.

skills.title: Search Before Exploring GitLab Projects
skills.principle: When locating a named directory, do not guess a project from its description. Open a likely repository only after checking its identity, then use GitLab’s “Find file” control and enter the directory name in “Find by path.” Open the matching result and verify the breadcrumb shows the requested directory; if no result appears, return to the project list and test another repository instead of repeating navigation.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab task requests a specific repository directory but the starting project list does not identify the correct project or the directory is absent from the visible root listing.

skills.title: Use Current Accessibility Targets
skills.principle: In GitLab repository browsing, select the target directory or file using its currently observed accessibility-tree link/bid, not a guessed text label. After each click, verify that the URL, breadcrumb, or table changed before continuing. If the target is not visible, use GitLab’s “Find file” or search instead of repeatedly clicking stale or nonexistent targets.
skills.when_to_apply: When navigating a GitLab repository and an attempted click reports that an element or bid cannot be found, or the page observation remains unchanged after an action.

skills.title: Navigate GitLab Repository Directories
skills.principle:
1. Start from the repository root and open the likely source or content directory.
2. Inspect the resulting file listing for a directory matching the requested content label.
3. Open that directory and verify the breadcrumb and listing show the target path and relevant files.
4. Once the target directory is visibly confirmed, report completion and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab tasks asking you to locate a named folder or content collection in a repository, when the repository root and accessible directory listings are available.

skills.title: Verify Repository Paths Before Navigating
skills.principle: In GitLab repository tasks, use the repository tree or “Find file” to locate the requested directory by its exact name. Inspect accessibility roles and URLs to distinguish directories (`/-/tree/...`) from files (`/-/blob/...`). Open matching directory entries and confirm the breadcrumb or page heading reflects the target before exploring further.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to open a directory or featured-content location in a GitLab project and the current page lists repository files or unrelated project-navigation links.

skills.title: Use Current Repository Evidence
skills.principle: When locating requested documentation in GitLab, inspect the current accessibility tree before every interaction. Prefer visible file names, semantic link labels, or Find file over stale element IDs. If a guessed path reports that the file does not exist, use the repository listing or search to identify the actual file, then verify its rendered contents before concluding the requested topic is absent.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab repository page contains many files or links and element IDs may change after navigation, especially when the requested document or topic is not immediately visible.

skills.title: Use Search Results Scope Correctly
skills.principle: After submitting a GitLab search, inspect the result counts and switch to the scope containing matches. Here, Projects showed zero while Issues showed matches, so select the Issues navigation entry and open the result whose title or content matches the requested article. Use current accessibility-tree labels or bids, not guessed project paths or stale identifiers.
skills.when_to_apply: When searching GitLab for an article or topic and the search page reports zero project results but nonzero issue results, or when repeated clicks fail because guessed labels or identifiers are not present.

skills.title: Find Articles by Repository Structure
skills.principle: In a GitLab project containing website source files, navigate from the repository root into the likely content directory (such as `src/posts`), scan filenames for the requested topic, open the semantically matching Markdown file, and summarize its rendered content. Confirm the file contains the requested subject before reporting findings.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when a GitLab task asks you to learn from a dedicated article and the initial project page exposes repository directories rather than the article directly.

skills.title: Open Dropdown Destinations Correctly
skills.principle: When a navigation control expands a menu, select the destination link inside the expanded menu rather than assuming the parent control navigated. Verify the URL, page heading, or main content changes before searching, scrolling, or reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when a GitLab navigation item such as Help shows expanded=True and reveals nested links, especially when the page remains unchanged after activating the parent item.

skills.title: Locate Content by Repository Filename
skills.principle: In a GitLab repository, navigate through visible directory entries to the content area, inspect filenames for an exact topical match, open that file, and verify its rendered text addresses the request before reporting completion. If an element reference is stale, use the current accessibility tree to select the same entry by its visible name or role.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to read or summarize a topic stored in a GitLab repository and the repository exposes directory listings with meaningful filenames.

skills.title: Switch Search Scope When Wiki Is Empty
skills.principle: When a project wiki is empty or returns zero results, do not keep scrolling or open creation forms. Use the search results’ available scopes—especially Code, Issues, or Commits—to locate the requested topic in repository content. Open matching results and verify the page contains the requested platform-specific information before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When researching a topic in GitLab and the Wiki shows no pages or zero matches, while search results indicate content exists in another scope such as Code or Issues.

skills.title: Use GitLab Commits for Repository Recency
skills.principle: Open the repository’s “Commits” view rather than relying on a directory’s last-commit label. Read the first commit entry on the target branch, open it if its message is truncated, and report the full message shown on the commit detail page.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked for the latest commit message for an entire GitLab repository, especially when currently viewing a subdirectory or file browser whose displayed commit may only apply to that path.

skills.title: Read the First Visible Commit Message
skills.principle: On GitLab’s commits page, inspect the first visible commit entry and read its commit-message link directly. Confirm it is the newest entry by its date and list position. Do not click author avatars, hidden responsive elements, or stale accessibility IDs; if the message is already exposed in the accessibility tree, report it without additional navigation.
skills.when_to_apply: When retrieving the latest commit message and the commits page already shows a dated commit list with message links in the accessibility tree.

skills.title: Use the Target Project’s Issues Link
skills.principle: From the project listing, select the Issues link associated with the target project card, not the global Dashboard Issues navigation entry. Prefer the observed project-specific href or open the project first and use its project navigation. Confirm the resulting page identifies the target project and its issue tracker; stop if a 404 appears rather than repeatedly guessing URLs.
skills.when_to_apply: When GitLab shows both global Issues navigation and project cards containing issue links, especially when the task names a specific project. Verify the link’s surrounding project identity and href before activating it.

skills.title: Verify Target Directory in Main Tree
skills.principle: Open the repository’s “Repository” file tree and confirm the branch selector is set to the requested branch. Inspect the current path listing for the target directory; if it is absent, report that it does not exist rather than navigating elsewhere. If present, open it and list the directory names shown.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab tasks asking for contents of a path on a specific branch, especially when the requested directory may be absent. Requires access to the target repository and its repository file tree.

skills.title: Read GitLab Directory Listings
skills.principle:
1. Open the target project’s Repository and confirm the requested branch and path in the branch selector and files breadcrumb.
2. Inspect the repository table and collect entries represented as directory links, excluding files.
3. Report the directory names exactly as displayed, then stop once the listing is complete.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab tasks asking for directory names under a specified repository path and branch, when the Repository files table and path breadcrumb are visible.

skills.title: Use Repository Commits Navigation
skills.principle: From a GitLab repository page, use the project navigation sidebar and select the “Commits” link under “Repository.” Confirm completion when the page title, breadcrumb, or URL shows the repository’s Commits view and commit history, then report success and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to open a GitLab repository’s commit history and the project page is already available with repository navigation visible.

skills.title: Inspect Both GitLab Registries
skills.principle:
1. Open the project’s “Packages and registries” navigation entry.
2. Inspect “Package Registry” and record its visible package count or empty-state message.
3. Open “Infrastructure Registry” and record whether Terraform modules exist.
4. Report both observed results, then stop once each registry has been viewed.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view a GitLab project’s Packages and Registries section, especially when the task requires checking both package contents and Terraform module contents.

skills.title: Stop After Reaching The Target Page
skills.principle: Once the requested GitLab page is open, verify its heading and key state, then report completion and stop. Do not follow documentation links, scroll for extra information, or perform unrelated actions after the target view is confirmed.
skills.when_to_apply: When a task asks you to view a specific project section and the destination page visibly shows the expected heading, such as “Package Registry,” with its current contents or empty state.

skills.title: Export Open Issues as CSV
skills.principle:
1. Open the project’s Issues page and keep the Open issues tab selected.
2. Click “Export as CSV” to open the export confirmation dialog.
3. Confirm the selected issue count and click “Export issues.”
4. Verify the success alert states that the CSV export started and will be emailed; then report completion and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to export a project’s open GitLab issues as CSV, provided the Issues page exposes the Open tab and an “Export as CSV” control.

skills.title: Complete CSV Export Through Modal
skills.principle:
1. Open the issues page with the desired status filter selected, then choose “Export as CSV.”
2. When the “Export issues” modal appears, stop interacting with the obscured background button.
3. Locate the modal’s current “Export issues” link or confirmation control by its accessible label and activate it.
4. Treat the confirmation that the export will be created in the background and emailed as completion; do not reuse stale element IDs.
skills.when_to_apply: For GitLab issue CSV exports when “Export as CSV” opens a confirmation modal. Use the modal’s refreshed accessibility-tree elements, especially after repeated renders or stale-ID errors.

skills.title: Open Repository Merge Requests
skills.principle:
1. Locate the target repository in the project list and open it.
2. In the repository’s project navigation, select “Merge requests.”
3. Confirm the merge-request page shows the “Open” state and its open-count tab; this page lists the repository’s open merge requests.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view open merge requests for a specific GitLab repository and the repository is reachable from the projects dashboard or search results.

skills.title: Inspect Merge Request Pipeline Status
skills.principle:
1. Open the project’s Merge requests page and select the requested merge request by its title or reference.
2. Open its “Pipelines” tab and wait or scroll until the pipeline table appears.
3. Inspect the latest pipeline row for its status, pipeline identifier, timestamp, commit or branch, and individual stage results.
4. Report the observed status and relevant failed or successful stages, then stop.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when checking a specific GitLab merge request’s latest pipeline, after locating the correct project and merge request. Confirm the pipeline table is loaded before reporting results.

skills.title: Verify Merge Request Before Pipeline Inspection
skills.principle:
1. Identify the requested merge request explicitly from its number, title, or branch; do not substitute the newest repository pipeline.
2. Open that merge request or its related pipeline entry and confirm the displayed merge request matches the target.
3. Read the latest pipeline status directly from the pipeline summary or status indicator, then report it and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When checking GitLab CI/CD status for a specific merge request, especially when the pipeline list contains multiple branches, commits, or similarly recent entries.

skills.title: Stop After Reaching Requested Page
skills.principle: Once the repository’s CI/CD navigation is selected and the resulting page visibly shows the CI/CD pipelines view, treat the task as complete. Confirm the page title or URL matches the requested destination, report completion, and terminate instead of exploring pipelines or jobs unnecessarily.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view a specific GitLab repository section and the resulting page visibly contains the requested section, such as a CI/CD pipelines page.

skills.title: Terminate After Page Confirmation
skills.principle: After navigating to the requested GitLab section, verify the page title, URL, and relevant navigation state. Once they confirm the target page is displayed, report completion and terminate immediately instead of issuing repeated no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for page-viewing tasks when the observed page already shows the requested repository section, such as a GitLab CI/CD Pipelines page, and no additional interaction is required.

skills.title: Verify Export After Confirmation
skills.principle:
1. Open the project’s Merge requests page and select “Export as CSV.”
2. In the “Export merge requests” dialog, activate the confirmation action.
3. If the click reports a navigation timeout, inspect the refreshed page before retrying; an alert such as “Your CSV export has started” confirms success.
4. Report completion and any stated delivery method.
skills.when_to_apply: When exporting GitLab merge requests through the UI, especially when the confirmation click may trigger background processing or a navigation timeout.

skills.title: Verify Navigation Before Exporting
skills.principle: After selecting the relevant GitLab “Merge requests” entry, verify that the page heading, URL, and accessibility tree show the merge-request list. If navigation only expands a menu or remains on the repository, choose the project-level merge-request link instead. Then locate the export/download control and confirm the CSV download state before stopping.
skills.when_to_apply: When exporting a GitLab merge-request list, especially when both dashboard and project navigation contain “Merge requests” links or clicking one may expand a menu instead of navigating.

skills.title: Retrieve Open Merge Requests RSS Feed
skills.principle:
1. Open the target GitLab project and select its project-level “Merge requests” navigation entry.
2. Ensure the “Open” state is selected, then activate “Subscribe to RSS feed.”
3. Use the resulting Atom page’s address-bar URL, including its feed token and open-state parameter, as the subscription URL.
4. Report the complete URL to the user; do not attempt to fill a nonexistent page field.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked for a GitLab project’s RSS feed for open merge requests, after locating the correct project and confirming the merge-request list exposes “Subscribe to RSS feed.”

skills.title: Use Current Page State Before Acting
skills.principle: After navigation succeeds, inspect the new accessibility tree and continue from its current controls. Do not reuse bids or selectors from the previous page. If the target page is already open, use its visible navigation, such as “Merge requests,” then locate the RSS control and verify the resulting subscription state.
skills.when_to_apply: When a click changes the page or the accessibility tree shows the target repository is already open, especially after earlier bid or selector errors.

skills.title: Use Repository Documentation Directly
skills.principle: In a GitLab project, identify a documentation file whose name matches the requested information (for example, a technology or architecture document), open it, read the rendered headings and lists, and report the relevant contents. Stop once the requested facts are confirmed rather than continuing unrelated repository exploration.
skills.when_to_apply: When answering questions about a GitLab project’s technologies, conventions, setup, or design and the repository contains a clearly named documentation file matching the topic.

skills.title: Use Root Documentation First
skills.principle:
1. When asked about a repository’s technology stack, inspect the root file list for documentation named TECHNOLOGY, README, or similar before exploring source directories.
2. Open the matching documentation file and extract the explicitly stated technologies.
3. After navigation or errors, reread the current accessibility tree and select fresh element references instead of reusing stale bids.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab repository questions about technologies, setup, or architecture when the repository root is accessible and contains documentation files.

skills.title: Verify Tags Before Opening Commit
skills.principle: Open the target repository’s Repository navigation, select “Tags,” and check the resulting tag list. If the requested tag appears, open it and follow its commit reference. If the page explicitly says the repository has no tags, report that the requested tag and associated commit are unavailable.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view a commit associated with a GitLab tag, after identifying the target repository and before attempting to inspect commit history.

skills.title: Use Root Listing for Documentation Files
skills.principle: In a GitLab repository, return to the repository root when nested directories do not contain the requested documentation. Scan the root file table for a clearly named documentation file, open it, and verify its rendered heading and substantive content before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to check project documentation and the current GitLab repository view is inside a nested directory without an obvious matching file.

skills.title: Retrieve GitLab Clone Command
skills.principle:
1. On the repository page, open the “Clone” control.
2. In the expanded options, locate the “Clone with HTTP” repository URL.
3. Construct `git clone <HTTP repository URL>` and provide the complete command.
4. Stop once the command is clearly reported; no additional repository navigation is required.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked for a GitLab repository’s Git clone command and the repository page exposes a “Clone” control with HTTP or SSH URL options.

skills.title: Read Clone URL Directly
skills.principle: When the GitLab Clone menu is open, read the visible repository URL textbox and construct the requested `git clone <URL>` command directly. Prefer the HTTP option when the page warns that SSH requires an unconfigured key. Use the copy button only if it is visibly enabled; otherwise do not retry hidden controls.
skills.when_to_apply: For GitLab tasks requesting a repository’s Git clone command, after opening the project’s Clone menu and when SSH access is unavailable or copy controls are not visibly actionable.

skills.title: Edit Source Files, Not Compiled Output
skills.principle: For this Eleventy site, edit files under `src/`, then save them while the development watcher is running. Node.js regenerates the website automatically, reports build errors in the command line, and refreshes the local preview. Do not edit `dist/`: those generated changes are overwritten by the next source-file save.
skills.when_to_apply: When updating an Eleventy-based GitLab website locally, after installing dependencies and starting its documented development watcher; confirm regeneration messages and the refreshed local preview.

skills.title: Use Repository Documentation First
skills.principle: For procedural questions, inspect the repository’s README or contributor documentation instead of repeatedly opening commit history. Find the section matching the request, then report its concrete commands and safeguards. For this site, the “Updating the website” section explains that saving files regenerates the site and edits belong in `src/`, not `dist/`, which is overwritten.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked how a GitLab-hosted project or website is updated and the repository contains accessible README or documentation files. Prefer documentation inspection before navigating commits or unrelated repository views.

skills.title: Stop Terminal-Running Development Servers
skills.principle: When a local development server is running in a terminal, stop its foreground process by pressing Ctrl+C in that same terminal. If it was launched through another process manager or method, use that method’s corresponding stop command instead.
skills.when_to_apply: Apply when asked how to quit a local development server and the server was started interactively in a terminal; identify the terminal or launcher before choosing the stop action.

skills.title: Handle Terminal-Only Server Instructions
skills.principle: When the requested operation concerns a local development server and the browser shows no server controls, provide the terminal procedure directly: focus the terminal running the server and press Ctrl+C. Send the guidance once, then terminate instead of repeating messages or attempting irrelevant browser navigation.
skills.when_to_apply: Apply when a user asks how to stop a local server, the current GitLab page contains no server-management control, and the server is assumed to be running in a terminal outside the browser.

skills.title: Find Latest GitLab Release via Tags
skills.principle: Open the repository’s Repository > Tags page and inspect the tags list. GitLab displays release tags with their dates and release links; use the first entry when the list is visibly ordered newest first. Report its version and date, confirming the entry is marked “Release” rather than relying only on tag naming.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked for a project’s most recent GitLab release and the repository is accessible. Navigate to Repository > Tags, especially when no dedicated Releases navigation entry is visible.

skills.title: Use GitLab Releases for Latest Version
skills.principle: Open the target project, select its Releases link, and read the first release entry when the list is sorted by released date descending. Treat that top entry’s version and displayed date as the most recent release, then report them and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked for a GitLab project’s latest or most recent release and the project page exposes a Releases link or release count. Verify the releases page shows descending date order before using the first entry.

skills.title: Use GitLab Search for Task Keywords
skills.principle: When a GitLab repository is already relevant, search within GitLab for the task’s distinctive keywords instead of navigating unrelated sections. Enter the query in the global “Search GitLab” field, review matching issues, commits, or files, and open the result whose title directly matches the requested topic. Confirm the page contains the requested guide before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: Apply when asked to find repository content and the current project may contain it, especially when navigation shows a global “Search GitLab” field and the task includes distinctive topic keywords.

skills.title: Stay Within GitLab Search Scope
skills.principle: Use GitLab’s global search, choose the appropriate project or “all GitLab” suggestion, and inspect matching issue, code, or wiki results. If a project-scoped search is sparse, broaden the GitLab scope using the current filter controls. Do not leave GitLab for an external search engine; report only after reviewing the available GitLab results.
skills.when_to_apply: When the task asks you to find information in GitLab and the initial project-scoped search returns few or irrelevant matches.

skills.title: Inspect Repository Templates for Page Content
skills.principle: When a GitLab repository mirrors a requested website page, locate the matching page template in the file listing and inspect its source. Use semantic headings and nearby descriptions to identify the requested topic, then summarize the relevant sections and note when links require the rendered site for full details.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab tasks asking about content on a repository-backed website page, especially when the repository tree exposes a clearly named template such as a resources or documentation page.

skills.title: Use GitLab Tags for Release Dates
skills.principle:
1. Open the repository’s “Tags” navigation entry.
2. Locate the requested version tag, using “Filter by tag name” when needed, and open it.
3. Read the timestamp shown beside the tag’s commit on its details page; report it as the release date and time.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked when a repository version was released and GitLab provides repository navigation with a “Tags” entry. Confirm the requested version tag and read its displayed commit timestamp.

skills.title: Verify Navigation Before Continuing
skills.principle: After selecting a navigation item, inspect the next accessibility tree and URL immediately. If the page has not changed, activate the intended submenu link or use the page’s search field; do not repeat waits. Confirm the destination contains the requested topic before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when navigating GitLab menus or help pages, especially when a top-level Help control opens a submenu and the task requires a specific resource or accessibility topic.

skills.title: Search All GitLab Content
skills.principle:
1. Enter distinctive task keywords in GitLab’s global “Search GitLab” field and submit.
2. Inspect result-scope counts; if Projects has no matches, open the populated scope such as “Issues” or “Merge requests.”
3. Select the result whose title semantically matches the requested post, then verify the destination page heading before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when locating a post or discussion in GitLab and global search returns multiple content types, especially when project results are empty but issue or merge-request results are populated.

skills.title: Report Once the Match Is Confirmed
skills.principle: After opening a candidate file, verify its title or visible content matches the requested topic. Then immediately report the file and relevant result to the user, and terminate. Do not repeat no-op actions after confirmation.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when a GitLab repository listing leads to a file whose path, title, or rendered content visibly matches the user’s requested item.

skills.title: Refresh Element References After Navigation
skills.principle: After each navigation or page update, re-read the current accessibility tree and locate the target by its visible role or label. Use the newly observed element reference for the next action; never reuse a bid from an older page state. If an action reports a missing element, immediately re-observe and retry with the current reference.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when browsing GitLab repository trees or any dynamic web UI where navigation, loading, or rerendering may change accessibility-tree element references.

skills.title: Refresh Element References After Navigation
skills.principle: After every navigation or failed interaction, re-read the current accessibility tree and identify the target by its visible label and current role before clicking. Do not reuse stale bids from earlier pages. If a tooltip blocks the target, move focus or hover away, wait for it to disappear, then retry; verify the URL or page content changed afterward.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when exploring GitLab repository trees, especially after returning to parent directories, encountering locator errors, or seeing tooltip overlays that intercept clicks.

skills.title: Filter GitLab Issues by Label
skills.principle:
1. Open the repository’s Issues section from project navigation.
2. Select the visible label link matching the requested label, using its current accessibility element ID rather than text alone.
3. Confirm filtering succeeded by checking the URL, active filter, issue count, and displayed issue list.
4. Report the verified results and stop once the goal is complete.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to find repository issues with a specific label and the GitLab project Issues page is accessible. Use the active filter and count as completion evidence.

skills.title: Use Structured GitLab Label Filters
skills.principle: On a GitLab project’s Issues page, apply the target label through GitLab’s structured filter or by selecting an existing label link, rather than relying on plain-text search. Confirm the filter is reflected in the URL or visible query state, then inspect issue cards for the requested label and use pagination to cover all results.
skills.when_to_apply: When finding project issues by an exact label, especially when plain-text issue search leaves the list unchanged or the results still contain unrelated labels.

skills.title: Read Issue Count From Navigation
skills.principle: When a GitLab project page is already open, inspect the project navigation for the “Issues” entry. Use the adjacent numeric badge as the current open-issues count, then report it without opening extra pages unless the count is absent or ambiguous.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab tasks asking for a repository’s current open-issue count when the project page’s accessibility tree shows an “Issues” navigation entry with a numeric badge.

skills.title: Open GitLab Web IDE
skills.principle: From the GitLab project repository, activate the link labeled "Web IDE." Confirm navigation succeeded when the IDE view appears with the project file sidebar and the instruction to select a file for editing.
skills.when_to_apply: When the task is to access browser-based code editing for a GitLab project and the repository page exposes a "Web IDE" navigation link.

skills.title: Use Current Accessibility IDs
skills.principle: After each page transition, re-read the latest accessibility tree and activate the numeric bid associated with the desired control. Match visible labels such as file names to their current numeric button IDs; never pass the label text as a bid. If activation fails, inspect the refreshed tree before retrying.
skills.when_to_apply: Whenever BrowserGym exposes numeric accessibility bids, especially in GitLab’s Web IDE file sidebar, after navigation or any failed click.

skills.title: Find an Issue’s Latest Update
skills.principle:
1. Open the project’s Issues list and locate the target issue by its exact title.
2. Open the issue details and wait until the Activity entries finish loading.
3. Compare activity timestamps chronologically; use the newest comment or system event, not the creation timestamp.
4. Report the newest entry’s full date and time, optionally including its relative label and author.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab tasks asking when an issue was last updated, after the target issue is identifiable in the project’s Issues list and its Activity section is accessible.

skills.title: Inspect a GitLab Repository File
skills.principle:
1. Locate the target file in the repository’s current directory listing, using its filename and path.
2. Open the file’s blob view and verify the breadcrumb and displayed source identify the requested file.
3. Summarize the relevant headings or content categories visible in the source, then report completion without unnecessary navigation.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to inspect a specific file in a GitLab repository and the repository tree is already open or provides a visible matching file entry.

skills.title: Use Current Semantic Targets
skills.principle: On GitLab project lists, locate the target repository or file using the visible project name, repository search, or “Filter by name,” rather than guessing accessibility-tree IDs. After every navigation or failed action, reread the current accessibility tree and select a currently exposed link. Once inside the repository, use file search or the repository tree to find the requested file.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab task requires finding a file across projects and element clicks fail, produce stale-bid errors, or the page remains unchanged. Verify the current page before each interaction.

skills.title: Navigate GitLab Repository Directories Carefully
skills.principle: When locating a repository content section, choose the directory matching the target name rather than a similarly named template file. If a wrong directory opens, use the visible “Go to parent” control, re-scan the file table, and open the intended directory. Confirm completion when its breadcrumb and contents show the requested section’s files.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when a GitLab task asks you to view a repository section and the file list contains both a target directory and similarly named templates or files.

skills.title: Use Current Accessibility Bids
skills.principle: When a click by visible text fails with “Could not find element,” do not repeat the same label or scroll blindly. Re-read the latest accessibility tree, identify the target link’s current element bid and role, then click that bid. Verify navigation by checking the URL or updated breadcrumbs before continuing.
skills.when_to_apply: Use this on GitLab repository file lists or any BrowserGym page when the target is visible in the accessibility tree but text-based clicking repeatedly returns a missing-element error.

skills.title: Verify Analytics Page Before Acting
skills.principle: Inspect the current accessibility tree and URL before clicking. If the page already shows the Analytics section, such as a Value Stream Analytics heading with project metrics, treat the task as complete, report the visible views and metrics, and stop. Only navigate when Analytics is not already open.
skills.when_to_apply: For GitLab tasks asking to visit project Analytics, especially when the current page may already be an Analytics view and the accessibility tree shows Analytics navigation or metric headings.

skills.title: Navigate to Project Analytics
skills.principle:
1. Open the target project from the project list.
2. In the project navigation sidebar, select “Analytics.”
3. Confirm the Value Stream Analytics page loads and report the displayed metrics or the explicit empty-state message when data is unavailable.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to view statistics or metrics for a GitLab project and the project list is the starting page. The target project must be identifiable before opening its Analytics navigation entry.

skills.title: Inspect GitLab Announcement Files
skills.principle: In a GitLab repository, locate the directory matching the requested page, open its announcement or content files, and read a representative substantive item. Summarize the observable updates and mention other listed topics without claiming every file was reviewed. Once the requested information is confirmed, report completion and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to check project updates stored in a GitLab repository, especially when the repository tree exposes a clearly named content directory such as announcements.

skills.title: Search For Exact Page Names
skills.principle: When a requested GitLab page is not visible in the current navigation, use the global “Search GitLab” field with the exact page name and inspect matching results. Open only a result whose scope and label match the request, then verify the destination heading before reviewing its updates.
skills.when_to_apply: Apply when the task names a specific page, such as Announcements, but the current dashboard or project sidebar does not expose that page directly.

skills.title: Locate and Review a GitLab Repository File
skills.principle:
1. From the repository tree, identify the most likely content directory based on the requested file type.
2. Open that directory and scan the file listing for the exact requested filename.
3. Select the file link and verify its page displays the filename and contents.
4. Summarize the relevant information only after the file content is visible.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to inspect a specific file in a GitLab repository and the repository tree or a likely directory is already accessible.

skills.title: Search GitLab for the Exact File
skills.principle: Use the visible “Search GitLab” field to search the exact filename before browsing unrelated Help pages. Select the matching project or repository result, open the file from the repository tree, and verify the page displays the requested file contents.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view a specific file in GitLab and the current page exposes global search, especially when the file’s project or location is unknown.

skills.title: Read and Summarize a GitLab Document
skills.principle:
1. Locate the repository file matching the requested document by its meaningful filename or visible content.
2. Open it in GitLab’s blob viewer and inspect all sections, scrolling until the document’s final headings or text are visible.
3. Summarize the major expectations and operational details accurately, then send the summary to the user.
4. If message submission fails, retry with simpler plain text and verify the action is non-empty.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to read or explain a document stored in a GitLab repository, especially when the file is long and requires scrolling through the blob viewer.

skills.title: Verify Search Results Before Reading
skills.principle: When locating a policy or document, distinguish documentation results from issue or merge-request mentions. After searching, inspect result type and title; refine the scope or select the exact document result. Open it only when the page contains the requested document, then read its content instead of scrolling unrelated search listings.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab tasks asking you to read a named policy or document, especially when global search returns mixed issues, merge requests, projects, or autocomplete suggestions.

skills.title: Use Current Element References
skills.principle: When a visible target cannot be clicked by its text, inspect the latest accessibility tree and activate the target using its current element reference or exact observed URL. After activation, verify that the URL or breadcrumb reflects the requested directory before continuing.
skills.when_to_apply: Use this for GitLab repository navigation when repeated text-based clicks fail with a missing-element error, especially after the page has re-rendered or accessibility-tree element references changed.

skills.title: Locate Articles by Repository Structure
skills.principle: In GitLab, use the repository’s semantic directories to narrow the search (for example, a posts directory), then select the file whose name matches the requested topic. Open it and verify the displayed title or content addresses the task. Once confirmed, report completion and stop instead of navigating to unrelated files.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to locate and display a specific article or document in a GitLab repository, especially when the repository tree exposes meaningful directories and descriptive filenames.

skills.title: Navigate GitLab Repository Files
skills.principle: In a GitLab repository, use the visible file tree and breadcrumb context to locate the target file: open the relevant directory, select the file link by its displayed name, and verify the resulting page shows the filename and code content before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view a specific file in a GitLab project and the repository tree is visible. Use directory listings and breadcrumbs to confirm location before opening the target file.

skills.title: Use Observed GitLab Repository Controls
skills.principle: After each navigation, inspect the current accessibility tree and act only on controls actually present there. For repository content, use the visible “Find file” control or an observed file/directory link, then verify the resulting path before continuing. If a label is absent, do not retry it; reassess the page and choose an available control or direct observed URL.
skills.when_to_apply: When browsing GitLab repositories and a desired article or file is not immediately visible, especially after a click fails because the requested label or bid is absent.

skills.title: Use File Links for GitLab Articles
skills.principle: When a GitLab repository list shows a matching commit message, do not open the commit metadata as the article. Locate the actual file path, such as the matching Markdown post, and activate its file link or use “Find file.” Verify navigation by checking that the resulting URL and page content represent the article rather than a commit diff.
skills.when_to_apply: When locating a specific article in a GitLab repository and the matching text appears in commit metadata, especially alongside a visible post filename or “Find file” control.

skills.title: Verify Navigation Before Searching
skills.principle: After activating a navigation menu, inspect the updated accessibility tree and select the actual destination link, not merely the menu container. Confirm the URL or page heading changed before searching. If the page did not navigate, correct the menu selection; use the editable searchbox element rather than its surrounding form.
skills.when_to_apply: When a menu click opens a submenu or leaves the current page unchanged, especially before attempting to search for a specific GitLab help article.

skills.title: Search Repository Before Browsing
skills.principle: Use GitLab’s repository search or “Find file” to locate topic-specific documents directly. If browsing folders, prioritize content directories such as `src/posts`, then match the exact filename or visible title. Open the matching document and verify its rendered content before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to read a specific guide in a large GitLab repository and the initial directory contains many unrelated files or folders.

skills.title: Terminate After Confirmed Completion
skills.principle: Once the requested file or page is open and its relevant content is visible, summarize the verified findings once and stop. Do not continue scrolling, resend duplicate messages, or perform exploratory actions after completion is established.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when a GitLab repository task’s target document is open and the accessibility tree shows the requested content, especially after a successful summary has already been sent.

skills.title: Use GitLab Search Suggestions
skills.principle:
1. Click the global “Search GitLab” field and enter a query.
2. Select the suggestion that searches the current project or choose the all-GitLab option.
3. Confirm the Search page loads and exposes content-type tabs such as Code, Issues, and Merge requests.
skills.when_to_apply: When starting from a GitLab project page and needing the Search page for projects, issues, merge requests, or other searchable content; the global search field must be visible.

skills.title: Locate and Read GitLab Articles
skills.principle:
1. Open the repository’s likely content directory, such as `posts`, when the requested article is stored as source files.
2. Select the file whose visible name semantically matches the requested topic, then open it.
3. Read the displayed content and scroll until the final section is visible.
4. Summarize the article’s main sections and report completion once the end is confirmed.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to read or summarize an article in a GitLab repository and the initial view shows a repository file tree. Use semantic filenames and verify the full file content before responding.

skills.title: Use Observed GitLab Element Bids
skills.principle: Use only element bids currently present in the accessibility tree; do not pass guessed repository paths or filenames to click. For a target file, click the observed directory link first, then inspect the refreshed tree for the file. If it is not visible, use GitLab’s “Find file” control and search by filename. Ensure the action syntax is valid before retrying.
skills.when_to_apply: When navigating a GitLab repository and the desired file or directory is not directly visible, especially after a click returns the same page or reports an unknown bid.

skills.title: Review GitLab Project Activity
skills.principle:
1. From a project page, open the “Project information” navigation entry.
