2. Select “Activity” and verify the page title or URL indicates the project activity feed.
3. Summarize visible recent events, such as merge-request changes, member joins, and timestamps, then report completion.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to check recent updates for a GitLab project and the project navigation exposes “Project information” or an “Activity” entry.

skills.title: Read Issue Counts From Status Tabs
skills.principle: Open the target project's Issues page and inspect the status tabs. Use the “All” tab count for the total; corroborate it with the “Open” and “Closed” counts when present. Report the counts only after confirming the page belongs to the requested project.
skills.when_to_apply: When retrieving a GitLab project's total issue count, especially when the project navigation badge may show only the open-issue count.

skills.title: Use Current Project Issue Counts
skills.principle: On GitLab’s project list, locate the target project by its visible name, then inspect that project card’s Issues link and displayed number directly. Treat the current accessibility tree as authoritative; use the current element reference or semantic label, not a stale hard-coded bid. If the count is visible, report it without unnecessary navigation.
skills.when_to_apply: When retrieving a project’s issue count from a GitLab project listing and the target card already exposes an Issues link with a numeric count.

skills.title: Read Project Issue Count
skills.principle: On GitLab project listings, locate the target project and inspect its project-statistics links. The numeric link whose destination represents the project's issues is the issue count; report that number directly once the project name and metric meaning match.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when a GitLab project list visibly includes the target project and its statistics, including a numeric Issues link or equivalent project issue navigation.

skills.title: Read Fork Count From Project Listing
skills.principle: Locate the target project row in GitLab’s Projects list, then read the number associated with its forks control or the link ending in `/-/forks`. Distinguish it from adjacent stars, merge requests, and issues counts before reporting the value.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when the GitLab project list is visible and the target project appears as a row with repository metrics, including a forks link or count.

skills.title: Read GitLab Project Summary Count
skills.principle: On GitLab’s Projects page, use the navigation entry labeled “Starred” and read its adjacent count. Treat that count as the user’s total starred projects, then report it without opening individual project records unless the count is absent or ambiguous.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked for the number of starred projects and the GitLab Projects navigation is visible, especially when the “Starred” entry includes a numeric badge.

skills.title: Report Visible Counts and Stop
skills.principle: When the requested count is already visible in the page’s relevant navigation label or summary, extract that number, provide it directly in the final response, and terminate. Do not repeat no-op actions after confirming the result.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab counting tasks when the relevant page is open and an accessibility-tree label such as a project category visibly includes the requested count.

skills.title: Read Project Description Directly
skills.principle: From GitLab’s project list, locate the target project by its displayed namespace and name, then open its project page. Read the visible description paragraph near the project heading or README preview and report its text. Treat paragraphs, headings, and static text as read-only; do not use form actions such as fill on them.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to view or report a GitLab project description and the project list or search results visibly identify the target. Confirm the opened page matches the requested project before extracting text.

skills.title: Stop After Confirming Project Description
skills.principle: Once the target GitLab project page displays its description, verify the text is visible, report completion, and terminate immediately. Do not repeat no-op actions after the goal is satisfied.
skills.when_to_apply: When viewing a GitLab project description and the project page visibly contains the description text, especially after navigating from a project list.

skills.title: Report the Open Merge Request Count
skills.principle: On the target GitLab project's Merge requests page, read the number beside the “Open” tab. Once that labeled count is visible and matches the requested project, report it to the user immediately and terminate the interaction.
skills.when_to_apply: When counting open merge requests in a GitLab project, after navigating to that project's Merge requests page and observing an “Open” tab with a numeric count.

skills.title: Read To-Do Count From Navigation
skills.principle: For a GitLab request asking only for the number of pending to-dos, inspect the navigation menu and read the numeric count displayed beside the “To-Do List” link. Report that count directly; opening the list is unnecessary unless details are requested.
skills.when_to_apply: Use on GitLab pages where the navigation menu is visible and the “To-Do List” entry includes a numeric badge. Verify the badge is present before reporting the count.

skills.title: Select Actual Group Filter Option
skills.principle: On GitLab’s To-Do List, open the “Group” filter and select the target from an actual matching option. Treat group names displayed within todo rows as metadata unless the accessibility tree identifies them as links. If the picker says “No matching results,” do not press Enter or click row text; clear the query, inspect available options, and verify the resulting todos belong only to the selected group.
skills.when_to_apply: When filtering GitLab todos by group, especially when visible group names appear in rows but the Group picker search returns no matches. Requires being on the To-Do List page.

skills.title: Select Group Picker Results Explicitly
skills.principle: In GitLab’s To-Do List, open the “Group” filter and treat “Search groups” as an autocomplete, not a free-text filter. Search the displayed group name, select a matching group option, then verify the list refreshes and every visible to-do belongs to that group. If no option appears, clear the search and inspect the available picker entries before concluding filtering failed; pressing Enter alone does not apply arbitrary text.
skills.when_to_apply: When filtering GitLab to-dos by group and the target group is visibly represented in list items, but the group search shows “No matching results.”

skills.title: Count Project-Specific To-Dos
skills.principle: Open GitLab’s “To-Do List” and inspect each listed item’s project label. Count only entries whose project matches the target project, then report the total and optionally identify matching titles or issue/merge-request references. Use the list’s displayed total only as a completeness check, not as the target-project count.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked how many GitLab to-dos belong to a particular project and the To-Do List page displays multiple entries with project names.

skills.title: Use Observed Navigation Targets Exactly
skills.principle: Activate the observed “To-Do List” link, or copy its exact URL from the accessibility tree. Before proceeding, verify that the resulting page is the GitLab to-do list; avoid reconstructing deployment URLs, since a small host mismatch can prevent navigation and leave the task incomplete.
skills.when_to_apply: When starting from a GitLab dashboard and needing to inspect to-dos, especially when the accessibility tree already exposes a labeled “To-Do List” link and its destination.

skills.title: Compare Exact To-Do Timestamps
skills.principle: Open GitLab’s To-Do List and inspect every visible item’s precise timestamp, not only relative labels such as “2 years ago.” Compare the dates and times chronologically; report the item with the earliest timestamp and include its displayed creation time.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked for the oldest to-do in GitLab and the list is visible. Ensure all relevant items are loaded and use exact timestamps when relative age labels are tied.

skills.title: Report the Oldest To-Do Directly
skills.principle: On GitLab’s To-Do List, compare the visible creation timestamps and select the earliest one. Report that item’s title and linked issue or merge request; do not click the list container merely to highlight it, since identification alone completes the task.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to identify the oldest pending GitLab to-do and the list displays each item’s timestamp, title, and related work-item link.

skills.title: Count Project Issues Assigned to You
skills.principle:
1. Open the target project’s Issues page using the project navigation, not the dashboard’s global issue link.
2. Inspect each visible issue for the assignee indicator matching the current user, such as “Assigned to [user].”
3. Count matching issues and report the total, optionally listing their titles or numbers for verification.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked how many issues in a specific GitLab project are assigned to the current user, after confirming the project’s Issues list is accessible and populated.

skills.title: Use Structured Assignee Filtering
skills.principle: On the project’s Issues page, use the filter control to select the assignee criterion and choose the current user, rather than entering a username as free-text search. Apply the filter, then read the resulting issue count or count the filtered issue rows. Verify that every displayed issue shows the current user as assignee and that the selected state (Open, Closed, or All) matches the request.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked how many GitLab issues in a project are assigned to the current user, especially when the ordinary search leaves the unfiltered issue list unchanged.

skills.title: Read Issue Counts From Dashboard Tabs
skills.principle: Navigate to the GitLab issues dashboard for the relevant user or scope. Read the numeric label attached to the requested status tab, such as “Closed,” rather than counting listed issues manually. Report that displayed count once the page shows the status tabs and their totals.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked for the number of issues in a status and the GitLab issues dashboard displays status links or tabs with counts. Ensure the dashboard scope matches the requested user or project.

skills.title: Stop After Confirming Issue Count
skills.principle: Navigate to the GitLab Issues dashboard, verify the page shows the relevant assignee filter and a visible “Closed” count, then report that count immediately. Do not repeat navigation or click stale element identifiers after the requested value is already observable.
skills.when_to_apply: When checking a GitLab issue total and the Issues dashboard visibly displays the requested state count, especially after navigation succeeds or repeated actions have produced errors.

skills.title: Use GitLab Issue State Tabs
skills.principle:
1. Open the GitLab dashboard’s Issues page from the main navigation.
2. Identify the state tabs, such as Open, Closed, and All, using their labels and counts.
3. Select the tab matching the requested issue state.
4. Confirm completion by checking the URL/state and visible issue rows show the selected status, then report completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view issues by status on GitLab and the dashboard navigation exposes an Issues entry with state tabs. Verify the selected tab’s state in the resulting page before finishing.

skills.title: Stop After Confirming Target State
skills.principle: Once the requested page state is visibly confirmed, report completion and terminate immediately. Do not issue repeated no-op actions or continue interacting with the page after the goal is achieved.
skills.when_to_apply: When a navigation task’s destination is visible and its defining label, filter, URL state, or result list confirms completion.

skills.title: Select GitLab’s All Issues Filter
skills.principle:
1. Open the GitLab Issues page and inspect the status filter options.
2. Select the option labeled “All” rather than “Open” or “Closed.”
3. Confirm the URL or page state indicates `state=all` and the list includes issues with differing statuses.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view every GitLab issue regardless of status, especially when the Issues page initially shows a status-specific view or other active filters.

skills.title: Select and Verify the All Issues Filter
skills.principle: On GitLab’s Issues dashboard, treat the presence of an “All” option as insufficient. Activate the “All” filter, then verify the resulting page state or URL includes the all-status selection before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view issues regardless of status and the dashboard shows separate Open, Closed, and All controls, especially when the current URL lacks an explicit all-status filter.

skills.title: Subscribe via GitLab Calendar Link
skills.principle:
1. Open the GitLab Dashboard Issues page.
2. Locate and activate the “Subscribe to calendar” link, preserving the displayed issue filters and due-date scope.
3. Confirm the destination is an ICS calendar feed, then provide its complete URL for subscription.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to subscribe to GitLab issues by due date, especially upcoming deadlines, and the Dashboard Issues page exposes a “Subscribe to calendar” link.

skills.title: Stop After Calendar Subscription
skills.principle: From GitLab’s Issues dashboard, locate and activate the “Subscribe to calendar” link. Confirm the resulting page contains an ICS calendar response such as “BEGIN:VCALENDAR”; then report completion and terminate instead of issuing repeated no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to subscribe to GitLab issues with upcoming due dates and the Issues dashboard exposes a “Subscribe to calendar” link. Verify the ICS response before stopping.

skills.title: Verify Dashboard Navigation Before Stopping
skills.principle: Check the current URL and page state first. If already at GitLab’s root Dashboard URL, report completion immediately. Otherwise activate the navigation link labeled “Dashboard,” then confirm the URL is the root and the page shows the Projects dashboard before reporting success and stopping.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to open the GitLab Dashboard and the current page may already be a dashboard subsection such as Starred Projects or Projects.

skills.title: Terminate After Confirming Target State
skills.principle: Verify the page title, URL, and distinctive content match the requested destination. If they already match, report completion and terminate immediately rather than issuing repeated no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for navigation tasks when the observed page already shows the requested destination and its URL or accessibility-tree content confirms the match.

skills.title: Use GitLab Merge Request Navigation
skills.principle:
1. From GitLab navigation, select the “Merge requests” entry.
2. When its menu expands, choose the assignment-specific option such as “Assigned to you.”
3. Confirm the dashboard heading is “Merge requests” and assigned requests are listed; use Open, Merged, Closed, or All tabs for status filtering.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view the signed-in user’s GitLab merge requests and the navigation menu exposes “Merge requests” with an assignment-specific submenu option.

skills.title: Stop After Confirming Target Page
skills.principle: Once navigation produces the requested page heading and URL, verify that observable state briefly, then report completion and stop. Do not open a specific item or perform extra management actions unless the task explicitly requests them.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for navigation-only tasks when the target page is visibly confirmed, such as GitLab showing the “Merge requests” heading and a dashboard merge-request URL.

skills.title: Verify Destination Before Stopping
skills.principle: Use the current accessibility tree to confirm whether the requested destination is already open. If not, activate the navigation entry matching its visible label. After navigation, verify the page title, URL, or distinctive content, then report completion and stop without redundant actions.
skills.when_to_apply: For navigation tasks, especially when the initial page may already match the requested destination. A loaded page title, URL, and relevant content should confirm completion.

skills.title: Stop After Reaching Explore
skills.principle: Once GitLab’s Explore page is open and public project listings are visible, verify the page heading or URL, report completion, and terminate. Do not continue scrolling or follow pagination unless the task explicitly requests inspecting additional projects.
skills.when_to_apply: When the task is to navigate to GitLab Explore and the observation shows the Explore page with project listings, filters, or the Explore navigation entry.

skills.title: Open GitLab Project Topics
skills.principle: From the GitLab Projects page, select the navigation link labeled “Topics.” Confirm the destination by checking for the Topics heading and its project-topic content. If the page reports “There are no topics to show,” communicate that the section is available but currently empty, rather than taking unrelated actions.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to browse GitLab projects by topic and the Projects dashboard is visible, especially when the navigation includes a “Topics” link.

skills.title: Stop After Reaching Target Page
skills.principle: After selecting the requested navigation entry, verify the URL and page heading match the destination. If the destination is loaded—even when it displays an empty-state message—consider navigation complete, report completion, and terminate instead of exploring unrelated sections.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for navigation tasks where the goal is to open a named GitLab page, especially when the destination visibly confirms itself through its URL, heading, or empty-state content.

skills.title: Navigate to a GitLab Repository
skills.principle:
1. Locate the target project in the current project list using its visible name or description.
2. Open the project link, then select Repository to display the file tree and README.
3. Inspect the source directory or contribution documentation when the user asks about code or contributing.
4. Confirm the repository page visibly shows the code structure and relevant guidance, then report completion.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when starting on a GitLab dashboard or project list and asked to view a repository’s code or contribution instructions. Confirm the target project is visible before opening it.

skills.title: Use Exact Links After Action Errors
skills.principle: When a GitLab click fails with an empty-action or missing-element error, stop repeating the same text-based click. Use the exact accessible element reference from the current accessibility tree, or navigate directly to the element’s observed href. Verify the URL and page heading changed before continuing.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when a repository or file is visibly listed in the accessibility tree but BrowserGym cannot resolve a text-based click, especially after an action error or repeated unchanged page state.

skills.title: Locate and Verify a GitLab Repository
skills.principle:
1. Inspect the visible project list and identify the repository by its owner/name or descriptive text.
2. Activate the repository link, then verify the destination using the page title, breadcrumb, and repository contents.
3. Once the target repository is confirmed, report completion and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to navigate to a specific GitLab repository and the project may already appear in a dashboard, starred-project list, or search results.

skills.title: Stop After Reaching Target Repository
skills.principle: Once the target GitLab repository page is visible, confirm its project name and repository content, then report completion and stop. Do not open README sections or external resource links unless the user explicitly asks for a specific document or resource.
skills.when_to_apply: When the request is to navigate to a named GitLab repository and the repository page is already displayed, with its project title and repository navigation or files visible.

skills.title: Read GitLab Project Description
skills.principle: On a GitLab project’s main page, identify the project heading and inspect nearby paragraphs for the description. Prefer the concise descriptive text associated with the project overview, then report it exactly and stop once confirmed.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to retrieve a GitLab project description and the project’s main page is open or can be reached. Verify the text belongs to the target project rather than README content or repository files.

skills.title: Recover From Empty Action Errors
skills.principle: When a user-facing action returns “Received an empty action,” inspect and correct the action serialization or invocation format before retrying. Submit the repaired action once, verify execution succeeded, then stop; do not repeat an unchanged payload.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when the requested information is already visible and a send-message or other terminal action fails with an empty-action or equivalent execution error.

skills.title: Read GitLab Repository File Table
skills.principle:
1. Open the target project, then select the project-navigation “Repository” entry if the file tree is not already visible.
2. Read the repository tree table’s “Name” column, distinguishing files from directories by their links and displayed entries.
3. Report the observed names only after confirming the table is present; do not open “Add to tree” or other editing controls.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to list files in a GitLab repository and the project page or Repository view is accessible. Use the existing file table directly if it is already displayed.

skills.title: Extract Visible Repository Listing
skills.principle: When the GitLab repository tree is already visible, read the table's “Name” column directly and report every listed file or directory. Do not issue a no-op browser action; convert the observed accessibility-tree content into the final response immediately.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for repository file-listing tasks when the GitLab tree page and its files table are present in the current accessibility tree.

skills.title: Verify Existing Project Star
skills.principle: Open the target GitLab project’s starrers view from its project-list star control. Check whether the current user appears with an “It’s you” indicator; if present, treat the goal as complete and avoid toggling the star. Otherwise, return to the project and activate its star control.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to star a GitLab project and the project list exposes a star count or starrers link, especially when the current starred state is unclear.

skills.title: Stop After Confirming Project Starred
skills.principle: On a GitLab project page, inspect the star control before acting. If it says “Unstar,” the project is already starred: report completion and stop. If it says “Star,” click it once, then verify it changes to “Unstar” before terminating. Never toggle an already-correct state.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to star a GitLab project and the project page is open, especially when the star control may already show either “Star” or “Unstar”.

skills.title: Read Repository Commit Count
skills.principle: On a GitLab project overview, inspect the repository statistics navigation and read the number attached to the “Commits” link. Use that displayed count directly when it clearly answers the request; no navigation into commit history is needed unless the statistic is absent or ambiguous.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked for a repository’s total commit count and the GitLab project overview is already open, look for a visible “Commits” statistic in the project navigation.

skills.title: Use GitLab’s Direct Commit Count
skills.principle: On a GitLab project overview, locate the repository summary link labeled “N Commits” and use its displayed number as the total. Do not enter the commit history or sum date-grouped entries unless the overview lacks a count; report the number once observed.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked for a repository’s total commits and the project overview visibly includes a “N Commits” summary link or statistic.

skills.title: Open Repository Images Directly
skills.principle: On a GitLab repository page, identify the requested image from the file listing or an embedded README image. Open the image link, then verify the resulting page displays only the image or shows its image filename and dimensions. Once displayed, report completion and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to view a repository logo, screenshot, or other image and the GitLab page exposes either an image file or an embedded image linking to its raw asset.

skills.title: Stop After Verifying Visual Content
skills.principle: Once the target file page visibly contains the requested image, treat the task as complete. Report that it is displayed and terminate instead of issuing repeated no-op actions or waiting for another state change.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when a GitLab repository file page shows the requested image in an image element and the task only asks to view it; no download or modification is required.

skills.title: Verify Project Open Issues
skills.principle:
1. From the target GitLab project, open the project-level “Issues” navigation entry, not the global dashboard Issues link.
2. Confirm the open-issues count from the project navigation or the Issues page’s empty-state/list content.
3. Report the observed count to the user and terminate once verified.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to check open issues for a specific GitLab project and the project page exposes an “Issues” navigation entry or count.

skills.title: Use Project Issue Count
skills.principle: Open the target GitLab project and inspect its project navigation. Read the number shown beside “Issues”; treat that count as the current open-issue total, then report whether any open issues exist. If the count is zero, no further navigation is needed.
skills.when_to_apply: When checking open issues for a GitLab project and the project page is accessible. Confirm the project identity before relying on the “Issues” navigation count.

skills.title: Use README Installation Instructions
skills.principle: On a repository page, inspect the README’s Installation section before exploring unrelated files. Extract the documented browser menu path, required extension file, and installation gesture, then report those steps and identify any repository download link if available.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked how to install software hosted in a GitLab repository and the repository page visibly renders a README or documentation containing an Installation section.

skills.title: Use Accessibility Bids, Not Visible Text
skills.principle: When BrowserGym exposes numeric accessibility bids, target the element’s current bid rather than its visible label. For informational tasks, report the README’s installation instructions directly once the relevant section is observed; only activate a download link if downloading is explicitly required.
skills.when_to_apply: Apply on GitLab repository pages when a visible filename or link repeatedly causes “Could not find element” errors, or when the task asks for instructions rather than performing the installation.

skills.title: Use README Browser Sections
skills.principle:
1. Open the target GitLab project and inspect its README.md, preferably the rendered file.
2. Scan headings and linked text for browser-specific sections such as Safari, Firefox, or Opera.
3. Report each explicitly named alternative version and its linked repository, confirming the README provides the evidence.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked whether a repository or extension supports platforms beyond its primary one, provided the project README is accessible.

skills.title: Use Visible README Evidence Directly
skills.principle: When a repository README visibly lists browser-specific versions and links, extract those browser names and URLs directly from the accessibility tree and answer the question. Do not wait or navigate unnecessarily; if opening a source is required, activate the link associated with the relevant browser heading, not the heading itself.
skills.when_to_apply: Use on GitLab repository pages when the task asks whether software supports alternatives to a default platform and the README already contains installation or version sections.

skills.title: Open and Verify Repository Code
skills.principle:
1. Navigate to the repository’s relevant directory using its visible directory entry or breadcrumb.
2. Inspect the file listing and open the code or configuration file matching the user’s request.
3. Confirm the destination by checking the breadcrumb and visible file contents, then report completion and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab tasks asking to view code in a repository directory, when the directory is visible in the file table or navigation breadcrumbs.

skills.title: Download a GitLab Repository File
skills.principle:
1. Locate the requested file in the repository file listing and open its file page.
2. On the file page, choose the “Download” link or the size-labeled download link for the raw file.
3. After the download link is activated, report completion and stop; the page may remain unchanged while the browser downloads the file.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for downloading a specific artifact from a GitLab repository when the target file is visible in the repository listing and its file page provides a Download link.

skills.title: Verify GitLab File Downloads
skills.principle: Open the target repository file, then use its explicit “Download” link (prefer the non-inline download option). Confirm the browser shows a completed download or downloadable file state; if nothing changes, inspect download status or use the raw download URL instead of repeatedly clicking the same link.
skills.when_to_apply: When downloading a binary or extension file from a GitLab repository, especially after the file page exposes both “Download” and “Download (size)” links but no visible page navigation confirms success.

skills.title: Read File Update Metadata
skills.principle:
1. Open the repository’s relevant directory, using the file table to locate the requested file.
2. Read that file’s “Last commit” and “Last update” cells, including the exact timestamp and commit message.
3. Report the metadata and stop once the requested update is confirmed.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab tasks asking when a repository file was last updated, provided the repository tree exposes file metadata in its directory table.

skills.title: Verify and Select Exact File Result
skills.principle: After using GitLab’s “Find by path,” inspect the filtered result list and click the exact target path, especially when it is nested in a directory. Verify the opened file’s breadcrumb and filename before reading its commit timestamp or history; do not assume pressing Enter selected the intended result.
skills.when_to_apply: When locating a repository file by name in GitLab, particularly when similarly named files exist or Enter may activate an unintended result. Confirm the destination page matches the requested path before extracting update information.

skills.title: Identify the Correct Repository First
skills.principle: Before opening repository files, locate the project that actually contains the requested filename. Use GitLab project filtering or global search rather than choosing an arbitrary repository. In the confirmed project, open Repository > Find file, enter the exact path or filename, and select a matching result. If results show another file or no exact match, return to project search instead of opening it.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view a specific file in GitLab and the current project is unknown. Requires access to project listings or GitLab search; verify the repository and exact filename before inspecting code.

skills.title: Navigate GitLab Repository Files
skills.principle:
1. Inspect the repository file table and identify the directory likely containing the requested file.
2. Open that directory, then select the file by its visible filename.
3. Confirm the breadcrumb and code view show the requested file and configuration.
4. Report the result and stop once the target file is visibly open.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab task asks you to view a specific repository file and the initial project page shows a browsable file table, especially when the file may be nested in a source directory.

skills.title: Use Find File for Repository Navigation
skills.principle: When a requested filename is not visible at the repository root, use GitLab’s “Find file” control instead of creating files, browsing unrelated projects, or repeatedly scrolling. Search for the exact filename, then open the matching result and verify the file-view page or path.
skills.when_to_apply: When viewing a GitLab repository and the target file is absent from the current directory listing, especially when nested directories or branches may contain it.

skills.title: Commit Web IDE Changes
skills.principle: After editing a GitLab file in the Web IDE, verify the intended code is present and syntactically coherent, then select “Create commit...”, provide a meaningful commit message, commit to the intended branch, and confirm the changed-file or commit state before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when a repository-edit task has produced a changed file in GitLab’s Web IDE. The task is incomplete while “Create commit...” remains unused or the repository does not show the saved change.

skills.title: Edit and Commit Through GitLab Web IDE
skills.principle:
1. Open the target file with “Open in Web IDE,” then interact with the editor textbox itself rather than its tabpanel.
2. Focus the editor, use keyboard editing commands or select-all and type the intended complete content.
3. Verify the editor reflects the change and that “Create commit...” becomes enabled with changed files listed.
4. Commit the change and confirm the resulting commit or repository file state.
skills.when_to_apply: When modifying a repository file in GitLab and the standard file view offers “Open in Web IDE.” The editor may expose content through an accessible textbox while surrounding panels are non-clickable.

skills.title: Download a GitLab Directory ZIP
skills.principle:
1. Open the target directory in the repository tree before downloading; the repository-level Download button archives the entire repository.
2. Click Download and, in the expanded menu, activate the visible “zip” link—not the menu container.
3. Confirm the menu closes or the ZIP download begins before stopping.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to download a specific GitLab directory as ZIP and the repository tree is visible. Navigate into that directory first, then use its Download menu and the labeled “zip” link.

skills.title: Navigate Project Merge Requests
skills.principle:
1. Open the target project from the project list.
2. In the project navigation, select “Merge requests,” not the global dashboard link.
3. Check the resulting page for listed requests or an explicit empty-state message, then report the observed status.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to inspect pending code changes for a specific GitLab project and the project is reachable from the projects list or dashboard.

skills.title: Recover From Invalid GitLab Clicks
skills.principle: After a browser action returns an empty-action or missing-element error, stop repeating it. Re-read the fresh accessibility tree, use the current element reference exactly (for example, the bid alone, without appended label text), and verify the control’s scope. For project-specific merge requests, open the target project first, then select its project-level “Merge requests” navigation entry and confirm the page changed.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab navigation click fails, the page remains unchanged, or the requested section belongs to a specific project rather than the global dashboard.

skills.title: Verify CI/CD Page State
skills.principle: Open the project’s CI/CD navigation entry and confirm the destination is the Pipelines page. Report the observable pipeline state, including an explicit empty-state message such as “There are currently no pipelines,” rather than assuming pipelines exist.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view a GitLab project’s build pipelines or automation and the project navigation exposes a CI/CD entry. After navigation, inspect the page heading or pipeline list for its actual state.

skills.title: Verify CI/CD Navigation Then Stop
skills.principle: Click the project’s “CI/CD” navigation entry, then verify the resulting page shows the pipelines view (for example, a “Pipelines” heading or pipeline tabs). Once this state is visible, report completion and terminate instead of clicking the already-selected “Pipelines” link or issuing repeated no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to open a GitLab project’s CI/CD or pipelines area and the accessibility tree shows the CI/CD navigation entry or confirms the pipelines page is already open.

skills.title: Verify Repository Folder Before Acting
skills.principle: Inspect the current repository URL and file listing first. If the target folder is already open, use its breadcrumb or path and visible contents to confirm completion, report the relevant files, and stop. Otherwise, select the folder link by its displayed name, then verify the destination page and contents.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab repository browsing tasks when asked to open a directory or view source files, especially when the initial page may already display the requested folder.

skills.title: Use Current Repository Navigation Targets
skills.principle: On GitLab, open the target project, expand the visible “Repository” navigation entry, then activate the currently observed “Commits” link. Use the exact accessible label or current element reference with valid action syntax, and verify the URL or page heading shows the project’s commit history before stopping.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view a GitLab project’s commits and the project list or issue page is visible. Reinspect the accessibility tree after each navigation because element references and visibility can change.

skills.title: Use Project Branch Navigation
skills.principle: From a GitLab project page, locate the repository summary or Repository navigation and activate the link labeled with the branch count or “Branches.” Confirm the destination by checking the page title and visible branch tabs or listings, then stop once the branches page is displayed.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view a GitLab project’s branches and the project page exposes a branch-count link or Repository submenu. The destination should show branch listings or Overview, Active, Stale, and All tabs.

skills.title: Verify Branch Tab Before Clicking
skills.principle: On GitLab’s project Branches page, inspect the accessible label and destination for each tab before acting. Select the tab labeled “All” and verify the resulting page or URL indicates all branches; do not rely on stale element IDs or assumed tab ordering.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view every repository branch and the Branches page offers separate Overview, Active, Stale, and All tabs. Confirm the selected tab’s label and resulting page state before stopping.

skills.title: Stop After Reaching Target File
skills.principle: After opening the requested repository file, verify the page identifies the target filename and displays its contents. Once confirmed, report completion and terminate immediately; do not repeatedly toggle rendered/source views or issue no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when a GitLab repository file page is already open and the breadcrumb, filename, and visible content confirm the requested file was reached.

skills.title: Select a File Before Editing
skills.principle: In GitLab Web IDE, treat the repository tree as the entry point to editing: select the target file or expand its directory, then wait for the editor pane to appear. The top-level “Edit” button only indicates the current mode; repeated clicks or waiting without selecting a file will not open an editor.
skills.when_to_apply: When the GitLab Web IDE shows the repository file tree, “0 changed files,” and the message instructing you to select a file before editing.

skills.title: Enumerate Visible Explore Projects
skills.principle: Read the current GitLab Explore page’s project list from the accessibility tree. For each project list item, extract the displayed owner and project name from its heading or project link, preserve page order, and report only items currently visible without following pagination.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to list projects visible on a GitLab Explore page and the current accessibility tree exposes project list items, headings, or project links. Do not use the Next control unless the task requests additional pages.

skills.title: Use Current Pagination Controls
skills.principle: After reaching the end of a GitLab project list, use the currently observed link labeled “Next” rather than reusing an old element identifier. Verify the URL and project-list heading after navigation; if the click leads elsewhere or the task only concerns the current page, return the captured projects and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When enumerating GitLab Explore projects and pagination is present. First determine whether the request concerns the current visible page or all pages; before each navigation, refresh the accessibility tree and confirm the control’s current role and destination.

skills.title: Verify Project Details in GitLab
skills.principle: When a GitLab project listing already shows the requested description and star count, use those values as leads, then open the project page and verify the description paragraph and star-count link before reporting both fields.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab tasks asking for metadata about a specific project, when the project is identifiable in Explore or search results and its listing exposes partial details.

skills.title: Use Accessibility Bids for Inputs
skills.principle: When an element is visible in the accessibility tree, target its numeric accessibility bid rather than treating its label as a bid. For example, fill the searchbox using the observed bid, then verify the value or filtered results. If the action fails, re-read the current tree and choose the refreshed bid instead of repeatedly scrolling blindly.
skills.when_to_apply: Use on GitLab pages when a labeled input appears in the accessibility tree but BrowserGym reports that the label cannot be found as a bid.

skills.title: Read Project Update Timestamp
skills.principle: On GitLab's project listing, locate the target project by its full owner/name, then read the adjacent “Updated” time element. Report the exact timestamp shown, optionally including the relative age displayed alongside it.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when the requested GitLab project appears in an accessible project list and its row visibly contains an “Updated” label with a timestamp.

skills.title: Search and Verify Project Updates
skills.principle: Use the visible “Filter by name” field or global “Search GitLab” to search the requested project name and namespace. Open the matching project result, then read the project’s “Updated” timestamp and report it. Do not stop after announcing an intended search; perform the search and verify the result page.
skills.when_to_apply: When GitLab Explore shows a project list but the target project is not immediately visible, and the task asks for its latest update time.

skills.title: Verify GitLab Project Star Count
skills.principle:
1. Locate the target project in GitLab Explore and open its project page.
2. Read the numeric link beside the star control, then open it if exact verification is needed.
3. Confirm the starrers page states the total, including public and private counts, and report that total.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked for a GitLab project's star count and the project is discoverable through Explore or search. Use the starrers page when the project-page number needs confirmation.

skills.title: Read Project Stars From GitLab
skills.principle:
1. Locate the exact target project in the GitLab project list and open its project page.
2. On the project overview, identify the star control and read the adjacent numeric link, which represents the total stars.
3. Report that number and stop once the project identity and count are confirmed.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab tasks asking for a project's star count when the target is identifiable in a project list or search result and its overview page is accessible.

skills.title: Verify Project Before Counting Issues
skills.principle: Search GitLab for the exact project name and submit the search. If the results explicitly show no matching projects, report that the project was not found or is inaccessible; do not infer an issue count from the absence of a project.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked for open issues on a GitLab project and the project is not immediately visible, use the global search first and inspect the Projects result before attempting issue navigation.

skills.title: Follow Search Results Semantically
skills.principle: Use the observed role and accessible name, not stale or guessed element IDs. In GitLab, enter the project name in the actual project-search field, select the matching search-result menu item, verify the project heading and URL changed, then activate that project's visible “Issues” navigation link. Re-read the accessibility tree after every navigation; never reuse IDs from another page or construct an unverified project URL.
skills.when_to_apply: When locating a GitLab project and counting its issues from a dashboard or search page, especially after search suggestions appear or the page changes.

skills.title: Choose Explore’s Most Stars Filter
skills.principle: On GitLab Explore, distinguish the dashboard’s “Starred” link from Explore’s project ranking. Open “Explore,” then select “Most stars.” Confirm the URL or page state shows the Explore projects starred view and projects ordered by stars before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to reach starred or most-starred projects specifically within GitLab Explore, especially when both dashboard “Starred” and Explore navigation links are visible.

skills.title: Stop After Confirming Navigation
skills.principle: After activating a navigation link, inspect the resulting page state. If the URL and heading/content confirm the requested destination, report completion and terminate. Do not repeat clicks or reuse accessibility IDs from the previous page, since IDs may become stale or refer to different elements.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab navigation tasks when a click changes the URL or page heading to the requested section, especially when subsequent observations already show the target page.

skills.title: Select GitLab Trending Projects
skills.principle: On GitLab's Projects Explore page, locate the navigation links labeled “All,” “Most stars,” and “Trending.” Select “Trending,” then verify the URL or refreshed project list reflects the trending view before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to view trending GitLab projects and the Projects Explore page shows the “Trending” navigation option. Stop after the refreshed page clearly displays the trending project list.

skills.title: Terminate After Confirming Goal
skills.principle: Once the page URL and accessibility tree confirm the requested section is open, report completion and terminate immediately. Do not repeat noop actions or wait for additional page changes after the goal is visibly achieved.
skills.when_to_apply: Use after navigating to a requested GitLab section when the resulting URL and visible navigation state clearly match the target.

skills.title: Verify Project Before Opening Issues
skills.principle: Use the current accessibility tree to locate GitLab’s project search or name filter, search for the target project, and open the exact observed project link. Then select its Issues page and read the open-issue count. Do not reuse stale element bids or guess a namespace/slug URL; if search returns no project, report that explicitly.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked for issue counts on a GitLab project and the project is not already visible. Requires a live page observation; refresh references after each navigation or failed action.

skills.title: Filter GitLab Projects by Name
skills.principle:
1. On GitLab’s project Explore page, use the “Filter by name” searchbox instead of scrolling through project pages.
2. Select the matching project result, then open its project-level “Merge requests” navigation entry.
3. Confirm the destination page and report the visible open-merge-request count or empty-state message.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to inspect merge requests for a named GitLab project and the starting page is a project listing. Requires access to Explore, project search, and project navigation.

skills.title: Verify Project Context Before Reporting
skills.principle: After searching GitLab for a project, activate the matching search result, then verify the page context shows that project. Open its project-level “Merge requests” navigation entry, and report completion only after the URL, heading, or list clearly identifies the target project. Do not infer success from a stale control or unchanged dashboard.
skills.when_to_apply: When locating a GitLab project through global search, especially after navigation or dynamic results change accessibility-tree element references. Confirm the project-specific merge-request page before ending the task.

skills.title: Verify Destination Before Navigating
skills.principle: Inspect the current URL and page heading before clicking navigation. If they already identify the requested destination, report completion immediately and avoid redundant clicks. Otherwise, activate the navigation entry matching the destination, then confirm the resulting URL or heading before finishing.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to open a GitLab dashboard page or other navigation destination, especially after an attempted click times out but the refreshed accessibility tree already shows the requested page.

skills.title: Emit Valid Browser Actions
skills.principle: When a visible GitLab navigation link is identified, send a syntactically valid browser action directly, such as clicking the link by its current accessibility reference or navigating to its observed destination. Do not wrap the action in another JSON object, truncate quotes, or repeatedly resend the same malformed payload. Confirm navigation by checking that the URL or page heading changes.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when the accessibility tree shows the target navigation entry but execution returns an empty-action or parsing error; correct the action serialization before retrying.

skills.title: Verify Starred State After Clicking
skills.principle: Open the target project from the project list, then activate its Star control. Confirm completion by checking that the control changes from “Star” to “Unstar” (and, if already “Unstar,” report success without clicking).
skills.when_to_apply: When starring a GitLab project and its project page is available, especially when the current state may already be starred.

skills.title: Filter GitLab Projects by Name
skills.principle: On GitLab’s Projects Explore page, enter the requested text in the “Filter by name” searchbox. Confirm the field retains the value, the URL includes the corresponding name filter, and the results list updates to matching projects before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to filter GitLab Explore projects by name and the “Filter by name” searchbox is available. Use the updated results and URL parameter as completion evidence.

skills.title: Emit Complete Valid Browser Actions
skills.principle: Construct the full BrowserGym action with correctly closed arguments and quotes before submitting it. For a GitLab project filter, target the observed “Filter by name” searchbox, enter the requested name, then verify the project list updates. If the tool reports an empty action, fix the serialized action format instead of repeatedly retrying the same malformed payload.
skills.when_to_apply: When an accessibility tree exposes the target searchbox but submitted actions produce empty-action or parsing errors, especially during GitLab project filtering.

skills.title: Use GitLab’s Sort Menu
skills.principle: On the GitLab Projects page, open the current sort control (for example, “Name”), choose “Most stars,” and verify the control now displays “Most stars” and the URL includes the stars-descending sort state. Once confirmed, report completion and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to order GitLab projects by popularity and the Projects page shows a sort control with options including “Most stars.”

skills.title: Activate and Verify Sort Control
skills.principle: When a page appears pre-sorted, perform the explicit sorting action anyway: click the visible “Most stars” control or corresponding navigation entry, then verify the resulting page state shows the selected sort and descending star counts. Only after this confirmation should you report completion and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: Use on GitLab project listings when the requested sort label is visible but the current URL, navigation state, or refreshed result state does not conclusively show that the requested action was executed.

skills.title: Rank Projects by Open Issues
skills.principle: On GitLab’s Explore Projects page, inspect each project card’s issue-count link, pairing the displayed count with its project name. Collect all visible entries, sort counts in descending order, and report the requested top projects. If a Next control exists and a global ranking is required, continue through subsequent pages before ranking.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to compare or identify GitLab projects with the most open issues, provided project cards expose issue-count links and pagination may contain additional projects.

skills.title: Compare Issue Counts Across Projects
skills.principle: On GitLab’s project listing, read each project card’s issue-count link, distinguishing it from stars, forks, and merge requests. Collect the visible counts, include zero-count projects when relevant, then sort projects numerically from highest to lowest before reporting the comparison.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to compare open issues across GitLab projects and the project listing exposes issue counts directly. Check additional pages if the requested comparison spans projects not visible on the current page.

skills.title: Clone a GitLab Repository via HTTP
skills.principle:
1. Search GitLab for the target repository and open the matching project result.
2. Open the repository’s “Clone” control and inspect the SSH and HTTP clone URLs.
3. If SSH access requires an unavailable key, copy the HTTP URL, then run `git clone <copied_url>` in a local terminal.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to clone a GitLab repository and the project page is accessible. Prefer HTTP when the page indicates SSH push or pull requires adding an SSH key.

skills.title: Verify Repository Before Cloning
skills.principle: After searching, activate the result labeled with the exact target repository, then verify the page heading, owner/path, and URL before acting. Only open the repository’s “Clone” control after confirmation, copy its HTTPS URL, and run `git clone <URL>` in an available terminal. If navigation lands on another project, return to search and retry rather than using stale element IDs.
skills.when_to_apply: When cloning a GitLab repository from search results, especially after dynamic suggestions or navigation, and a terminal or command execution environment is available.

skills.title: Update GitLab Profile Information
skills.principle:
1. Open the signed-in user menu and select “Edit profile.”
2. Modify the requested profile field, such as “Job title,” while preserving unrelated values.
3. Click “Update profile settings” to submit the form.
4. Confirm completion by checking for the “Profile was successfully updated” status message.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab task requires changing user profile details and the account is already signed in; use the user menu’s “Edit profile” entry and verify the save confirmation.

skills.title: Use GitLab’s Authenticated User Menu
skills.principle: On GitLab, access profile editing through the authenticated user/avatar menu or observed profile link in the header, rather than guessing a settings URL. If redirected to sign-in, complete authentication first; then open the profile and choose its edit/settings control, confirming the profile form appears before changing fields.
skills.when_to_apply: When updating user profile information from a GitLab dashboard, especially when direct navigation to a guessed settings path returns 404 or the page shows sign-in controls.

skills.title: Verify Available Project Filters
skills.principle: Inspect the GitLab Projects page for controls matching the requested criterion. Distinguish name search, sorting, and ownership tabs from visibility filtering; if no visibility control is present, accurately report that limitation instead of claiming the filter was applied.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to filter GitLab projects by visibility and the current Projects page shows only name search, sorting, or ownership tabs, with no visibility-specific control.

skills.title: Operate GitLab Visibility Listboxes Correctly
skills.principle: On GitLab Explore, click the “Visibility” button, then activate the desired option by its visible role/name (for example, “Private”), not with select_option on the listbox container. Confirm completion when the button label changes from “Any” to the chosen visibility and the project results refresh; stop once this state is visible.
skills.when_to_apply: When filtering GitLab Explore projects by visibility and the accessibility tree exposes a button plus a custom listbox with options such as Any, Private, Internal, and Public.

skills.title: Locate and Open a GitLab Project
skills.principle:
1. In GitLab Explore, use the project name and description to identify the matching list entry.
2. Open the project link, then select README when an overview is needed.
3. Confirm completion when the project page or README displays the requested project and its description.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to view a specific GitLab project from an Explore or project-list page, especially when the project can be recognized by its name, owner, or description.

skills.title: Stop After Project Page Loads
skills.principle: Once the target GitLab project page is displayed, verify its heading or project identity matches the request, then report completion and terminate. Do not navigate into Repository, README, or other sections unless the task explicitly requests those details.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view or open a specific GitLab project and the resulting page visibly shows the requested project name or heading.

skills.title: Verify Data Availability Before Reporting
skills.principle: When the current GitLab page lacks the requested information, inspect relevant navigation such as “Topics” or project-specific sections. If no accessible control or result exposes the data, clearly report that it is unavailable on the current page rather than inventing results.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab requests to list tags, topics, or other metadata when the current Explore or project page shows no matching fields, filters, or results.

skills.title: Use GitLab Topics for Project Tags
skills.principle: From the GitLab Projects dashboard, select the visible “Topics” navigation entry to open the project-tags listing. Review the resulting topic page rather than scrolling project cards or opening an arbitrary repository; confirm the page heading and topic list are displayed.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to see all project tags/topics and the GitLab Projects dashboard shows a “Topics” link, use that global navigation entry first.

skills.title: Check Personal and Explore Snippets
skills.principle:
1. Open GitLab’s main navigation menu and select “Snippets.”
2. Inspect “Your snippets” for personal entries.
3. Select “Explore snippets” to check publicly available entries.
4. If both views are empty or show “No snippets found,” report that no snippets are available and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to browse GitLab snippets and the snippets entry is not visible in the current page. Requires access to GitLab’s main navigation and both personal and explore snippet views.

skills.title: Stop When Snippets Are Empty
skills.principle: Navigate to the project’s “Snippets” page and inspect its content. If the page shows the “Code snippets” empty state with only “New snippet” and “Documentation,” report that no existing project snippets are available and terminate. Do not create a snippet or substitute repository files for snippets.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to browse existing GitLab project snippets and the project navigation exposes “Snippets”; especially when the resulting page visibly indicates an empty collection.

skills.title: Read README From Project Overview
skills.principle:
1. Select the target project from the GitLab project list using its visible name or description.
2. On the project repository page, verify the README is listed and inspect the rendered README article, which may already appear below the file table.
3. Summarize the README’s main topics and report completion once its rendered content has been observed.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to read a GitLab project README and the project is discoverable through Explore or another project list. Prefer the rendered README on the repository overview before opening the file separately.

skills.title: Terminate After Reading README
skills.principle: Once the GitLab README page visibly displays its rendered contents, read the relevant text, report completion, and terminate. Do not issue repeated no-op actions after the target file and content are already confirmed.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab repository’s README link has opened successfully and the accessibility tree shows the README filename plus rendered headings or paragraphs.

skills.title: Open the Target GitLab Project
skills.principle:
1. Locate the target project in the GitLab project list using its visible owner and repository name.
2. Activate the project-name link, rather than an issue, merge request, or statistics link.
3. Confirm the project page loads by checking its heading, repository navigation, and project details.
4. Once confirmed, report completion and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view a GitLab project from an Explore or project-list page, especially when multiple similarly named links or related statistics appear.

skills.title: Stop After Project Details Load
skills.principle: When the target GitLab project page appears, verify its heading and breadcrumbs identify the requested project. The project overview already satisfies a “view details” request; report completion and terminate instead of opening README or issuing repeated no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when navigating from GitLab’s project list to a requested project, once the page title, project heading, or breadcrumbs visibly confirm the target project is open.

skills.title: Verify Destination Before Acting
skills.principle: Inspect the current page title, URL, and visible content before navigating. If they already confirm the requested destination, report completion immediately and stop. Otherwise, select the visible navigation control whose label and destination match the goal, then verify the resulting page state.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for navigation tasks when the initial page may already be the requested destination or when a navigation control is visible. Confirm completion from the resulting page title, URL, and relevant content.

skills.title: Use Direct Links for Navigation
skills.principle: When the accessibility tree exposes the target page as a direct link, activate that link or navigate to its observed href instead of repeatedly interacting with parent menus or guessed text labels. After navigation, verify the page title, URL, or main heading matches the requested destination, then stop.
skills.when_to_apply: Use this on GitLab when a target such as “New project” is already exposed as a link, especially after menu clicks fail, produce empty actions, or report missing element bids.

skills.title: Use GitLab’s Most Stars View
skills.principle: On GitLab’s Explore Projects page, select the navigation link labeled “Most stars” rather than relying on the current name sort. Confirm completion when the URL indicates the starred-projects view and the project list displays star counts in descending order, then report completion and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view GitLab projects with the most stars and the Explore Projects page is showing another view, such as “All” or alphabetical name sorting.

skills.title: Report Once Timestamp Is Visible
skills.principle: When the filtered project result clearly shows the target project and its “Updated” timestamp, read that timestamp, provide it as the answer, and terminate. Do not repeat no-op actions or navigate elsewhere after the required evidence is visible.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab project-update queries when filtering by name yields a matching project card with an observable “Updated” time.

skills.title: Use GitLab’s Starred Projects Link
skills.principle: From the GitLab dashboard, locate the Projects navigation tabs and select the link labeled “Starred” with its project count. Confirm the resulting page is the starred-projects view by checking the URL or selected tab and verifying starred projects are listed, then report completion and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view a user’s starred GitLab projects and the dashboard is available. If starting on an error page, return to the GitLab Home or Dashboard first, then use the visible “Starred” projects link.

skills.title: Terminate After Page Confirmation
skills.principle: After navigation, verify the destination using the URL and a distinctive page control or heading. Once the requested page is confirmed, report completion and terminate instead of issuing repeated no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for navigation tasks when the accessibility tree shows the requested destination, such as GitLab’s starred-projects URL and its “Starred” navigation entry.

skills.title: Verify Sort State Before Acting
skills.principle: On a GitLab projects page, inspect the sort control’s current label and expanded menu before changing anything. If it already shows the requested criterion, report completion and stop. Otherwise open the control and select the matching menu option, then verify the label or resulting URL reflects that sort.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to reorder GitLab projects and the page exposes a sort button or menu; first confirm the current sort state to avoid toggling or undoing an already-correct setting.

skills.title: Terminate After Confirming Sort
skills.principle: Select the project-list sort control, choose “Most stars,” and verify the control shows “Most stars” or the page reflects descending-star sorting. Once confirmed, report completion and terminate instead of issuing repeated no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: On GitLab’s Projects page when changing the list order. After selecting the requested sort and observing its selected label or refreshed sorted list, stop immediately.

skills.title: Star From the Project Header
skills.principle:
1. Locate the target project in the project list and open its project page, rather than selecting the star-count link, which opens the starrers list.
2. On the project page, activate the clearly labeled “Star” button near the project header.
3. Confirm completion when the button changes to “Unstar” and the star count updates, then stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When starring a GitLab project from an Explore or project list page, especially when the visible star count links to the starrers list and the actionable Star control is on the project page.

skills.title: Verify License In Project Details
skills.principle:
1. Search GitLab Explore projects using a distinctive license term, then inspect candidate results rather than trusting search matches.
2. Open a candidate project and check its repository file list for a LICENSE entry labeled with the requested license.
3. Cross-check the README for a corresponding license badge or link, then report the project only after confirmation.
skills.when_to_apply: When finding GitLab projects by license and Explore search returns candidates without explicit license metadata. Requires access to project details and repository files or README content.

skills.title: Inspect Project License Badges
skills.principle: On GitLab Explore → Projects, identify matching projects by reading each project card’s visible license label, such as “MIT License.” Do not use global search for the license phrase, because it searches project content and may return zero projects despite matching license badges. Check additional pages with Prev/Next when needed.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to find GitLab projects using a specific license and the Explore Projects listing displays license metadata on project cards.

skills.title: Use Dashboard Then Yours Filter
skills.principle:
1. From GitLab Explore or another page, activate the top navigation link labeled “Dashboard.”
2. On the dashboard Projects view, select “Yours” to show the current user’s projects.
3. Confirm completion when the dashboard Projects page displays the user-specific project list and the Yours filter is selected.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to open GitLab’s dashboard and view the current user’s own projects, especially from an Explore page. Requires an authenticated GitLab session with dashboard navigation visible.

skills.title: Stop After Dashboard Confirmation
skills.principle: Once the GitLab dashboard visibly shows the user’s personal projects, treat the task as complete. Report completion and terminate immediately instead of issuing repeated no-op actions or waiting for further changes.
skills.when_to_apply: When navigating to GitLab’s dashboard and the Personal project view is visible, confirmed by the dashboard state and displayed user-owned project listings.

skills.title: Paginate Through All GitLab Stargazers
skills.principle: Search for the target project, open its stargazer count link, then inspect each page and use the currently observed “Next” control. Continue until “Next” is disabled or absent; verify the total stargazer count and current page contents before reporting completion. Re-locate controls after every navigation instead of reusing stale element identifiers.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab project’s stargazers are listed across multiple paginated pages and the task requires viewing every stargazer.

skills.title: Stop at the Last Pagination Page
skills.principle: Track the current page and pagination controls after each navigation. Continue through each numbered page, but stop when the final page is reached or the Next control points to the current page or a fragment-only URL. Verify the last page’s entries, then report completion instead of clicking Next again.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when a GitLab list such as project stargazers spans multiple paginated pages and the final page exposes a disabled or self-referential Next link.

skills.title: Verify Recency Across All Pages
skills.principle: When a list has no date filter, inspect each item’s visible “Updated” timestamp, compare it with the requested cutoff, and record qualifying items. Follow pagination links such as “Next” until all pages are checked; only then report that no matches exist, including the scope and newest observed update.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab project searches requiring all items within a relative date range when the current list is name-sorted or paginated and lacks a direct recency filter.

skills.title: Sort by Update Date Before Paginating
skills.principle:
1. Open the project sort control currently labeled “Name” and choose the update-time option, preferably newest first.
2. Record every visible project whose “Updated” timestamp falls within the requested range.
3. Follow the observed pagination link, such as “Next,” only after confirming it exists in the current accessibility tree; re-inspect after navigation.
4. Stop when pagination ends, then report the complete collected list instead of repeating no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab Explore project tasks requiring all projects within a relative update period, especially when results span multiple pages and the list is initially sorted by name.

skills.title: Open GitLab To-Do List
skills.principle:
1. Locate the navigation link labeled "To-Do List," using its visible pending-item count as confirmation.
2. Activate the link and verify the page heading is "To-Do List" and the displayed pending list matches the navigation count.
3. Once the list is visible, report completion and stop without changing any items.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view GitLab to-do items from the navigation menu and the menu exposes a visible "To-Do List" link, preferably with a pending-count indicator.

skills.title: Terminate After Goal Confirmation
skills.principle: Once the page visibly matches the requested state, treat the task as complete. Report completion and terminate immediately instead of repeating noop actions or waiting for additional observations.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when a GitLab page visibly shows the requested content, such as the To-Do List heading and its item list, and no further modification or navigation is requested.

skills.title: Verify Submission After Timeout
skills.principle: After submitting a GitLab issue, inspect the resulting page before retrying if the click reports a timeout. Confirm the target issue title, open status, and displayed issue number; navigation may have completed despite the error. Report success and stop once these indicators appear.
skills.when_to_apply: When creating a GitLab issue and the final “Create issue” click times out or otherwise reports an uncertain result, especially when the page may have navigated.

skills.title: Verify Project Before Navigating
skills.principle: Use GitLab’s project search or the dashboard’s “Filter by name” field to locate the target project and confirm its exact namespace. Open the verified project link, then select its “Issues” navigation entry. If a guessed URL returns “Page Not Found,” stop guessing paths and search again before declaring the task infeasible.
skills.when_to_apply: When creating an issue for a project not visible in the current list, especially when the project namespace or URL is uncertain and direct navigation returns a 404.

skills.title: Verify Destination Before Reporting
skills.principle: Use a semantically matching navigation entry such as “New project” or “Create new...” to reach the requested page. After navigation, verify the page heading, title, or URL matches the goal; then report completion and stop without extra actions.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab task requests opening a specific page and the current accessibility tree offers labeled links that plausibly lead there. Confirm the destination using visible page semantics before responding.

skills.title: Use GitLab’s Create New Menu
skills.principle:
1. Open the GitLab “Create new...” navigation control.
2. Select “New project/repository” from the expanded menu.
3. Confirm navigation succeeded when the page heading reads “Create new project” and project options such as blank, template, and import are visible; then stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to navigate to GitLab’s project creation page from another GitLab page, especially when the “Create new...” control is visible in the main navigation.

skills.title: Open and Verify Starred Projects
skills.principle: Select GitLab’s “Starred” projects navigation entry rather than browsing Explore results. After navigation, verify the page URL or heading indicates starred projects, then read the displayed project list and report the visible count and names. Stop once the list is confirmed.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to browse or identify a user’s starred GitLab projects and the Projects navigation contains a “Starred” link with an optional count.

skills.title: Stop After Starred List Loads
skills.principle: For a GitLab task to browse starred projects, click the “Starred” navigation entry and verify the resulting page shows the starred-project list. Once the list is visible, report completion and stop; do not open a project, repository, or issue unless explicitly requested.
skills.when_to_apply: Apply when the task only asks to browse starred projects and the GitLab page visibly shows the starred-project section and its project entries.

skills.title: Select the Matching GitLab Project
skills.principle:
1. In GitLab’s project explorer, locate the list entry whose visible owner and project name match the requested repository.
2. Activate that project’s name link, not a related statistics or metadata link.
3. Confirm navigation succeeded by checking the page heading, repository content, and URL path identify the requested project, then report completion.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to navigate to a GitLab repository from an explorer or project list, especially when multiple similarly named projects or pagination may be present.

skills.title: Stop After Repository Confirmation
skills.principle: After selecting the target project, verify that the page heading, breadcrumb, or URL shows its repository files (for example, a “Files” view). Once confirmed, report completion and terminate. Do not repeat clicks using stale accessibility IDs after navigation; reacquire current elements only if the target state is not confirmed.
skills.when_to_apply: When navigating to a GitLab project repository, especially after clicking a project result or “Repository” entry and the resulting page visibly shows repository files or a repository breadcrumb.

skills.title: Access a GitLab Project Wiki
skills.principle:
1. Locate the target project in the project list and open its project page.
2. In the project navigation, select the link labeled “Wiki.”
3. Confirm the wiki page loaded by checking its title, URL, or breadcrumb; report any visible empty-state or permission message.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to access a GitLab project’s wiki and the project is discoverable through Explore, search, or another project list.
