skills.title: Stop After Reaching the Wiki
skills.principle: In GitLab, locate the target project, open its project navigation, and select “Wiki.” Once the page URL or heading confirms the requested wiki is open, report completion and terminate. If the wiki is empty, that still satisfies an access request; do not open an issue, consult Help, or perform unrelated actions.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to access or open a GitLab project wiki. Completion is confirmed by the Wiki page heading, breadcrumb, or URL, regardless of whether wiki pages exist.

skills.title: Open GitLab Web IDE via Fork
skills.principle:
1. Open the target project and select the “Web IDE” link.
2. If “Fork project?” appears, choose “Fork project” when direct editing is unavailable.
3. While “Forking in progress” is shown, wait and refresh only as needed.
4. Confirm completion when the IDE page appears with the repository file tree, then stop.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when opening a GitLab project’s Web IDE, especially when the project is not directly editable and GitLab requires creating a fork first.

skills.title: Stop After Web IDE Opens
skills.principle: From the target GitLab repository, open the repository's Web IDE link (for example, “Edit fork in Web IDE”). Confirm the IDE page shows the project name, branch, and file tree. Once these are visible, the task is complete; report completion and stop instead of clicking Edit, focusing files, or taking unrelated actions.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to open a GitLab project in the Web IDE and the repository page exposes a Web IDE action. Apply after the IDE title, project context, branch, and file list are visibly loaded.

skills.title: Stop Once Target Directory Opens
skills.principle: When the repository page shows the requested directory in its breadcrumb and the files/directories table lists its contents, treat exploration as complete. Report completion and terminate instead of opening individual packages or files, unless the task explicitly requests deeper inspection.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab repository-navigation tasks asking to explore or open a directory, once the page path and contents table visibly confirm the requested directory.

skills.title: Stop After Confirming the Description
skills.principle: Once the project page or README visibly contains the requested description, send one concise summary to the user and terminate. Do not repeat messages, issue empty actions, or use no-op actions after completion; these add failure risk without advancing the task.
skills.when_to_apply: When viewing a GitLab project page or README and the requested description is already visible in the accessibility tree, especially after a successful navigation or file-opening action.

skills.title: Read Project Metadata Directly
skills.principle: On GitLab’s project listing, locate the target project by its displayed namespace and name, then read the adjacent “Updated” timestamp from that same project card. Report the timestamp exactly as shown, without opening the project unless the listing lacks the required metadata.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when a GitLab Explore or project-list page visibly contains the target project and each project card includes an “Updated” label with a timestamp.

skills.title: Read Project Update From Explore List
skills.principle: Locate the target project in GitLab's Explore projects list and read the timestamp shown beside its "Updated" label. Use the project name and surrounding row to ensure the timestamp belongs to the correct project, then report the displayed date, time, and timezone.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab Explore projects page is available and the target project appears in the visible list with an "Updated" timestamp.

skills.title: Cycle Visibility Filters Reliably
skills.principle: On GitLab’s Projects Explore page, use the button beside “Visibility:” to open the listbox and select each required option: Public, Internal, and Private. After every selection, verify the button label and refreshed project list or URL reflect the chosen visibility before reopening the dropdown. Use current labels from the latest accessibility tree rather than stale element IDs.
skills.when_to_apply: When filtering GitLab project listings by visibility, especially when demonstrating multiple levels. The Projects Explore page must expose the “Visibility:” dropdown and options such as Public, Internal, and Private.

skills.title: Use Explore Visibility Dropdown
skills.principle:
1. Open GitLab’s Explore projects page, where the “Visibility:” control offers Any, Private, Internal, and Public.
2. Click the visibility button to open its listbox, then click the desired option itself, such as “Private”; do not use select_option on the button.
3. Confirm the button label changes and the project results refresh.
skills.when_to_apply: When filtering GitLab projects by visibility and the dashboard lacks public/internal/private filters. Use Explore projects and interact with the custom listbox by clicking its visible option.

skills.title: Use GitLab’s Dashboard Link
skills.principle: From any GitLab page, locate the global navigation link labeled “Dashboard” and activate it. Confirm completion when the page title or URL indicates “Dashboard” and the main content shows the user’s project list, then report success and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to open the personal GitLab dashboard and the current page exposes the global “Dashboard” navigation link. Verify the destination page before claiming completion.

skills.title: Stop After Dashboard Navigation
skills.principle: Click the GitLab “Dashboard” link, then verify the resulting page using observable state such as the “Projects · Dashboard · GitLab” title, dashboard URL, or personal project controls. Once confirmed, report completion and terminate instead of issuing repeated no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: When navigating from a GitLab Explore page to the personal dashboard and the resulting accessibility tree shows the dashboard title, root dashboard URL, or dashboard project tabs.

skills.title: Open Project Issues From Explore
skills.principle:
1. Locate the target project in GitLab’s Explore Projects list using its visible name.
2. Activate that project’s issues-count link or the project’s Issues navigation entry.
3. If issue rows show loading placeholders, wait until titles and labels appear.
4. Confirm the Issues page and selected status tab before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view tracked issues for a GitLab project and the project is discoverable through Explore Projects or the project list.

skills.title: Stop After Issues Page Loads
skills.principle: Once the project’s Issues page is open and issue entries are visible, the viewing task is complete. Confirm the page identity and visible issue list, report completion, and terminate rather than repeatedly scrolling through every issue or changing the item-count control.
skills.when_to_apply: For GitLab tasks asking to view a project’s tracked issues, after selecting the target project’s project-navigation “Issues” link and observing the issues list.

skills.title: Use Observed Bids for GitLab Links
skills.principle: When navigating GitLab from an accessibility tree, activate the observed link element using its current accessibility bid or role/name, not its href URL. After an element-not-found error, re inspect the latest tree, identify the exact namespace and project link, then click that element and verify the page changes before continuing.
skills.when_to_apply: Use this when GitLab lists duplicate project names or BrowserGym reports that a URL-based click cannot find an element. The current accessibility tree must contain the target project link.

skills.title: Use GitLab Explore Projects Listing
skills.principle: Open GitLab’s Explore → Projects page and verify that the project listing is displayed. Confirm the relevant visibility and sorting state, then stop once the listing is visible; use Prev/Next pagination only when the task explicitly requires inspecting additional pages.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view public projects in GitLab and the Explore Projects page is available, with the project list and its visibility controls or pagination visibly rendered.

skills.title: Traverse Every Project Results Page
skills.principle: Start from the GitLab Explore projects list, select the public visibility filter if needed, then inspect each page and activate “Next.” Continue until “Next” is absent or disabled, confirming the final page before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view all public GitLab projects and results are paginated. Ensure the visibility filter is public, and do not finish while a usable “Next” control remains.

skills.title: Use GitLab Topics for Topic Searches
skills.principle: When asked to find projects by topic, use GitLab’s “Topics” navigation or a project’s topic link rather than the global “Search GitLab” box. Select or enter the requested topic, then verify the resulting project list and topic association before reporting results. Do not invent a topic when the request omits one; clarify the required topic.
skills.when_to_apply: Apply to GitLab tasks requesting projects with specific topics, especially when the topic value is missing or the dashboard offers both global search and “Topics” navigation.

skills.title: Navigate Topics to Personal Dashboard
skills.principle: From GitLab’s Topics page, activate the header link labeled “Dashboard.” Confirm completion when the page title indicates “Projects · Dashboard · GitLab,” the URL is the dashboard root, and the user’s projects are displayed.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when the task requires navigating from GitLab Explore → Topics to the signed-in user’s personal dashboard and the Topics page is currently visible.

skills.title: Verify Dashboard State Before Continuing
skills.principle: After selecting GitLab’s “Dashboard” navigation link, inspect the new accessibility tree and URL. If the page title indicates “Dashboard,” the URL is the dashboard route, and dashboard content such as project tabs is visible, treat the task as complete, report success, and stop. Do not repeat clicks based on stale assumptions.
skills.when_to_apply: When navigating from GitLab Explore or Topics to the personal dashboard, especially after a click produces a refreshed accessibility tree or root dashboard URL.

skills.title: Move Back Exactly One Page
skills.principle: For a request to go to the previous page, activate Prev once and verify the page indicator or destination changed to its immediate predecessor, then stop. Report that no previous page exists only when Prev was unavailable in the starting state.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to move back one page in a paginated project listing, with the current page and pagination controls visible.

skills.title: Stop After Verified Page Navigation
skills.principle: After clicking the current “Prev” link, inspect the refreshed page and verify the URL or visible listing changed to the immediately preceding page. Once that transition is confirmed, report completion and terminate. Do not continue clicking, reuse stale accessibility IDs, or navigate further unless the task explicitly requests multiple pages.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to move one page backward in a paginated GitLab listing and the current page exposes a “Prev” link. After navigation, a changed page indicator or URL confirms completion.

skills.title: Choose the Correct Explore Entry
skills.principle: On GitLab’s Projects navigation, select the link labeled “Explore,” not the adjacent “Topics” entry. Verify the destination heading or URL shows the general project-exploration page before searching for a star-count sorting control. If the page shows topic listings, return to Projects navigation and choose the correct entry.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view or rank GitLab projects by stars and the Projects navigation contains both “Explore” and “Topics” links. Verify the resulting page before continuing.

skills.title: Disambiguate Duplicate GitLab Projects
skills.principle: When multiple projects share the requested name, compare their namespace or owner and select the repository matching the intended organization or canonical source. Open its project link, then verify the destination by checking the page heading, breadcrumb, and repository URL before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: Use on GitLab Explore or search pages where duplicate project names appear under different owners or namespaces, especially when the task implies an official, canonical, or organization-specific repository.

skills.title: Terminate After Goal Confirmation
skills.principle: Once the target GitLab project page is visibly open and matches the requested owner and repository, treat navigation as complete. Report completion and terminate immediately rather than issuing repeated no-op actions or waiting for additional observations.
skills.when_to_apply: Use after a navigation task when the page title, URL, breadcrumb, or project heading visibly confirms the requested GitLab project.

skills.title: Use Accessibility Links After Click Errors
skills.principle: When a text-based click fails, inspect the current accessibility tree for the matching link’s actual bid, then click that bid. Confirm navigation by checking the resulting URL, breadcrumb, or page heading before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when navigating GitLab repository file trees or similar lists, especially after a selector or text-based click returns an element-not-found error.

skills.title: Navigate to a Project’s Releases
skills.principle:
1. Identify the intended repository by matching its project name and authoritative owner when duplicate projects appear.
2. Open the repository and locate the project navigation entry labeled “Releases” or showing a release count.
3. Select it, then verify the page title, URL ending in “/-/releases”, and visible release entries before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view releases for a GitLab project, especially when search results contain duplicate project names. The target repository must be identifiable before using its project navigation.

skills.title: Stop Once Releases Are Visible
skills.principle: After opening the target GitLab project, select its “Releases” link and verify the releases page shows release entries. Once this observable state is reached, report completion immediately and terminate; do not keep scrolling or gather unnecessary additional releases unless the task explicitly requests specific versions or details.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab tasks asking to view a project’s releases when the Releases page is accessible and at least one release entry is visible.

skills.title: Reach an Organization via Breadcrumbs
skills.principle:
1. From a GitLab project list, open a project whose listing shows the target organization as its namespace.
2. On the project page, click the organization link in the "Breadcrumbs" navigation, not the project name.
3. Confirm completion when the page title and main heading show the target organization and its profile sections or projects are visible; then stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to open a GitLab organization profile and the organization is discoverable through a project listing or the current project's breadcrumb navigation.

skills.title: Stop After Confirming Destination
skills.principle: Verify completion using the page title, URL, and main heading. Once they identify the requested organization page, send one concise completion message and terminate immediately; do not repeat messages, issue no-op actions, or continue interacting.
skills.when_to_apply: When navigating GitLab from a project or listing to an organization page, after the destination page visibly matches the requested organization and the URL reflects its profile route.

skills.title: Access Web IDE Through a Fork
skills.principle:
1. Open the target GitLab repository and select the "Web IDE" link.
2. If GitLab shows "Fork project?", choose "Fork project" when direct editing is unavailable.
3. Wait for "Forking in progress" to finish, then verify the page title is "IDE · GitLab" and project files appear in the sidebar.
4. Report completion once the IDE and file tree are visible; do not edit files unless requested.
skills.when_to_apply: When viewing a GitLab repository’s Web IDE and the account lacks direct write access, causing GitLab to require a fork before opening the editable IDE.

skills.title: Verify Deployment Before Monitoring
skills.principle:
1. Open the correct target project, then select the project navigation’s “Monitor” entry.
2. Check the Metrics page for dashboards or an explicit empty-state message.
3. If it says “No deployed environments,” report that monitoring data is unavailable and deployment is required before dashboards can appear.
skills.when_to_apply: When checking GitLab monitoring for a project, especially when multiple similarly named repositories exist. Confirm the intended project first and use the Metrics page’s observable deployment status.

skills.title: Navigate to GitLab New Project
skills.principle: From a GitLab projects listing, activate the visible “New project” link (or equivalent “Create new...” navigation entry). Confirm completion when the page title or main heading indicates “New Project” or “Create new project,” and the creation options are visible; then report completion and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when the task asks to open GitLab’s project-creation page and the current observation shows a projects listing with a “New project” or “Create new...” link.

skills.title: Terminate After Goal Confirmation
skills.principle: Once the target page is visibly confirmed—such as by its title, URL, or breadcrumb—treat the task as complete. Report completion and terminate immediately instead of issuing repeated no-op actions, which can prolong the trajectory and cause failure.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for navigation tasks when the current accessibility tree clearly shows the requested destination and no additional interaction is required.

skills.title: Use GitLab’s Starred Projects View
skills.principle:
1. From GitLab Projects, select the “Starred” navigation entry rather than scanning the general project list.
2. Confirm the destination is the starred-projects view and use its displayed count as a completeness check.
3. Read each project’s namespace and name from the result list, then report all entries and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to list a user’s starred GitLab projects and the Projects navigation exposes a “Starred” entry with a count.

skills.title: Verify Starred Projects Page
skills.principle: Use the visible “Starred” navigation link by its accessible label, ensuring the click action is syntactically valid. After activation, verify the page changes to the starred-projects view and enumerate the projects actually shown. Report completion only after this state is confirmed.
skills.when_to_apply: When listing a user’s starred GitLab projects and the current Projects page shows a “Starred” navigation entry, especially after an attempted click produces an action error or no visible page change.

skills.title: Sort GitLab Projects by Recent Updates
skills.principle:
1. On GitLab’s Projects Explore page, open the current sort control, such as “Name.”
2. Select “Updated date” from the “Sort by” menu.
3. Verify the control now shows “Updated date” and the list’s first projects have the newest visible “Updated” timestamps.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to find or view recently updated GitLab projects and the Projects Explore list is available. Ensure the resulting sort is descending by confirming newer update times appear first.

skills.title: Use the Actual Project Sort Control
skills.principle: On GitLab’s Projects page, distinguish scope tabs such as “Personal” from the sorting control. Open the sort menu, choose “Updated” descending/latest, and verify the visible project cards’ “Updated” timestamps decrease from top to bottom. Do not treat a URL parameter alone as sufficient if it also changes the project scope.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to sort GitLab projects by latest update and the page contains both project-scope tabs and a separate sort button or menu.

skills.title: Verify Project Update Dates Across Pages
skills.principle:
1. Inspect each project card’s “Updated” metadata, preferring the exact timestamp over approximate relative text.
2. Paginate with the visible “Next” control while project results remain, recording projects that satisfy the requested recency window.
3. Report matches, or report none only after checking all relevant pages and confirming every visible project falls outside the window.
skills.when_to_apply: When searching GitLab Explore projects by update recency, especially when results are name-sorted and no date filter is available. Ensure the project list and pagination controls are accessible.

skills.title: Stop When Scrolling Produces No Change
skills.principle: Track the visible project names and update dates after each scroll. If the accessibility tree remains unchanged, treat the list as exhausted or scrolling ineffective; stop repeating the action, compile projects whose displayed dates satisfy the requested window, and report the results.
skills.when_to_apply: When searching GitLab project lists by update date and repeated scrolling returns the same projects, dates, or page state. Ensure the project cards expose update timestamps before evaluating the date range.

skills.title: Use Semantic Tabs, Then Verify URL
skills.principle: On GitLab’s Projects Explore page, locate the navigation links labeled “All,” “Most stars,” and “Trending” by their current accessible names. Select “Most stars,” then verify navigation succeeded by checking the URL contains the starred-projects route and the project list is displayed. If already on that route, report completion without clicking again.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to open GitLab’s Most stars projects view and the Projects Explore navigation tabs are visible, or when the current URL already indicates the starred-projects route.

skills.title: Verify Destination Before Repeating Actions
skills.principle: After activating a navigation link, inspect the resulting URL and page content before acting again. If the URL matches the requested view and its expected label or content is present, treat the task as complete and stop. Do not repeat clicks merely because the same navigation link remains visible.
skills.when_to_apply: Use after navigating GitLab Explore views or similar pages, especially when the resulting URL already identifies the requested destination, such as a projects view filtered by stars.

skills.title: Verify Destination Page Before Acting
skills.principle: Inspect the current accessibility tree and URL before navigating. If the requested page is already open, confirm it using the page heading, URL, and visible content, then report completion without redundant navigation. Otherwise, activate the navigation entry matching the requested page and verify the resulting heading and content.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for navigation tasks when the initial page may already match the requested destination. Verify the page heading, URL path, and meaningful content before deciding whether navigation is necessary.

skills.title: Stop After Confirming Target Page
skills.principle:
1. From GitLab Projects, select “Explore,” then choose the “Trending” tab.
2. Verify the page URL or visible “Trending” selection confirms completion.
3. Report completion and terminate immediately; do not repeat no-op actions after the target page is reached.
skills.when_to_apply: When a navigation task’s target page is visibly loaded and the URL or selected navigation entry confirms it, especially for GitLab Explore pages.

skills.title: Verify Navigation Before Reporting
skills.principle: When a target navigation link is visible, do not assume it is active merely because it appears in the current menu. Activate the link, then verify the resulting URL and page heading/content match the requested destination before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab navigation tasks when the target entry is listed on the current page but the address bar and visible content still show a different page.

skills.title: Use Direct Navigation After Click Failures
skills.principle: If a visible navigation link repeatedly produces an empty-action error, stop retrying the same click. Use the link’s observed destination URL with direct navigation, then verify the page title, URL, and main heading match the requested destination before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When navigating GitLab from a dashboard, the target link is visible with a destination URL, but click attempts repeatedly return empty-action errors or leave the page unchanged.

skills.title: Use the All Merge Requests View
skills.principle:
1. Navigate to GitLab’s Merge requests dashboard without assignee or reviewer filters.
2. Select the “All” state tab, which should update the view to include every project and merge-request state.
3. Confirm the page URL or visible state reflects broad scope and `state=all`, then report the resulting page status.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view all GitLab merge requests from a general dashboard, especially when the navigation link defaults to an assignee-specific filter.

skills.title: Verify Navigation Before Confirming
skills.principle: After selecting a navigation entry, inspect the updated page state rather than assuming navigation succeeded. Confirm the URL, page heading, and relevant merge-request content changed; if the menu only expands, select the appropriate submenu or retry. Report completion only after the destination visibly shows the requested view.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when a GitLab navigation click may expand a menu without changing pages, especially when viewing merge requests from the Explore or project list.

skills.title: Use the Profile Menu Link
skills.principle: On GitLab, select the signed-in username in the top navigation to open its menu, then choose the username link (showing the handle) rather than settings options. Confirm navigation by checking that the page heading shows the user’s name and profile sections such as Overview, Activity, or Personal projects.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view the current user’s GitLab profile from another page and the top navigation shows a signed-in username or avatar.

skills.title: Use Direct Navigation After Click Errors
skills.principle: When a visible profile link repeatedly produces empty-action or bid errors, use its observed destination URL with direct navigation instead of retrying the same click. Verify the page title, URL, and profile heading show the target user, then stop; do not issue repeated no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: When viewing a GitLab user profile and the account-menu or username link is visible but clicking it fails, provided the accessibility tree exposes the link’s destination URL.

skills.title: Stop After Confirming Navigation
skills.principle: After clicking the target project link, inspect the next accessibility tree and URL. If the project page heading and destination path are present, report completion and terminate; do not repeat the click using a stale element identifier.
skills.when_to_apply: When navigating from a GitLab project list and the resulting page visibly shows the requested project name, project navigation sidebar, or matching project URL.

skills.title: Open Repository From Project List
skills.principle:
1. Locate the target repository in GitLab’s project list using its displayed name.
2. Open the repository link, then verify the repository root shows the files-and-directories table.
3. Report completion only after confirming the directory structure and file entries are visible.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to view a GitLab repository’s files and the repository must first be selected from an Explore or project-list page.

skills.title: Use Direct Navigation After Lookup Failures
skills.principle: When a visible project link repeatedly fails element lookup, use its observed destination URL with direct navigation instead of retrying guessed text or CSS selectors. Confirm the URL and page heading change to the target repository, then stop once the repository file listing is visible.
skills.when_to_apply: Use on GitLab Explore pages when the target project is visibly listed with a usable href but click actions return empty-action or element-not-found errors.

skills.title: Use Current Accessibility Bids
skills.principle: After locating a repository directory in GitLab, use its current numeric accessibility bid or the observed directory link URL, not the visible text as a bid. If an action fails, refresh the accessibility tree and select the matching link again; scrolling alone will not create a missing element. Confirm navigation by checking the breadcrumb or URL for the target directory.
skills.when_to_apply: When navigating GitLab repository file listings, especially after an action reports that a text-based element bid cannot be found.

skills.title: Complete GitLab ZIP Downloads Efficiently
skills.principle:
1. Open the repository’s “Download” menu and wait for its expanded state.
2. Select the visible “zip” archive link, whose URL indicates a ZIP download.
3. Treat the click as completion even if the repository page remains unchanged; downloads commonly occur without navigation.
4. Stop after the single ZIP-link click instead of repeatedly toggling the menu.
skills.when_to_apply: When downloading a GitLab repository archive and the “Download” control exposes archive-format links such as “zip”; prerequisite: the target repository page is open.

skills.title: Complete Archive Download Without Repeating
skills.principle: On a GitLab repository page, open the “Download” menu only when collapsed, then select the visible “zip” link once. A download may leave the repository page unchanged and close the menu; treat that post-click state as completion rather than reopening the menu or repeating the download.
skills.when_to_apply: When downloading a repository archive from GitLab and the ZIP link was visible and clicked, especially when the page remains on the repository after the click and no explicit download confirmation appears.

skills.title: Verify License Through Repository File
skills.principle: Open the target GitLab project, locate the repository’s LICENSE entry or displayed license label, and inspect it when needed. Confirm the license from explicit page text such as “This project is licensed under the …” or the file’s heading, then report the result and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked for a GitLab project’s license and the project is discoverable from the dashboard, search, or project list. Prefer explicit license metadata or the repository LICENSE file over inference.

skills.title: Target Search Inputs by Role
skills.principle: Use the accessibility tree’s current role and label to identify the project filter (for example, the visible searchbox named “Filter by name”), not nearby or stale element IDs. Fill that input, verify the results update, then open the matching project and inspect its license. If no match appears, use GitLab’s actual global search control rather than guessing a URL.
skills.when_to_apply: When locating a GitLab project from a dashboard or Explore page, especially after navigation changes or when element IDs refer to links such as “Topics” instead of the visible search field.

skills.title: Verify Navigation Before Acting Again
skills.principle: After selecting a project link or using direct navigation, inspect the updated URL, page title, and project heading. If they identify the requested GitLab project, treat navigation as complete and stop. Only retry when the observed state still shows the source page or an error.
skills.when_to_apply: When navigating from a GitLab project list to a target project, especially after a click or goto appears successful. Confirm the destination state before issuing additional clicks, scrolling, or navigation commands.

skills.title: Search GitLab Before Declaring Missing
skills.principle: Use GitLab’s “Search GitLab” or “Filter by name” control with the project name, then verify the owner or namespace in the results and open the matching project link. Do not infer absence from the initially visible dashboard list or limited scrolling; report not found only after the search returns no matching project.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to navigate to a GitLab project that is not visible in the current dashboard list, especially when the project may belong to another namespace or user.

skills.title: Select the Matching GitLab Project
skills.principle: On a GitLab project listing, scan visible entries for the requested namespace and repository name. Click the project link whose accessible label matches both. Confirm completion when the destination shows the project title, repository navigation, and file listing; then report completion and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to open a specific GitLab project from an explore or project-listing page, especially when the target may already be visible among multiple similarly named repositories.

skills.title: Use the Project Link, Not Its List Item
skills.principle: On GitLab’s project list, select the link whose accessible name matches the target project, rather than the surrounding list item or another nearby bid. After clicking, verify navigation by checking that the URL and page heading identify the target project; if unchanged, re-inspect the current accessibility tree and choose the correct link.
skills.when_to_apply: When opening a specific GitLab project from a projects list, especially when accessibility-tree bids identify both a project link and its containing list item.

skills.title: Recover From Completed Navigation
skills.principle: After a project-link click reports a timeout, inspect the refreshed accessibility tree and current URL before retrying. If the target project page loaded, use its project navigation and select the role-labeled “Issues” link. Confirm completion by checking the URL contains the project’s issues path and the page shows issue tabs or an issue list.
skills.when_to_apply: When navigating within GitLab from a project listing and a click times out while waiting for navigation; the browser may already have reached the project page.

skills.title: Use Valid Actions and Verify Navigation
skills.principle: On GitLab, select the target project from the project list, then select its project-level “Issues” navigation entry. Use a syntactically complete browser action with the currently observed element reference. After each click, verify the URL, page title, or visible navigation state changed; if an action errors or the page remains unchanged, retry using the refreshed accessibility tree rather than repeating malformed or stale actions.
skills.when_to_apply: When navigating from GitLab project exploration to a repository subsection such as Issues, especially after an action error or when accessibility-tree element references may have changed.

skills.title: Replace Auto-Populated Project Slugs
skills.principle: When a project name auto-populates the slug, inspect the slug before editing. Select all existing text or clear the field, then enter the intended URL-friendly slug exactly once. Verify the displayed slug is not duplicated before selecting “Create project.”
skills.when_to_apply: Use on GitLab project-creation forms where entering a project name may automatically populate the required “Project slug” field before manual editing.

skills.title: Recover From GitLab Name Conflicts
skills.principle: When GitLab reports that the project name or namespace is already taken, choose a genuinely unique project name, explicitly replace the project slug with a matching unique slug, verify both field values, then click “Create project” again. Confirm creation by checking that the page leaves the form and shows the new project.
skills.when_to_apply: Use during GitLab project creation whenever submission returns “Name has already been taken” or “Project namespace name has already been taken,” especially after editing fields that may append instead of replace.

skills.title: Use Most Stars to Filter Projects
skills.principle:
1. On GitLab Explore Projects, select the “Most stars” navigation entry when no direct star-count filter is available.
2. Verify the resulting project cards show star counts above the requested threshold.
3. Report completion only after the visible results satisfy the threshold; stop without further navigation.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab project-list tasks requiring a minimum star count, especially when the page offers “Most stars” but no explicit numeric star filter.

skills.title: Use Explore for Star Thresholds
skills.principle: On GitLab, distinguish sorting from name filtering: the “Most stars” control only orders projects, while “Filter by name” searches names. For a star threshold, open Explore, select “Most stars,” then inspect the displayed star-count links and continue through pages only while counts exceed the requested threshold. Verify every visible result meets the threshold before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to find GitLab projects above a star-count threshold, especially if the dashboard shows only sorting and a “Filter by name” field. Use Explore and verify star counts rather than entering query syntax into the name filter.

skills.title: Use Project Descriptions for Language
skills.principle: On GitLab’s project exploration page, locate the target project and inspect its visible description. If the description explicitly names the implementation language, use that statement as the answer. Open the project only when additional confirmation is useful, then report the language concisely with the supporting wording.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked which programming language a GitLab project uses and the project list or overview visibly includes a descriptive sentence naming its implementation language.

skills.title: Use GitLab’s Project Name Filter
skills.principle: On GitLab’s Projects page, use the page-level “Filter by name” searchbox to locate the requested project, not the global “Search GitLab” textbox. Inspect the filtered results; if no matching project appears, report that it is unavailable instead of opening an unrelated project or creating one.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to check out a GitLab project from the user’s projects and the project list is visible, especially when multiple search controls exist.

skills.title: Read License Labels Directly
skills.principle: Match the requested license against displayed project license labels, opening a license file when necessary. Cover the requested listing pages and collect matching projects; use a license search qualifier only when this interface demonstrates support, rather than interpreting zero keyword results as proof that no licensed projects exist.
skills.when_to_apply: When finding GitLab projects by license and project cards or repository pages display license information.

skills.title: Verify Licenses Across Project Pages
skills.principle: Use the Projects Explore list and inspect each project card’s displayed license label directly. Do not use “Filter by name” with a license term; it searches project names and can return unrelated licenses. Record cards labeled “MIT License,” then follow Prev/Next pagination and repeat until all pages are checked.
skills.when_to_apply: When GitLab asks you to view all projects using a particular license and the Explore page exposes license labels on project cards, especially when no dedicated license filter is visible.

skills.title: Verify Navigation Before Continuing
skills.principle: Use the current accessibility tree to activate the link by its visible role and label, then verify the URL, page heading, or content changed. If the observation is unchanged, treat the action as unsuccessful, reacquire the current element reference, and retry rather than proceeding with assumptions or stale element IDs.
skills.when_to_apply: When navigating GitLab project areas such as Explore, Topics, or dashboard filters, especially after scrolling or any action that may change accessibility-tree references.

skills.title: Filter Projects by Topic
skills.principle:
1. Open GitLab’s Projects > Topics page.
2. Select the link for the requested topic.
3. Confirm the resulting page shows the topic heading and a “Projects with this topic” section, indicating the filter is applied.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to filter or browse GitLab projects by a topic/tag and the Projects navigation includes a Topics entry.

skills.title: Validate Element Roles Before Acting
skills.principle: Use the accessibility tree’s role and label to identify controls before interacting. Fill only inputs, textareas, or editable comboboxes; click only links or buttons. If an action fails, re-inspect the refreshed tree for the actual control instead of retrying the same heading or static element. For project topics, distinguish selecting an existing topic from creating or assigning one.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab topic or project-filter task presents headings and links with similar text, especially after a failed fill or click. Re-inspect the page before choosing the next control.

skills.title: Filter GitLab Projects to Personal
skills.principle:
1. From GitLab’s Projects area, select “Yours” if starting in Explore.
2. On the projects dashboard, choose the “Personal” filter rather than “All.”
3. Confirm the URL or page state indicates the personal filter is active and the list shows projects owned by the current user, then report completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to open personal projects and the GitLab Projects dashboard offers “All” and “Personal” views. If starting in Explore, first navigate through “Yours.”

skills.title: Filter GitLab Projects to Personal
skills.principle: From GitLab’s Projects page, select “Yours,” then select the “Personal” filter. Confirm the resulting page shows the personal-project list and the URL includes the personal-project filter. Once confirmed, report completion and terminate instead of issuing repeated no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to open or go to personal projects and the GitLab Projects page exposes “Yours” and a “Personal” filter. Verify the filtered list or URL before stopping.

skills.title: Use Direct Navigation After Stale Clicks
skills.principle: When a visible navigation link repeatedly fails because its accessibility bid is invalid, stale, or produces an empty action, stop retrying the same bid. Use the destination URL exposed in the current observation instead, then verify the new page by checking its heading and relevant content before terminating.
skills.when_to_apply: Use this on GitLab dashboard tasks when a sidebar link is visible but clicks fail with empty-action, missing-element, or stale-bid errors, and its destination URL is available in the accessibility tree.

skills.title: Identify and Open the Target GitLab Project
skills.principle: On GitLab’s Explore projects page, locate the project whose name and description match the requested topic, then activate its project-name link. Confirm the destination by checking the project heading and README content before reporting the requested information.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to learn about a specific GitLab project from an Explore listing, especially when several similarly named projects exist and the target’s description provides distinguishing context.

skills.title: Stop After Confirming Target Page
skills.principle: Navigate using the observed project link’s actual accessibility bid or its href, then verify the destination heading and relevant README content. Once the requested project page and information are visible, report completion and terminate; do not repeatedly click visible text as though it were an element bid.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab navigation task asks you to open a project or learn from its README, and the destination page already shows the project heading or requested description.

skills.title: Find Contribution Instructions in README
skills.principle: On GitLab, locate a repository whose description matches the contribution question, open its project page, and inspect the rendered README. Extract the documented workflow in order, including fork, clone, branch, edit, commit, push, and pull-request steps, plus any linked GUI tutorials or support resources. Report only instructions visibly supported by the README.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked how to contribute to a GitLab project and the repository list exposes descriptions or a project README. Prefer a contribution-focused repository when several candidates are available.

skills.title: Verify Contribution Guidance Navigation
skills.principle: When contribution guidance is requested, use the visible Help menu entry labeled “Contribute to GitLab” rather than stopping at the menu. After activating it, verify that the destination page loads and contains contribution instructions before reporting the result.
skills.when_to_apply: Apply on GitLab dashboard tasks asking how to contribute, especially when the Help menu is expanded and “Contribute to GitLab” is visible. Confirm navigation instead of ending after the click.

skills.title: Navigate Repository Graph Examples
skills.principle:
1. Identify the GitLab project whose name or description matches the requested technology or examples.
2. Open its Repository and enter the relevant examples directory.
3. If present, open the graphs subdirectory to expose visual graph files.
4. Confirm the page lists the requested graph assets before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to view examples stored in a GitLab repository, especially visualizations organized under an examples or graphs directory. Verify the final directory contents before responding.

skills.title: Choose the Most Relevant Search Result
skills.principle: After searching GitLab, compare result titles and snippets with the requested topic before opening anything. Select the item whose title or preview directly matches the target, rather than the first result. On its page, verify the requested examples are visible in code, images, or attachments before continuing.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when a GitLab search returns multiple issues or merge requests, especially when the first result is only loosely related and another result directly names the requested topic.

skills.title: Search GitLab Before Concluding Missing
skills.principle:
1. Use the header “Search GitLab” field when the requested project or file is absent from the visible project list.
2. Search the exact filename first, then related keywords if needed.
3. Open a matching project and navigate to the target file to verify its contents before reporting completion or absence.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab dashboard does not visibly contain the requested file or example, and the header search field is available.

skills.title: Verify Target Page Before Navigating
skills.principle: Inspect the current URL, page title, and accessibility tree before acting. If they already identify the requested destination, report completion and stop. Otherwise, use the clearly labeled navigation link matching the requested page, then verify the resulting URL or heading before reporting success.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for navigation tasks when the initial page may already be the requested destination, especially in GitLab dashboards with labeled sidebar links and distinctive page headings.

skills.title: Open a Project’s GitLab Issues
skills.principle:
1. Locate the target project in GitLab’s project list using its visible namespace and name.
2. Select the project’s issue-count link or project navigation entry labeled “Issues.”
3. Verify the resulting page identifies the correct project and displays the requested issue list, such as the selected “Open” tab.
4. Report the visible issue titles and status, then stop once the issues page is confirmed.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to view issues for a specific GitLab project and the project may first need to be located from Explore or another project list.

skills.title: Use GitLab’s Project Name Filter
skills.principle: On GitLab’s Explore > Projects page, enter the target project name in the dedicated “Filter by name” searchbox. Verify the project list updates to show the matching project, then stop; do not substitute the global “Search GitLab” field, which navigates to a different search workflow.
skills.when_to_apply: When the task explicitly asks to use the project search filter and the Explore > Projects page exposes a “Filter by name” searchbox.

skills.title: Read Project Update From List
skills.principle: On GitLab’s project list, locate the project whose name matches the request, then read the timestamp beside its “Updated” label. Report the displayed date, time, timezone, and relative age when available; stop once the matching entry is verified.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when the GitLab project list is already loaded and the target project appears as a visible entry with an “Updated” timestamp.

skills.title: Select Sort Option, Then Stop
skills.principle: Open the project sort control and choose the explicit “Most stars” menu option, rather than repeatedly clicking the currently displayed sort label. Verify the page reflects the selection, such as the URL containing the stars-descending sort state and the menu closing. Once confirmed, report completion and terminate without further clicks.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab project list shows a sort button and dropdown, especially when the button already displays the requested sort and the task requires changing from another ordering.

skills.title: Open a GitLab Project’s Stargazers
skills.principle:
1. Locate the target project in the GitLab project list using its visible name.
2. Select that project’s stargazer count link, not its general project link.
3. Confirm completion when the page title or breadcrumb shows “Starrers” and the page displays the stargazer count and user list.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to view who starred a GitLab project and the project is discoverable in an Explore or project-list view.

skills.title: Stop After Confirming Stargazers
skills.principle: Once the target project’s “Starrers” page is visible and lists the stargazers, treat the task as complete. Report completion immediately instead of exploring pagination or navigating away. Only use “Next” when the request explicitly requires all pages or additional entries.
skills.when_to_apply: For GitLab tasks asking to view a project’s stargazers, after opening the project’s stargazer-count link and confirming the “Starrers” page is displayed.

skills.title: Find Project Fork Count
skills.principle:
1. Search GitLab globally for the requested project name and select the matching project result.
2. Open the project’s forks control, identified by the forks icon or count.
3. Read the explicit total on the forks page, including public, internal, and private breakdowns when shown, then report the total and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab tasks asking how many forks a named project has, when global search is available and the result may include similarly named projects.

skills.title: Report Confirmed Results Immediately
skills.principle: Once the target metric is visibly confirmed, provide the requested value in the task output and terminate. Do not issue repeated no-op actions or wait for another observation after completion.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when a GitLab project page or metric-specific detail page clearly displays the requested count, such as a forks summary, and no further interaction is required.

skills.title: Stop After Confirming Recent Projects
skills.principle:
1. Select the project view that visibly sorts by last updated, such as GitLab’s “Personal” view with descending update order.
2. Verify the first listed project and its visible update timestamp.
3. Open that project if “view” requires details, then stop and report completion; do not browse unrelated activity filters unless explicitly requested.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to search for and view recently updated GitLab projects, after the sorted project list and target project page visibly confirm the most recent item.

skills.title: Stop After Verifying Navigation
skills.principle: Click the GitLab project-category link matching the requested destination, then verify the resulting URL or selected state. Once the destination is confirmed, report completion and terminate instead of issuing repeated no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: When a navigation task reaches a page whose URL and visible category state match the requested destination, especially after selecting GitLab's Personal projects view.

skills.title: Navigate to Project Topics
skills.principle: From GitLab’s project exploration page, select the navigation entry labeled “Topics.” Confirm the destination by checking the page title or URL, then inspect the content. If it displays “There are no topics to show,” report that topics cannot currently be browsed because projects need topics added first.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to browse GitLab project topics and the project exploration navigation is visible. Stop after reaching the Topics page and report its empty-state message if no topics are listed.

skills.title: Stop After Confirming Empty Topics
skills.principle: When the GitLab Topics page displays “There are no topics to show,” treat the browse request as complete. Report that no topics are available and terminate instead of filtering, switching to Explore, opening projects, or inspecting unrelated Wiki pages.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when browsing GitLab project topics and the Topics page visibly shows an empty-state message confirming that no topics are available.

skills.title: Use GitLab’s Trending Projects View
skills.principle: From GitLab’s project exploration page, select the navigation link labeled “Trending” rather than relying on the current sort or pagination. Confirm the URL or page state shows the trending projects view, then report the visible project information and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to explore trending GitLab projects and the current page is an alphabetically sorted, paginated project list with an available “Trending” navigation link.

skills.title: Stop After Trending Page Loads
skills.principle: Select the GitLab Explore navigation entry labeled “Trending.” Verify the URL is the trending-projects page and project cards are visible. Once this state is confirmed, report completion and stop; do not keep scrolling unless the task explicitly requests additional projects or a specific item.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view GitLab trending projects and the Explore page exposes a “Trending” link with visible project listings after navigation.

skills.title: Locate and Verify GitLab Project
skills.principle:
1. Inspect the current GitLab project list for the target project’s visible name or repository link.
2. Select the matching project entry using its semantic label, not a fixed element identifier.
3. Confirm navigation succeeded by checking the page title, project URL, repository contents, and project navigation.
4. Report completion and stop once the target project page is confirmed.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to navigate to a GitLab project from an exploration or project-list page, especially when the target may already be visible and accessible.

skills.title: Stop After Goal Confirmation
skills.principle: Once the target project page is reached and its heading, breadcrumbs, or URL confirms the destination, treat the task as complete. Report completion and terminate immediately instead of issuing repeated no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: When navigating to a GitLab project or other target page, after the observed URL and page content clearly identify the requested destination.

skills.title: Open a GitLab Project Repository
skills.principle:
1. Locate the target project in the GitLab project list using its visible name or description.
2. Open the project’s link, then select the sidebar navigation entry labeled “Repository.”
3. Confirm completion when the repository tree appears, showing the branch and files/directories such as README or LICENSE.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to view a specific GitLab project repository and the starting page is a project listing or the project overview page.

skills.title: Navigate GitLab Code by Semantic Paths
skills.principle:
1. Open the target project, then follow repository directories whose names and README descriptions match the requested technology or component.
2. Prefer the source directory over build output, and select the main implementation file by its meaningful filename.
3. If a tooltip blocks a link click, use the link’s observed destination URL with direct navigation.
4. Confirm completion when the file view shows the expected filename, source content, and relevant implementation details.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when locating a specific source file in a GitLab repository, especially when the repository is unfamiliar or UI tooltips obstruct clicks. Verify the target path and file contents before reporting findings.

skills.title: Recover From Tooltip-Blocked Clicks
skills.principle: When a tooltip or overlay intercepts a target link, do not repeat the same click indefinitely. Move the pointer to a neutral area or dismiss the overlay, then retry using the refreshed accessibility target. If interception persists, navigate through the link’s observed destination URL instead, and verify the resulting breadcrumb or page heading.
skills.when_to_apply: Use in GitLab repository browsing when a visible file or directory link repeatedly times out because an accessibility-tree tooltip or overlay intercepts pointer events.

skills.title: Follow Repository Documentation Links
skills.principle: When asked to learn a repository-specific topic, open the matching project, scan its README for a relevant documentation link, then open the linked source file. Use the document’s headings and paragraphs to extract the requested guidance, verify the page matches the topic, and summarize only the observed content.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab research tasks where the target project is discoverable in a project list and its README links to focused documentation about the requested topic.

skills.title: Read Stars From Project Listings
skills.principle: Identify the target project by its displayed name, then read the numeric link associated with the star icon within the same project entry. Treat that number as the star count and report it directly; the link destination indicating starrers confirms its meaning.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when a GitLab project appears in an Explore or project-listing page and its entry shows repository statistics, including a star-associated numeric link.

skills.title: Create a GitLab Blank Project
skills.principle:
1. From GitLab Projects, select “New project,” then “Create blank project.”
2. Fill “Project name” and “Project slug,” replacing any auto-generated slug rather than appending to it.
3. Confirm the intended visibility and repository initialization settings, then select “Create project.”
4. Verify the project page and success alert identify the new project before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When creating an empty GitLab project from an authenticated Projects dashboard, especially when the form auto-populates or modifies the project slug.

skills.title: Verify Form Before Filling
skills.principle: Use the accessibility tree’s role and accessible name, not guessed or stale element IDs. Click the actual “Create blank project” link, then confirm the project form and its name textbox appear. Fill only the textbox identified by its label or role; if the expected form is absent, re-observe and correct navigation before retrying.
skills.when_to_apply: When creating a GitLab blank project and the page shows project-choice cards or element IDs that resolve to unrelated navigation links. Re-observe after navigation before entering project details.

skills.title: Navigate to Blank Project Form
skills.principle:
1. From GitLab Projects, select the relevant “New project” navigation entry.
2. On the project-type page, choose “Create blank project” rather than a template or import option.
3. Confirm the destination by checking the “Create blank project” heading, breadcrumb, and project-details form; then report completion without submitting it.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when the task asks only to reach GitLab’s blank-project creation page, starting from a Projects or project-list page. Stop once the blank-project heading and form are visible.

skills.title: Stop After Reaching Target Page
skills.principle: After navigation produces the requested page, verify its heading and key content, then report completion and terminate. Do not repeat no-op actions or continue interacting with the page once the goal is satisfied.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for navigation tasks when the current accessibility tree visibly shows the requested destination, such as GitLab’s “Create blank project” heading and form.

skills.title: Read Project Counts From Explore
skills.principle: On GitLab’s project Explore list, locate the target project by its visible name, then read the number attached to its merge-request link or merge-request icon. Use that displayed count directly when the project row clearly identifies the requested repository; avoid opening the project unless the count is absent or ambiguous.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked for a project’s merge-request count and the GitLab Explore project list is visible, with the target project row and its merge-request statistic displayed.

skills.title: Verify Project Scope Before Counting
skills.principle:
1. Search using GitLab’s global search or Explore when the project is absent from the current personal-project list.
2. Open the target project and use its project-level “Merge requests” navigation.
3. Read the project page’s “All” count; do not infer the total from dashboard labels such as “Assigned to you” or “Review requests for you.”
skills.when_to_apply: When asked for a project’s merge-request total and the initial project list or filter shows no matching project. Verify the project context before interpreting counts.

skills.title: Use the Correct Project Filter
skills.principle: On GitLab’s Projects page, identify the control by its accessible role and label before acting. Use the “Filter by name” searchbox to enter the target project, not the nearby “New project” link. Confirm that the filtered project appears, open it, and inspect its license information.
skills.when_to_apply: When locating a GitLab project from a Projects list, especially when a searchbox labeled “Filter by name” is visible alongside navigation links.

skills.title: Identify Relevant Projects from Visible Descriptions
skills.principle: Scan every visible project card on the GitLab Explore page, using both project names and descriptions to identify semantic matches for the requested topic. Collect each matching project’s displayed name and supporting description, then report the deduplicated list directly to the user.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to find projects related to a topic on the current GitLab Explore page and the project list with names and descriptions is visible.

skills.title: Use GitLab Project Name Filtering
skills.principle: On GitLab’s Projects page, use the “Filter by name” searchbox before manually paging through results. Enter the target keyword, then verify the project list updates and inspect displayed names and descriptions for relevance. Once matching projects are visible, report them and stop instead of repeatedly reopening the sort menu or clicking unrelated controls.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to find projects related to a keyword on GitLab’s Explore Projects page, especially when the current list is paginated or sorted and the “Filter by name” searchbox is available.

skills.title: Use GitLab’s Assigned Issues Link
skills.principle: From any GitLab page, locate the top-navigation link labeled “Issues” and activate it. Confirm the destination is the dashboard Issues page with an assignee filter for the current user and visible issue listings. Once the heading, assignee filter, and list are present, report completion and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view issues assigned to the current GitLab user and the top navigation contains an “Issues” link leading to the dashboard issues view.

skills.title: Terminate After Confirming Target Page
skills.principle: Once the page title, URL, and relevant content confirm the requested destination, treat navigation as complete. Report completion immediately and terminate the trajectory instead of issuing repeated no-op actions or waiting for further changes.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab navigation task is satisfied and the accessibility tree shows the requested page, such as Issues with the intended assignee filter and visible issue listings.

skills.title: Verify Filter Context Before Acting
skills.principle: On GitLab project lists, distinguish navigation tabs such as “All” and “Personal” from actual visibility filters. Locate the control labeled for visibility, inspect its available options, and use the interaction matching its element type (click a tab/link, select only a real `<select>`). If the target option is absent, navigate to the appropriate project-exploration/filter view rather than guessing or repeatedly clicking unrelated elements.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to change a GitLab project visibility filter and the current accessibility tree shows only name search, sorting, or ownership tabs without a visibility control or target option.

skills.title: Click Custom Listbox Options Directly
skills.principle: For GitLab’s custom visibility dropdown, open the current filter button, then click the visible option labeled “Public” rather than repeatedly issuing malformed `select_option` calls. Confirm completion when the filter button changes from “Any” to “Public” and the listbox closes or results refresh.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab Explore page shows a visibility button such as “Any” with a custom ARIA listbox, especially after an action-format or empty-action error.

skills.title: Use Accessibility Bids for Project Links
skills.principle: On GitLab’s project list, read each project’s issue-count link directly when the count is visible. If navigation is necessary, activate the observed accessibility-tree bid or link element, not its URL string. After each action, verify the page changed before continuing; otherwise re-inspect the current tree instead of guessing another project URL.
skills.when_to_apply: When comparing issue counts across GitLab projects and the project list exposes issue-count links. Use this before attempting navigation, especially after a click reports that an element or bid cannot be found.

skills.title: Verify Project View Before Navigating
skills.principle: Check the current URL and selected project-category tab first. If they already indicate the requested view, report completion and stop. Otherwise, select the semantic navigation link such as “Trending,” then confirm the URL and active tab show the requested category.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab Explore task requests a specific project view and the initial page may already be filtered or opened to that category.

skills.title: Verify Target View Before Further Actions
skills.principle: After selecting a navigation option, inspect the updated URL and page content. If they already show the requested view, treat the task as complete, report completion, and stop. Do not manipulate unrelated controls such as visibility filters or repeat clicks using stale element references.
skills.when_to_apply: When switching GitLab Explore views, especially after clicking “Trending.” Apply once the URL and visible project list confirm the requested view, even if the original action produced an error.

skills.title: Stop After Dashboard Confirmation
skills.principle: Once the personal dashboard is visibly confirmed—such as the GitLab URL containing the personal filter and the “Personal” view being active—report completion and terminate immediately. Do not issue repeated no-op actions or continue interacting with the page.
skills.when_to_apply: When navigating to a GitLab personal dashboard, after clicking “Dashboard” and selecting “Personal,” verify the resulting URL or active view before ending the task.

skills.title: Use GitLab’s Sort Dropdown
skills.principle:
1. Identify the current sort control and open its dropdown.
2. Choose the requested alternative, such as “Most stars,” from the visible options.
3. Confirm completion when the control label and resulting page state reflect the new sort, then stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When viewing GitLab’s project exploration list and asked to change sorting. The sort control must be visible; verify the selected label or URL reflects the requested ordering.

skills.title: Verify Sorting Then Stop
skills.principle: After choosing a different sort option, confirm the sort control displays the selected attribute and the visible items follow the expected order. Once both signals are present, report completion and terminate instead of repeating no-op checks.
skills.when_to_apply: Use on GitLab project-list pages after selecting any alternative sort option, when the sort control updates and the refreshed list visibly reflects the requested ordering.

skills.title: Subscribe to a GitLab Issues Calendar
skills.principle:
1. Open the target GitLab project and select its Issues navigation entry.
2. On the issues list, locate and activate the “Subscribe to calendar” link.
3. Confirm the destination displays iCalendar data beginning with “BEGIN:VCALENDAR”; provide the resulting URL for use with a calendar application.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to subscribe to a GitLab project’s issues calendar and the target project is accessible. The issues list must expose a “Subscribe to calendar” link.

skills.title: Terminate After Project Page Confirmation
skills.principle: Once the GitLab project page is visible and its heading or URL matches the requested project, treat the task as complete. Report completion and terminate immediately instead of issuing repeated no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view a GitLab project and the project page is visibly loaded, with the requested project name confirmed by the heading, breadcrumb, or URL.

skills.title: Read Repository Stars from Explore
skills.principle: On GitLab’s project listing, locate the target repository by its visible owner/name heading, then read the numeric link paired with the star icon in that same project row. Report that value as the repository’s star count without confusing it with forks, merge requests, or issues.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when the GitLab Explore projects list visibly contains the target repository and its project-row metadata, including the star-count link, is available in the accessibility tree.

skills.title: Verify Filter Results Before Clicking
skills.principle: After entering a repository name in GitLab’s project filter, inspect the updated accessibility tree for a matching project link. If the result list is empty, switch to Explore or global GitLab search rather than waiting. Click only the verified matching project link, then read the stars count from its project card or details page.
skills.when_to_apply: When a repository is absent from the current project list or a name filter shows an empty-state message. Confirm the target link exists before clicking, especially when nearby navigation entries such as Explore are present.

skills.title: Use Search Result Issue Counts
skills.principle: Search GitLab globally for the target repository, select the matching project result, and read the numeric link labeled for issues beneath that project. Treat this repository-level issue metric as the requested open-issue count when it links to the project’s issues page, then report it without unnecessary navigation.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked for a repository’s open issue count and GitLab search results show a unique matching project with an issues metric linking to its issues page.

skills.title: Use Project Name Filtering
skills.principle:
1. On GitLab’s Projects page, enter the target repository name in the “Filter by name” searchbox.
2. Select the matching project link from the filtered results; do not reuse stale or nonexistent element IDs.
3. Open the project’s “Issues” page and read the count for the “Open” state.
skills.when_to_apply: When the GitLab Projects view shows many repositories and the target is not immediately visible, especially after an element lookup fails.

skills.title: Verify Repository Identity and Latest Commit
skills.principle: When repositories share a name, identify the intended project by its owner before opening it. On the repository page, use the latest commit shown on the default branch and read its timestamp; treat that date as the last update when no explicit repository update field is available.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab tasks asking when a repository was last updated, especially when search results contain multiple same-named repositories or forks.

skills.title: Report Visible Repository Update Time
skills.principle: When a GitLab project list shows the target repository and its adjacent “Updated” timestamp, read that timestamp directly, state it in the final answer, and terminate. Do not focus or repeat no-op actions after the required value is visibly confirmed.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when the target GitLab repository appears in a project list with an adjacent “Updated” time, and the timestamp is readable without opening the repository.

skills.title: Use Header Dashboard Navigation
skills.principle: When GitLab is on another page, activate the visible header link labeled “Dashboard.” Confirm navigation succeeded by checking that the page title includes “Dashboard” and the URL is the GitLab root dashboard path, then report completion without further actions.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for tasks requiring the GitLab Dashboard when the accessibility tree shows a header “Dashboard” link or when the current page title and URL already indicate the dashboard.

skills.title: Recognize Dashboard Already Reached
skills.principle: After navigation, verify the current URL and page title before taking more actions. If the URL is the Dashboard route and the accessibility tree identifies “Dashboard,” treat the task as complete, report success, and stop. Do not repeatedly click the same link, scroll, wait, or navigate to the identical URL.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to open a GitLab page and the post-action accessibility tree already shows the requested page title and its expected route, especially when the destination is the current URL.

skills.title: Recognize Already-Displayed Project Lists
skills.principle: When GitLab’s Projects page visibly contains the requested category, use the existing navigation state rather than taking another action. Confirm the relevant tab or list label, verify that project entries are displayed, then report completion and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: Apply when asked to view projects and the current GitLab page already shows the requested project category, such as a visible “Starred” tab and populated project list.

skills.title: Terminate After Confirming Target Page
skills.principle: Once navigation reaches the requested GitLab page, verify the URL and visible content match the task, then report completion and terminate. Do not issue repeated no-op actions after the target state is already confirmed.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for navigation tasks when the browser shows the requested destination and its relevant content, such as the GitLab Projects page with the Starred projects list visible.

skills.title: Use Valid Navigation Actions
skills.principle: When a navigation click produces an empty-action error, issue a correctly formatted action or navigate using the observed destination link URL. Verify the resulting page by its heading and URL, then report completion and stop instead of repeating no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: For GitLab navigation tasks when the target link is visible but click execution fails, or when the target page is already confirmed by its heading and URL.

skills.title: Fork GitLab Repository Through Namespace
skills.principle:
1. Open the target repository and select the visible “Fork” action.
2. On “Fork project,” choose the destination namespace; retain valid defaults unless the task requires changes.
3. Submit “Fork project” and wait for navigation or a success alert.
4. If the page shows the forked repository under the destination namespace and confirms “The project was successfully forked,” report completion and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when a GitLab repository must be copied into the signed-in user’s namespace and the repository page exposes a “Fork” action. Verify the destination namespace is selected before submitting.

skills.title: Verify Fork Completion Before Retrying
skills.principle: After selecting GitLab’s “Fork” action, inspect the resulting page rather than clicking again. Confirm the project is under the user’s namespace and the page shows “Forked from” linking to the original repository. These observations establish success even if a “Fork” link remains visible; then report completion and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When forking a GitLab repository, especially after navigation to a same-named project under your account. Use the destination namespace, repository ownership, and “Forked from” indicator as completion evidence.

skills.title: Scan Project Cards for License Matches
skills.principle: Review each repository card on the current GitLab projects page and compare its displayed license label with the requested license. Record the repository’s namespace and name whenever the label matches, then report the complete matching list and count.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when the GitLab Explore projects page is already open and repository cards visibly include license text. No navigation or opening individual repositories is needed unless the license is not displayed.

skills.title: Use Current Semantic Targets
skills.principle: After navigation, re-read the accessibility tree and act on the currently exposed element by role or label. Do not reuse stale element IDs from an earlier page state. Verify action syntax, then confirm the resulting URL or expanded control before continuing; if no license filter exists, inspect candidate repository details or license files instead of repeatedly clicking navigation.
skills.when_to_apply: When filtering GitLab projects across navigation or dynamic page updates, especially after a click changes the accessibility tree or when the requested attribute is not visible in the project list.

skills.title: Open Your GitLab Profile
skills.principle:
1. From any GitLab page, activate the signed-in user name in the header.
