2. In the expanded account menu, select the entry showing the user name and username, rather than settings such as “Edit profile.”
3. Confirm navigation succeeded by checking the profile page heading, username, and profile details; then report completion and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view the signed-in user’s GitLab profile and the header account control is visible. Use the account menu when clicking the header name only expands options.

skills.title: Count Threshold Matches in Listings
skills.principle: Scan each visible project list item and read its star-count link, treating the count as the project’s stars. Increment a tally only when the value is strictly greater than the requested threshold, including boundary checks such as exactly 10. Report the final tally after all visible items are evaluated.
skills.when_to_apply: Use on GitLab project listing pages when asked to count items meeting a numeric star threshold and the accessibility tree exposes each project’s star-count link.

skills.title: Systematically Count Project Stars
skills.principle: Review each project card once, using the star-count link (the link ending in “/starrers”), not forks, merge requests, or issues. Increment a counter only when the displayed stars exceed the requested threshold. After every card on the current page is accounted for, report the final count and stop; do not use repeated no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: When counting projects matching a numeric star threshold on a GitLab Explore page, provided the full target page and its project cards are visible in the accessibility tree.

skills.title: Verify Dashboard by URL and Title
skills.principle: For GitLab navigation, confirm the destination using the current URL and page title, not the main content heading alone. The Dashboard can legitimately display a “Projects” heading; a root dashboard URL and title containing “Dashboard” indicate success. Stop immediately once both are confirmed.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to open GitLab’s Dashboard and the resulting page still shows a Projects heading. Check the browser URL and accessible page title before retrying navigation or performing extra actions.

skills.title: Stop After Confirming Project Page
skills.principle:
1. Search GitLab for the target project and submit the query.
2. Select the matching project result, verifying the resulting page shows the project name and repository navigation.
3. Once the project page is confirmed, report completion and terminate instead of issuing repeated no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab task asks you to check out or open a project and the project page is visibly loaded with its name and repository controls.

skills.title: Stop After Reaching Target Page
skills.principle: When the requested GitLab page is visibly loaded, verify its heading, URL, and relevant content, then report completion and terminate. Do not repeat no-op actions or continue navigating after the target state is confirmed.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for navigation tasks when the accessibility tree shows the requested destination and its expected content, such as GitLab Explore > Trending displaying project entries.

skills.title: Recognize the Existing GitLab Dashboard
skills.principle: When the current page already shows GitLab Dashboard indicators—such as the Dashboard navigation entry, a Projects heading, and project listings—treat the navigation goal as complete. Confirm the page matches the requested overview, report completion, and stop without unnecessary navigation.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for tasks asking to open or navigate to the GitLab Dashboard when the initial accessibility tree or URL already identifies the Dashboard and displays projects or activity content.

skills.title: Terminate After Confirming Dashboard
skills.principle: When the observed page already matches the requested destination, verify its URL and identifying heading or navigation label, then report completion and terminate. Do not repeatedly issue a no-op action, because the browser environment may reject it as an empty action and prevent successful termination.
skills.when_to_apply: For navigation tasks when the current accessibility tree already shows the requested GitLab destination, such as the Dashboard link, Dashboard URL, and Projects heading.

skills.title: Navigate GitLab Account Settings
skills.principle:
1. Open the signed-in user menu from the avatar or username.
2. Select “Edit profile” to enter User Settings.
3. Select “Account” in the settings sidebar.
4. Confirm the page shows “Account · User Settings” and account controls, then report completion and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when a GitLab task asks to manage account-level settings and the current page shows the signed-in user’s avatar or username menu.

skills.title: Stop After Reaching Profile Settings
skills.principle: Once the GitLab user menu is expanded, select “Edit profile.” Verify the page shows “User Settings” and “Edit Profile” breadcrumbs or profile settings controls. Then report completion and terminate; do not repeat noop actions.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to open GitLab account or profile settings and the accessibility tree confirms the Edit Profile page is loaded, including its settings sidebar or profile form.

skills.title: Navigate via GitLab To-Do Items
skills.principle:
1. Open GitLab’s “To-Do List” from the global navigation.
2. Inspect pending entries to identify the target project and its associated issue or merge request.
3. Activate that entry’s issue or merge-request link.
4. Confirm the destination by checking the project breadcrumb and page title, then stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to navigate to a project mentioned in GitLab’s To-Do List and the list contains pending entries with project names and linked issues or merge requests.

skills.title: Open the Project, Not Its Issue
skills.principle: When a To-Do entry shows both a project name and an issue or merge-request link, use the project identity or breadcrumb to open the project root. Do not click the work-item link unless the task asks for that item. Confirm the resulting page is the project overview (project name and project navigation visible), then stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When GitLab To-Do entries identify a project alongside linked issues or merge requests, especially when the task asks to navigate to the project rather than inspect a specific work item.

skills.title: Open a Merge Request from To-Do List
skills.principle:
1. Open GitLab’s “To-Do List” navigation entry.
2. Identify the requested merge-request item by its title, project, or reference; do not choose arbitrarily when the target is specified.
3. Activate that item’s “Merge Request” link.
4. Confirm the destination page shows the merge-request title and details, then report completion and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when a GitLab task requires opening a merge request listed in the current user’s To-Do List and the list contains identifiable merge-request links.

skills.title: Check To-Do State Before Scrolling
skills.principle: Inspect the To-Do List counts and visible empty-state message before searching. If “To Do” is zero and the page says all tasks are done, do not keep scrolling; verify whether the requested item can come from “Done,” otherwise recognize that no pending item is available.
skills.when_to_apply: When navigating to a GitLab item from the To-Do List, especially when the page shows a zero pending count or an explicit all-done empty state.

skills.title: Verify GitLab Projects Before Opening Issues
skills.principle: Use GitLab's global "Search GitLab" field to search the exact project path, submit the search, and inspect the Projects result count. Only open the project's Issues page after a matching project is found; if results show zero projects, report that the project or path could not be found instead of guessing URLs.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to inspect issues for a GitLab project whose namespace or name is not already visible as a confirmed project link.

skills.title: Search Before Scrolling Projects
skills.principle: Use GitLab’s project search controls instead of repeatedly scrolling. Enter the target namespace/project in “Filter by name” or the global search, then select the matching result or press Enter. Once the project page opens, use its “Issues” navigation and verify the issue list belongs to the requested project.
skills.when_to_apply: When a requested GitLab project is not immediately visible in the dashboard list, especially when the project belongs to another namespace or the list contains many repositories.

skills.title: Use Repository Merge Request Counts
skills.principle: From the project listing, identify the target repository and activate its merge-request count link. On the repository’s Merge requests page, read the Open, Merged, Closed, and All tabs, then summarize the visible requests and counts. Stop once the page state directly answers the request.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to inspect a GitLab project’s merge requests and the project listing exposes a merge-request count or link. Verify the destination is the target repository’s Merge requests page before reporting.

skills.title: Use Project-Specific Merge Requests Link
skills.principle: From a GitLab project listing, open the target project, then select its project-specific “Merge requests” entry or count. Do not use the global navigation item, which opens dashboard requests. Verify the URL and page heading identify the target project before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view merge requests for a particular GitLab project, especially from Explore results where both global and project-specific “Merge requests” links are visible.

skills.title: Verify Explore Filter Capabilities
skills.principle: Check the Explore page for a license-specific filter before searching. If only name filtering and project summaries are available, perform a bounded scan, avoid treating missing license text as proof of licensing, and report when the requested criterion cannot be verified there.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when searching GitLab Explore projects for a metadata attribute such as a license, but the visible controls lack a matching filter and project cards do not expose that attribute.

skills.title: Extract Explicit License Matches Efficiently
skills.principle: On GitLab Explore, inspect each project card for an explicit license label such as “MIT License,” record the associated project name, and ignore cards showing other licenses or none. Stop when scrolling produces no new cards or a pagination boundary is reached, then report the collected matches instead of repeating unchanged scrolls.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to find projects using a specific license on GitLab Explore and project cards visibly expose license labels. Ensure the results are recorded before terminating.

skills.title: Track Maximum Stars Across Project Cards
skills.principle: Inspect every project card on the current GitLab page and read its star-count control (the starrers link). Maintain the project with the greatest count, updating it whenever a larger value appears. Report the final maximum only after all visible cards have been checked; do not assume the URL or selected tab guarantees star ordering.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked which GitLab project has the most stars on the current page, especially when the page may be sorted by name or its visible ordering is uncertain.

skills.title: Use GitLab’s Most Stars View
skills.principle: Open the semantic “Most stars” navigation link, then verify the URL changes to the starred-projects view. Treat each project card’s first numeric metric link as its star count, compare visible cards in descending order, and use “Next” only if the requested results exceed the current page.
skills.when_to_apply: When exploring GitLab projects for highest star counts, especially if the current URL shows name sorting or a paginated “All” project list. Verify the starred view before comparing cards.

skills.title: Compare Issue Counts Across Projects
skills.principle: Scan every project card currently visible and read the numeric link associated with its issues. Compare the counts numerically, retain the project with the largest value, and report both the project name and count. Do not infer from sorting by name or inspect another page unless requested.
skills.when_to_apply: Use on GitLab project listings when the task asks for the project with the most open issues on the current page and each card exposes an issue-count link.

skills.title: Stop After Confirming the Maximum
skills.principle: Compare each project's visible open-issue count, retain the project with the largest value, and report it once identified. If the target and count are already confirmed in the current observation, do not click into additional details or repeat the same action; terminate the task.
skills.when_to_apply: When GitLab's project list visibly shows issue-count links or labels and the maximum can be determined directly from the current page.

skills.title: Filter Explore Projects and Verify Completion
skills.principle:
1. Open GitLab’s Projects > Explore page rather than the global search.
2. Enter the target keyword in the “Filter by name” searchbox and confirm the URL/results update.
3. Review matching project cards, scrolling as needed; inspect for pagination or “Next” controls before concluding.
4. Report completion only when further scrolling produces no new results and no continuation control is available.
skills.when_to_apply: When searching GitLab Explore for projects matching a name or keyword, especially when results may span scrolling content or pagination.

skills.title: Use Observed Sort Option
skills.principle: Open the current sort control and inspect the expanded menu. Select the observed link labeled “Updated date,” not an inferred label such as “Most recently updated.” Verify completion by checking that the page URL or displayed sort state reflects latest-activity descending and the project order changes.
skills.when_to_apply: When changing GitLab Explore project sorting and the menu is open in the accessibility tree. Use the exact visible option label and its current element reference, then confirm the resulting page state.

skills.title: Use the Yours Projects Tab
skills.principle: On GitLab’s Projects page, locate the navigation link labeled “Yours” (often showing a project count) and select it. Confirm completion when the URL changes to the dashboard projects page and the project list displays accessible personal or shared projects; then report completion without repeating the action.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view your own GitLab projects and the current page is Explore or another Projects view showing tabs such as Yours, Starred, Explore, and Topics.

skills.title: Verify Navigation Before Retrying
skills.principle: After activating a navigation entry, compare the resulting URL and page state with the requested destination. If the URL already matches the target (for example, the GitLab Projects page for the “Yours” tab), treat the task as complete and stop. Do not substitute similarly named filters such as “Personal” or “All” or repeat clicks without evidence of failure.
skills.when_to_apply: When navigating GitLab tabs or dashboard links, especially when the destination may reuse the current URL. Check the URL and visible selected content immediately after the first action.

skills.title: Report Visible Count and Stop
skills.principle: When the requested count is clearly shown in a labeled UI element, read that label’s associated number, provide it directly in the response, and terminate. Do not repeatedly issue no-op actions after the answer is established.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab list or dashboard tasks when an accessibility-tree label such as “Starred” visibly includes the requested count and no further interaction is needed.

skills.title: Verify Project Search Before Navigating
skills.principle: Use GitLab’s “Filter by name” field with the requested project name. Inspect the refreshed results: navigate only through a matching project link. If the filtered state shows no matching project, report that it is absent from the accessible project list rather than clicking a generic navigation item or claiming success.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to open a GitLab repository from a project dashboard and the repository may be missing or inaccessible in the current project list.

skills.title: Stop After Reaching Target Repository
skills.principle: After navigating to the requested GitLab project, verify the page title, project heading, breadcrumb, or URL identifies the target repository. Once confirmed, report completion and terminate instead of issuing repeated no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for simple GitLab navigation tasks when the target project is visibly loaded and its identity is confirmed by the current page state.

skills.title: Verify GitLab Star State
skills.principle: On the target project page, inspect the project-follow control before acting. If it says “Unstar,” the project is already followed; report completion without clicking. If it says “Star,” click it, then confirm it changes to “Unstar” before reporting success.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to follow or receive updates from a GitLab project, after locating and opening the correct project page and its star control.

skills.title: Find Projects Through Owner Profiles
skills.principle: When GitLab project search returns no matching projects, broaden the query to the likely owner’s name, switch to the Users results, open the matching profile, and inspect that user’s project list. This is more reliable than repeatedly scrolling the dashboard’s personal-project list.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when a target project is absent from dashboard results or global project search shows zero matches, but the task identifies a likely namespace or owner name.

skills.title: Verify Filter Availability First
skills.principle: Check the project page for a control matching the requested attribute before manually browsing. If no such filter exists, inspect only the visible/current project scope, avoid repetitive scrolling, and clearly report that the requested filtering is unsupported rather than claiming a complete result.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to list GitLab projects by an attribute such as license and the Projects page exposes only name filtering, sorting, or basic scope tabs.

skills.title: Complete Pagination Before Reporting
skills.principle: When a listing lacks the needed filter, scan each visible card for the target attribute, record matching item names, and follow the pagination control consistently. Continue until the first page is reached and no previous page exists; only then report the complete collected set.
skills.when_to_apply: Use on GitLab Explore project listings when the target license is displayed on cards but no license filter is available. Prerequisite: identify the pagination controls and maintain a deduplicated result list.

skills.title: Stop After Code View Is Confirmed
skills.principle: Once the GitLab repository’s Files view is open and a source file or directory is visibly displayed, the browse-code goal is satisfied. Confirm the repository path and visible code, then report completion and terminate instead of repeatedly scrolling or navigating without a specific requested target.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for open-ended GitLab tasks such as “browse the repository code” when the Repository > Files page shows the file tree or a source file’s contents.

skills.title: Use Targeted File Navigation
skills.principle:
1. Open the repository’s “Repository” and “Files” views, then select a relevant source directory or file.
2. Prefer “Find file” or “Open raw” for large files instead of repeatedly scrolling through the rendered code.
3. Stop once the requested code is visible and report completion; do not continue exploratory scrolling without a specific objective.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to browse GitLab repository code and the repository file tree or a source file is already accessible, especially when the rendered file is large.

skills.title: Use GitLab Dashboard Issues
skills.principle: From any GitLab page, select the global "Issues" navigation entry rather than opening individual projects. On the dashboard, read the Open, Closed, and All tabs to summarize assigned issue counts and inspect visible projects or issue types. Report the observed totals and themes once the dashboard confirms them.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to check a user's GitLab project issues and the global navigation includes "Issues". Ensure the resulting dashboard is filtered to the relevant assignee before reporting counts.

skills.title: Stop After Issues List Appears
skills.principle: Navigate to GitLab’s “Issues” view, then verify the page heading and issue entries are visible. Once the issue list is confirmed, report completion and terminate instead of repeatedly issuing no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to check project issues and the GitLab Issues page is accessible, showing an “Issues” heading and one or more issue entries.

skills.title: Access Project Package Registries
skills.principle:
1. Navigate to the target GitLab project rather than using global dashboard menus.
2. In the project navigation sidebar, select “Packages and registries.”
3. Confirm the Package Registry page loads, checking its package count and any available registry options such as “Infrastructure Registry.”
4. Report the observed registry state and stop once access is confirmed.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to access packages or registries in GitLab and the target project is identifiable. The project navigation sidebar must be visible or reachable first.

skills.title: Stop After Reaching Package Registry
skills.principle: Navigate from the target project’s sidebar to the semantic “Packages and registries” entry, then select “Package Registry” if needed. Confirm the destination by checking for the “Package Registry” heading or package count. Once the requested page is visible, report completion and terminate instead of retrying stale element IDs, scrolling, or exploring unrelated repository links.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab project page is available and the task is to access packages or registries, especially after the Package Registry page and its heading or package status are visible.

skills.title: Open and Verify GitLab README
skills.principle:
1. From the GitLab project listing, open the target project.
2. On its repository page, locate the file link labeled “README” or “README.md” and open it.
3. Confirm the page heading and rendered content identify the README, then summarize only information visible there and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to read a repository README in GitLab and the project is not yet open. Use the repository file listing or rendered README section, verifying the destination before reporting completion.

skills.title: Verify Project Navigation Before Reading README
skills.principle:
1. Select the project’s exact accessible-name link, not a nearby avatar, tab, or generic navigation control.
2. Verify the resulting URL and page heading identify the target repository before proceeding.
3. Open the repository file list or the README file entry; do not rely on repeated scrolling to locate it.
4. Confirm the README content is displayed before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When reading a README in GitLab from a project list, especially when multiple links or generic controls are nearby and navigation may silently land on the dashboard.

skills.title: Access GitLab Issues RSS Feed
skills.principle:
1. Open the target GitLab project and select the project-level “Issues” navigation entry.
2. On the issues list, locate and activate “Subscribe to RSS feed.”
3. Confirm the destination displays Atom/XML feed content and provide the resulting feed URL for use in an RSS reader.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to subscribe to a GitLab project’s issue updates and the project is accessible. Use the project Issues list, not the global dashboard, and verify the feed page loads successfully.

skills.title: Verify RSS Feed and Stop
skills.principle: On a GitLab project’s Issues page, click the visible “Subscribe to RSS feed” link. Confirm the resulting page displays an Atom/XML feed and its URL contains the project’s issues feed endpoint. Treat this as completion and terminate immediately; do not repeat no-op actions or attempt unsupported address-bar clipboard operations.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to subscribe to a project’s issues RSS feed and the Issues page exposes a “Subscribe to RSS feed” link. Completion is indicated by the resulting Atom/XML feed page.

skills.title: Use the Issues Calendar Entry Point
skills.principle: Start from GitLab’s Dashboard or the relevant project’s Issues navigation, then locate the explicit Calendar view or “Subscribe to calendar” control. Do not select an arbitrary project from Explore or search project integrations. Activate the subscription and verify the control or page state confirms it is enabled.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to subscribe to an issues calendar without a specified project, especially from Explore or another unrelated GitLab page. Use the Issues navigation first and proceed only when the calendar or subscription control is visible.

skills.title: Verify Submission Before Retrying
skills.principle:
1. In the target GitLab project, open the project-level “Issues” navigation and select “New issue.”
2. Fill the required title and, when provided, the description, then activate “Create issue.”
3. If the click reports a timeout, inspect the current page before retrying; navigation may already have succeeded.
4. Confirm the issue page shows the title, “Issue created,” and an open status before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When creating a GitLab issue and the submission click times out or appears ambiguous, especially after required fields are filled and the page may have navigated.

skills.title: Select GitLab Projects Through Custom Comboboxes
skills.principle: On GitLab’s Issues dashboard, open “Select project to create issue,” then treat the project picker as a custom combobox rather than a native select. Search using a distinctive project name, click the matching visible option, and verify the picker closes or the issue form loads before entering issue details. If “No matches found” appears, clear the query and search again instead of pressing Enter on unmatched text.
skills.when_to_apply: When creating an issue from GitLab’s dashboard and the project picker exposes an input with an expanded listbox, especially after a native select action fails or the typed project produces “No matches found”.

skills.title: Open GitLab Issues Directly by Number
skills.principle:
1. Identify the likely repository from project context, then open its Issues section.
2. If list search does not visibly filter results, navigate directly to the repository’s standard issue URL using the requested number.
3. Verify the page breadcrumb, issue number, title, and relevant description before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view a specific GitLab issue by number, especially when the issue list is paginated or its search control fails to update visible results.

skills.title: Validate Actions and Element Bids
skills.principle: Use the latest accessibility tree to identify the target control and submit a complete, correctly formatted browser action. After acting, verify that the URL or page heading changed. If an action fails or the bid is missing, reassess the current tree and choose a fresh semantic target instead of repeating the stale action.
skills.when_to_apply: When navigating GitLab from a project list to Issues or another section, especially after an empty-action error, stale element error, or unchanged page state.

skills.title: Filter Projects Before Checking Merge Requests
skills.principle:
1. Open GitLab’s project list and use the “Filter by name” control with the target project name.
2. Confirm whether a matching project or an explicit empty-state message appears.
3. Report that no open merge requests exist only when the filtered results provide sufficient evidence; otherwise continue navigating to the project’s merge-request view.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view open merge requests for a named GitLab project, especially when the initial dashboard does not display that project directly.

skills.title: Terminate After Confirming Filtered Results
skills.principle: After selecting the project’s “Merge requests” page, choose the “Open” state filter and verify the URL or visible Open tab reflects the filter. Once the open merge-request list is displayed, provide the completion response and terminate instead of repeating no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when a GitLab task asks to view items with a specific state and the page visibly shows the requested filtered list, such as an Open merge requests tab and matching state parameter.

skills.title: Handle GitLab Import Credentials
skills.principle: On GitLab’s “Import group” page, choose the direct instance-migration flow, enter the source GitLab URL, then require a personal access token with `api` and `read_repository` scopes. If the token is unavailable, explain the prerequisite and instruct the user to enter it and click “Connect instance” before proceeding.
skills.when_to_apply: When importing groups from another GitLab instance and the source URL is known but no usable personal access token is available.

skills.title: Validate Source URL Before Connecting
skills.principle:
1. On GitLab’s “Import group” page, enter the actual reachable base URL of the source instance, not a placeholder or unresolved hostname.
2. Provide a source token with the required `api` and `read_repository` scopes.
3. Click “Connect instance” only after both values are real, then verify the page advances or displays available groups.
4. If “Host cannot be resolved or invalid” appears, locate the URL field by its current accessible label after the UI rerenders, replace it, and retry.
skills.when_to_apply: When importing groups through GitLab’s direct instance migration form, before clicking “Connect instance,” especially if the form reports an unresolved or invalid source host.

skills.title: Verify GitLab Navigation State
skills.principle: Use the current accessibility tree and page title to determine whether the requested GitLab page is already open. If it is, confirm the matching heading, URL or active navigation label, report completion, and stop. Otherwise, activate the navigation link whose accessible label matches the requested page, then verify the resulting heading or URL.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to navigate to a GitLab page and the current observation may already show that destination, especially when an accessible page heading, title, URL, or active navigation item can confirm completion.

skills.title: Terminate After Confirming Navigation
skills.principle: Once the page heading and URL confirm the requested destination, provide the completion response immediately and terminate the interaction. Do not repeat noop actions or wait for additional observations after the goal is visibly achieved.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for simple navigation tasks when the observed page shows the requested destination, such as GitLab’s Issues heading and Issues URL, and no further user action is required.

skills.title: Use Expanded Navigation Options
skills.principle: When a navigation link expands a menu instead of navigating, select the submenu entry matching the task, then verify the destination URL and page heading. Once the requested page is visibly loaded, report completion and stop rather than repeatedly clicking the parent link.
skills.when_to_apply: Use on GitLab dashboard tasks when the target navigation item opens a dropdown and the current page remains unchanged after clicking the parent link.

skills.title: Verify Navigation and Use Direct Href
skills.principle: After selecting a navigation entry, verify the URL and page heading changed to the requested destination. If the click only expands a menu or leaves the dashboard unchanged, use the observed link href directly, then confirm the destination heading and content before stopping.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when navigating GitLab from a dashboard and a sidebar click leaves the current URL or page heading unchanged, especially when the control also opens a submenu.

skills.title: Verify GitLab Visibility Definitions
skills.principle: On GitLab’s group-creation form, read the descriptions for Private, Internal, and Public visibility. Follow “View the documentation” for authoritative details, then compare audience, authentication requirements, directory visibility, and subgroup constraints. Include the rule that child projects or groups cannot be less restrictive than their parent.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to explain GitLab group visibility levels and the group-creation form exposes visibility radio options or a “View the documentation” link. Avoid creating a group when the task only requests information.

skills.title: Verify Help Navigation Before Searching
skills.principle: When opening GitLab Help, distinguish the expanded menu trigger from its submenu link. Select the actual “Help” destination, then verify the page title or URL changes to the Help documentation before searching or scrolling. If the page remains the dashboard, correct the navigation target instead of repeating waits or scrolling.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab documentation questions when the Help control opens a menu. Apply whenever the observed URL and page content remain the dashboard after clicking, indicating navigation has not completed.

skills.title: Select Visibility via Its Label
skills.principle:
1. Complete required group fields; GitLab may auto-generate the Group URL.
2. Choose the required visibility by clicking its visible label when the radio input is covered or intercepts pointer events.
3. Confirm the radio reports checked, submit Create group, and stop after the success alert and group page appear.
skills.when_to_apply: When creating a GitLab group and a visibility radio click times out because its associated label intercepts pointer events. Requires the creation form and required group name to be available.

skills.title: Refresh UI State Before Clicking
skills.principle:
1. After every navigation or click, inspect the latest accessibility tree before acting.
2. Select controls by their current visible role or label, not remembered element IDs.
3. If an action fails or the page becomes blank, stop repeating it; re-establish the page and re-observe before continuing.
skills.when_to_apply: When navigating GitLab from a dashboard to Groups or another creation workflow, especially after failed clicks, navigation, or page transitions that may invalidate accessibility-tree element references.

skills.title: Select Styled Radio Labels
skills.principle: When a styled radio input’s click is blocked by its associated label, click the visible label instead. Confirm the radio’s accessibility state changes to checked, then complete the form and verify the resulting success alert or destination page.
skills.when_to_apply: Use on GitLab forms or similar pages when a radio input reports that a label intercepts pointer events, especially while configuring group or project preferences.

skills.title: Refresh Element References After Navigation
skills.principle: After every navigation or page update, inspect the new accessibility tree and locate controls by their current role or label. Do not reuse bids from an earlier tree; stale bids caused repeated click failures. For group setup, use the refreshed navigation or creation control, then verify the resulting page before continuing.
skills.when_to_apply: Use this on GitLab or any dynamic website when a click changes the page, accessibility-tree identifiers shift, or an element lookup reports that a bid cannot be found.

skills.title: Create a GitLab Group with Settings
skills.principle:
1. Choose “Create group,” enter the group name, and confirm the generated Group URL.
2. Set the required visibility and personalization fields to match the requested audience and purpose.
3. If a radio input is blocked by its label, activate the associated visible label instead.
4. Click “Create group” and verify the destination page shows a success alert naming the new group.
skills.when_to_apply: When creating a new GitLab group from the “New Group” page and the task specifies audience, visibility, or purpose settings. Confirm completion only after the group homepage displays a successful-creation message.

skills.title: Open Group Creation Form First
skills.principle: On GitLab’s “Create new group” page, select the “Create group” option before interacting with fields. Wait for the creation form to appear, then locate the group name, visibility, and submit controls from the refreshed accessibility tree. Do not reuse identifiers from an absent or collapsed form.
skills.when_to_apply: When the “Create new group” page shows separate “Create group” and “Import group” options but no group-name input yet.

skills.title: Follow GitLab Documentation Links
skills.principle:
1. Open GitLab Help rather than relying on a related configuration page.
2. Choose the relevant topic, such as “GitLab groups,” from Popular topics or documentation navigation.
3. Follow the page’s direct link to the specific feature documentation, such as “subgroups.”
4. Summarize the definition, supported use cases, permissions, and constraints visible on the feature page, then stop after reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to explain a GitLab feature and the current page is related but not authoritative, use Help documentation and follow progressively more specific topic links until the feature’s dedicated page is displayed.

skills.title: Verify Help Navigation Before Searching
skills.principle: When a navigation item expands a menu, select the actual submenu link labeled “Help,” not the parent control. Verify the page title or URL changed to GitLab Help before searching. Use the Help documentation’s own search or topic navigation, and confirm results are documentation pages rather than project, issue, or merge-request search results.
skills.when_to_apply: When researching GitLab concepts such as subgroups and clicking “Help” expands a menu instead of immediately navigating. Confirm the destination before entering search terms.

skills.title: Verify GitLab Mention Syntax
skills.principle: Use GitLab Help to reach Use GitLab → Plan and track work → Markdown, then inspect GitLab-specific references. Confirm documented syntax such as `@user_name` and `@group_name`; if subgroup syntax is absent, clearly label any hierarchical-path interpretation as an inference rather than documented behavior.
skills.when_to_apply: When answering GitLab documentation questions about mentions in issues or merge requests, especially when the relevant page documents users and groups but does not explicitly describe subgroups.

skills.title: Open Help Submenu Destination
skills.principle: When a navigation label opens a menu, distinguish the menu trigger from its destination link. Select the submenu item labeled “Help” to navigate, then verify the page heading or URL changes before searching documentation.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when GitLab’s “Help” control expands a menu instead of immediately navigating, especially when the task requires locating product documentation or feature guidance.

skills.title: Verify Subgroup Availability Before Expanding
skills.principle: Open the GitLab Groups dashboard, select the target group, and inspect the selected “Subgroups and projects” tab. Expand only an existing subgroup’s hierarchy control. If the tab shows only “Create new subgroup” and “Create new project” options, treat the hierarchy as empty and report that no subgroup can be expanded; avoid unrelated notification or sorting menus.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to expand a GitLab subgroup and the target group page is not yet open, or when the “Subgroups and projects” tab may contain no existing subgroup entries.

skills.title: Use GitLab Groups Hierarchy
skills.principle:
1. Open the global navigation and choose the “Groups” entry, rather than treating the navigation menu button itself as a subgroup.
2. Locate the target group in the groups hierarchy list and identify its row-level expand control.
3. Click that control and verify the row becomes expanded and nested subgroup entries appear.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to expand a GitLab subgroup from a hierarchy list, especially when the initial page shows only Projects and a global menu. Verify nested subgroup text appears after expansion.

skills.title: Open GitLab User Profile
skills.principle:
1. Identify the signed-in user's display-name or avatar link in the GitLab header.
2. If clicking it opens an account menu, choose the entry showing the user's display name and username.
3. Confirm navigation succeeded when the page heading shows the user and profile sections such as activity or projects.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to visit the current user's GitLab profile from another GitLab page, especially when the header identity control opens a dropdown before exposing the profile link.

skills.title: Select Profile From User Menu
skills.principle: Click the signed-in username/avatar to open its menu, then select the submenu link showing the username and handle (for example, “Username @handle”). Verify navigation by checking that the URL changes from the dashboard to the user profile path and that profile content is displayed.
skills.when_to_apply: When GitLab’s username/avatar control opens a dropdown instead of navigating directly, and the menu contains a dedicated username/profile link.

skills.title: Navigate to a GitLab Project
skills.principle:
1. From an unrelated GitLab page, open the Dashboard and use the Projects list or name filter.
2. Locate the target project by its displayed name, then activate its project link.
3. Confirm the project page by checking its heading, repository content, or project navigation sidebar, then stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to open a specific GitLab project and the current page is elsewhere. The Dashboard must expose the project list or search/filter controls.

skills.title: Confirm the Target Project Before Navigating
skills.principle: When asked to open a specific GitLab project, identify the requested project name or path before selecting an item. Use the dashboard’s “Filter by name” or GitLab search to locate an exact match, then open its project link. If no target is provided, ask for clarification instead of choosing an arbitrary project.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab navigation tasks when multiple projects are listed and the target project name or path is missing, ambiguous, or not directly visible.

skills.title: Locate and Open a GitLab Issue
skills.principle:
1. Navigate to GitLab’s Issues page from the global navigation.
2. Scan the issue list for the target title, using the visible project and issue reference to disambiguate matches.
3. Open the matching issue link and verify the page heading or title matches the requested issue.
4. Once the issue content is visible, report completion and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view a specific GitLab issue and the current page is elsewhere in GitLab. The Issues list must be accessible, and the target issue should be identifiable by title or project reference.

skills.title: Create a Top-Level GitLab Group
skills.principle:
1. On GitLab’s Create group page, enter the requested name in Group name.
2. Verify Group URL auto-populates appropriately; change visibility only if the task specifies it.
3. Click Create group.
4. Confirm the group page appears and a success alert states the group was successfully created before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to create a new top-level GitLab group and the Create group form is available. Use the success alert and resulting group page as completion evidence.

skills.title: Use GitLab’s Group Creation Flow
skills.principle: For a top-level group, choose GitLab’s group-creation path rather than “New project.” Use the “Create a group” link or navigate to the Groups creation page, enter the group name, submit, and verify the resulting group page or confirmation. Do not treat a project name field as a group-creation form.
skills.when_to_apply: When the task requests a new GitLab group, especially from the project dashboard or namespace picker. If a project form appears, back out and use “Create a group” instead.

skills.title: Use the Associated Label for Radios
skills.principle: When a styled radio input cannot be clicked because its label intercepts pointer events, click the label associated with the desired option instead. Then inspect the updated accessibility tree and confirm the target radio is checked before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: Use on GitLab forms or similar UIs when changing a selectable setting, the radio input click fails with pointer-event interception, and the accessibility tree exposes an associated label for the desired option.

skills.title: Trust the Actual Radio State
skills.principle: Read the radio group's explicit checked state, not merely the target label. If the requested visibility option is unchecked and another option is checked, select the requested option, then verify it reports checked before completing. Only report that no action is needed when the target control is explicitly checked.
skills.when_to_apply: When changing GitLab group visibility on a form exposing Private, Internal, and Public radio options, especially when accessibility-tree labels and checked states may be easy to confuse.

skills.title: Verify Dropdown Selection Before Acting
skills.principle: Inspect the labeled combobox and its selected value before making changes. If the requested option is already selected, treat the task as complete, report confirmation, and stop; otherwise select the requested option and verify the updated value.
skills.when_to_apply: Use on form tasks requiring a specific dropdown choice, especially when the page may already be preconfigured. The accessibility tree must expose the combobox value or selected option for confirmation.

skills.title: Verify and Set Purpose Selection
skills.principle: Inspect the combobox’s actual selected value, not merely whether the requested option exists. If the selected value is blank or differs from the requested purpose, open the purpose field and choose the matching option. Confirm the accessibility tree shows that option selected before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: Use on GitLab’s new-group form when asked to specify the group’s purpose, especially when the requested option is listed but the current selection may be blank or different.

skills.title: Follow Relevant Documentation Links
skills.principle: When the current page contains a link whose label and surrounding text directly match the requested documentation topic, activate that link. Verify completion by checking the destination heading, URL path, and page content match the requested topic, then report completion and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for navigation requests to a named GitLab help or documentation page when the current accessibility tree exposes a semantically matching link and the destination can be verified after navigation.

skills.title: Use Observed Links, Not Visible Labels
skills.principle: When a text-based click fails, do not retry the same label or invent a bid. Read the current accessibility tree, identify the exact link and URL for the relevant documentation topic, then navigate using that observed target. Confirm the destination title or topic before taking further actions.
skills.when_to_apply: Use on GitLab help or documentation pages when a link is visibly named but BrowserGym reports that its text or bid cannot be found, especially after navigation changes the accessibility tree.

skills.title: Follow Semantically Matched Documentation Links
skills.principle: When a task requests specific documentation, inspect the current page for a link whose label and surrounding section match the requested topic. Activate that link, then verify the destination through the page title, URL path, and relevant headings before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when already viewing a GitLab page that contains contextual links to help documentation, especially when the requested topic corresponds to a visible link such as “View the documentation.”

skills.title: Stop After Confirming Target Page
skills.principle: When the target documentation page is visible and its title or URL matches the requested topic, treat navigation as complete. Report completion and terminate immediately rather than issuing repeated no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: Use after clicking a documentation link when the resulting page visibly matches the requested subject, confirmed by its page title, URL, or relevant heading.

skills.title: Use Radio Labels When Inputs Are Blocked
skills.principle: When a radio input’s click is intercepted by its styled label, click the associated visible label instead. Then inspect the updated accessibility tree and confirm the intended option shows checked=true before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: Use on GitLab forms or similar pages when selecting a radio option, especially after a direct input click times out because the label intercepts pointer events.

skills.title: Follow the Group Creation Workflow
skills.principle: Do not infer a group-settings URL from a similarly named project. Use visible GitLab navigation to open the group-creation or onboarding workflow, then select the option labeled "Just me" when the user audience question appears. If a guessed URL returns 404, go back and locate the correct workflow instead of reporting infeasibility.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to choose an audience such as "Just me" for a GitLab group, especially from the dashboard where only projects are visible or a guessed settings URL produces a 404.

skills.title: Verify Link Targets After Navigation
skills.principle: Use the current accessibility tree to locate the link by its exact visible label and activate it. After navigation, re-scan the new page rather than reusing the prior element ID, then confirm the destination heading or URL matches the requested content before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When a task asks you to click a specifically labeled link, especially when the destination is documentation or another page whose content must be confirmed after navigation.

skills.title: Verify Navigation Before Acting Again
skills.principle: After activating a requested link, inspect the new page URL, heading, and content to confirm the destination satisfies the task. Once the requested information is visible, report completion and stop. If another action is needed, re-scan the current accessibility tree and use a newly observed element reference; never reuse identifiers from the previous page.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for link-following tasks, especially when navigation changes the page or accessibility-tree references. Apply after the first click and whenever the observed page no longer contains the original target.

skills.title: Verify Dashboard State Before Acting
skills.principle: Inspect the current URL, page title, and accessibility-tree content before navigating. If they already identify the requested destination and show its expected content, report completion immediately. Otherwise, activate the visible navigation link matching the destination, then verify the resulting page state before finishing.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for navigation tasks when the initial page may already be the requested destination. Prerequisite: the accessibility tree exposes a reliable destination label, URL, title, or expected page content.

skills.title: Confirm Dashboard State and Stop
skills.principle: When GitLab already shows the Dashboard navigation entry and dashboard content (such as the Projects heading), treat the navigation task as complete. Report completion and terminate immediately; do not repeatedly click the current-page link or issue noop actions.
skills.when_to_apply: For GitLab tasks requesting Dashboard navigation, when the observed URL, page title, or accessible tree already identifies the Dashboard and its content is visible.

skills.title: Terminate After Confirming the Target View
skills.principle: Once the requested GitLab page is visible and its relevant filter is confirmed—for example, the Issues page showing an assignee filter and issue list—treat the task as complete. Report completion and terminate instead of repeating no-op actions or reopening an already-correct filter.
skills.when_to_apply: When a navigation or filtering task visibly reaches the requested page and the accessibility tree confirms the intended state, such as an assignee-filtered Issues list.

skills.title: Create an Internal GitLab Group
skills.principle:
1. On GitLab’s Create group form, choose the Internal visibility option by clicking its associated label when the radio input is obstructed.
2. Fill Group name; confirm the Group URL textbox contains the desired slug, editing the textbox itself if necessary.
3. Click Create group and verify the destination page shows a success alert naming the new group.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when creating a top-level GitLab group requiring Internal visibility and a custom URL, with the Create group form available and required fields editable.

skills.title: Open Group Creation Form First
skills.principle: On GitLab’s “New Group” page, select the “Create group” option before searching for fields. The group name, URL, visibility, and submit controls appear only after that creation pane is activated; then inspect the updated accessibility tree and fill the visible form fields.
skills.when_to_apply: When the “New Group” page shows separate “Create group” and “Import group” options but no input fields, activate “Create group” before scrolling, focusing, or filling fields.

skills.title: Navigate Nested Help Menus
skills.principle:
1. Identify the top-level navigation control labeled “Help” and activate it.
2. If it expands a menu instead of navigating, select the nested “Help” link.
3. Confirm completion by checking the page title, URL, or visible Help documentation content, then stop and report success.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when GitLab’s navigation presents Help as a dropdown or menu rather than a direct link, and the target is the GitLab Help landing page.

skills.title: Stop After Verifying Navigation
skills.principle: After selecting the relevant navigation entry, verify the destination using the page title, URL, or distinctive content. Once the requested page is visibly confirmed, report completion and terminate instead of issuing repeated no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for simple navigation tasks when the destination page is loaded and its accessibility tree shows the expected title, URL path, or distinctive heading.

skills.title: Use Observed Profile URL Directly
skills.principle: When a visible username or navigation label cannot be clicked reliably, use the exact profile URL exposed in the accessibility tree with `goto`. Confirm completion by checking the destination title and profile-specific content such as an “Edit profile” link or username details, then stop.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab profile-navigation tasks when the header username appears in the accessibility tree but label- or element-based clicks fail, or when the profile link’s observed URL is available.

skills.title: Choose the Profile Link, Not Avatar
skills.principle: On GitLab, open the account menu and activate the semantic profile link labeled with the username or handle, such as “Byte Blaze @username.” Do not select the avatar image or its external image URL. Verify navigation by checking that the page URL is the user’s GitLab profile path and the page content identifies the user.
skills.when_to_apply: When navigating from a GitLab dashboard to the signed-in user’s profile and the account menu exposes both an avatar image and a textual profile link.

skills.title: Use Cancel To Reach Groups Dashboard
skills.principle: From an unintended GitLab New group form, activate the visible "Cancel" link rather than interacting with the form. Verify navigation succeeded by checking the page heading "Groups," dashboard tabs such as "Your groups," and the resulting groups list, then report completion and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: When the task is to open GitLab’s Groups dashboard and the current page is the New group form with a Cancel link leading to the groups dashboard.

skills.title: Use Exact Navigation Targets
skills.principle: When leaving an unintended GitLab form, use the currently observed element by accessible role and label, such as the "Cancel" link targeting the Groups dashboard, or copy the exact observed href. Avoid stale bids and verify the resulting URL or page heading before finishing.
skills.when_to_apply: When the task requires reaching a dashboard but the current page is a creation or edit form, especially after an element lookup fails or direct navigation is necessary.

skills.title: Choose the Canonical Documentation Link
skills.principle: Inspect the accessibility tree for links matching the requested topic. Prefer the broad, canonical documentation link over narrower related pages such as subgroups. Activate it, then verify the destination by checking the page heading and URL before reporting completion and stopping.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab task requests navigation to a documentation topic and the current page contains multiple related links, especially a general topic link alongside specialized subtopic links.

skills.title: Use Semantic Documentation Links
skills.principle: When a page contains a link whose label matches the requested documentation topic, select it rather than navigating through unrelated menus. If multiple matching links exist, choose any link targeting the same topic. Confirm completion using the destination URL and page heading, then report success and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: Apply when the requested GitLab documentation topic is already referenced by a visible, semantically labeled link and the resulting page exposes a recognizable topic heading or matching documentation URL.

skills.title: Use GitLab Docs Entry Point
skills.principle: When GitLab’s instance search cannot locate a documentation topic, open Help and follow the “docs.gitlab.com” link to the documentation site. Search for the requested topic there instead of guessing an instance URL or slug, and confirm the destination heading matches the requested page.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab documentation-navigation tasks when instance search returns no useful result, a guessed path produces a 404, or Help exposes a dedicated “docs.gitlab.com” link.

skills.title: Recover From 404 Via GitLab Dashboard
skills.principle:
1. When a GitLab URL shows “Page Not Found,” use the visible “Home” or “Dashboard” link instead of retrying the invalid path.
2. On the dashboard, select the “To-Do List” navigation entry, identifiable by its pending-item badge.
3. Confirm the “To-Do List” page displays the pending list and its “To Do” count before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to view pending GitLab to-dos and the initial URL is invalid or displays a 404 page; requires an accessible Home/Dashboard link and authenticated GitLab navigation.

skills.title: Terminate After Verifying Completion
skills.principle: Once the GitLab To-Do List is open, select the pending-state entry and inspect the resulting page. If the page shows the pending count and an empty-state message such as “Nothing is on your to-do list,” the task is complete; report the result and terminate instead of repeating no-op actions.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view pending GitLab to-dos and the To-Do List page visibly confirms the pending state, especially with a zero count or empty-state message.

skills.title: Recover From GitLab 404 Pages
skills.principle: When a requested GitLab route shows “Page Not Found,” recover through the visible Home link or GitLab navigation, then locate the relevant feature from the valid interface. Use the global search only if navigation does not expose it. Verify the destination page before reporting that the task is impossible, and stop after one clear user-facing status if recovery genuinely fails.
skills.when_to_apply: Apply when direct navigation lands on a GitLab 404 page while seeking a feature such as completed to-dos, and visible Home, navigation, or search controls remain available.

skills.title: Check To-Do State Before Searching
skills.principle: On GitLab’s To-Do List, inspect the visible state counts and content before scrolling. If “To Do” is zero and an all-done message appears, open “Done” and locate the target there instead of repeatedly scrolling. Use GitLab’s global search only to navigate to the related record, not as proof that the to-do is pending or completed.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab To-Do List shows no pending items, an all-done message, or unchanged accessibility content after scrolling; verify the Done view and target status before taking further actions.

skills.title: Open GitLab’s What's New Drawer
skills.principle:
1. If starting on an invalid or 404 page, use the visible GitLab Home or Dashboard link to reach the main dashboard.
2. Open the top navigation “Help” menu and select the “What’s new” button.
3. Confirm completion when a “What’s new” drawer appears with update titles, dates, descriptions, and tier information.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view GitLab’s latest updates, especially from a dashboard or after landing on a 404 page. The Help menu must be available in the authenticated GitLab interface.

skills.title: Use Help Menu for What's New
skills.principle: Open GitLab’s Help menu and inspect its expanded accessibility tree. Select the explicitly labeled “What’s new” button rather than scrolling or opening Help documentation. Confirm the resulting page or panel contains the latest updates before finishing.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view GitLab’s latest updates and the dashboard header lacks a direct link, especially after expanding the Help menu where “What’s new” is visible.

skills.title: Search GitLab Projects from a 404
skills.principle:
1. If the current GitLab page is missing or irrelevant, use the visible Dashboard or Home navigation to reach the main project dashboard.
2. Enter the requested keyword in the global “Search GitLab” field and submit with Enter.
3. On the results page, select the “Projects” scope and verify its result count and listed project name, description, and metrics.
4. Report the matching project details once the project result is visibly confirmed.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to find GitLab projects matching a keyword, especially when starting on a 404 page or another unrelated route and the global search field is available.

skills.title: Stop After Search Results
skills.principle: When the requested GitLab search returns matching projects, verify the results list and report the project names or links immediately. Do not open project details, README sections, documentation, or unrelated links unless the task explicitly requests further information.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab tasks asking to find projects matching a term, once the search results page visibly shows the Projects scope and one or more matching project entries.

skills.title: Infer Projects From Issue Search Results
skills.principle: Search GitLab globally for the integration phrase. If the Projects scope returns zero but Issues returns relevant results, inspect each issue’s project attribution and descriptions, collect distinct project names, and report them as projects associated with the integration topic. Clearly distinguish documented mentions or work from confirmed built-in integrations.
skills.when_to_apply: When GitLab project search finds no direct matches for an integration query, but global issue results contain project-qualified issues mentioning that integration.

skills.title: Verify Search Results Against Task Criteria
skills.principle: After searching GitLab for a keyword, open the Projects result scope and inspect each returned project’s description or README. Distinguish a project that merely mentions the external service from one that actually provides integration, then report only verified matches.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab search returns projects matching a service name but the task requires a specific capability such as integration; prerequisites are a submitted search and visible project results.

skills.title: Filter GitLab Issues by State
skills.principle:
1. Open the GitLab Issues page from the dashboard.
2. Select the state link matching the request, such as “Closed,” rather than using individual issue controls.
3. Confirm the page URL or issue list reflects the selected state and report completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab issue-list task requests a specific state and the Issues page exposes state links such as Open, Closed, or All.

skills.title: Terminate After Verified Completion
skills.principle: Once the requested filter is applied, verify the page state—such as the URL showing the target state and issue rows labeled CLOSED—then report completion and terminate. Do not continue issuing noop actions after the goal is visibly achieved.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab issue-list task reaches a page whose filter control and displayed results confirm the requested state, such as Closed issues.

skills.title: Find GitLab Issues Through Global Search
skills.principle:
1. If the starting URL is invalid, return to GitLab Dashboard rather than guessing issue URLs.
2. Open the global “Search GitLab” field and enter the target issue title.
3. Select the “Issues” result category, then choose the result whose title and project match the request.
4. Confirm the issue details page by checking its heading and displayed description before reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when locating a GitLab issue by title, especially from a 404 page or a dashboard filtered to assigned issues. Verify the exact issue result before stopping.

skills.title: Open the Actual Issue Result
skills.principle: After searching GitLab, distinguish the scope tab (for example, “Issues 2”) from individual result links. Select the result whose accessible name matches the target title, then verify navigation by checking that the URL leaves search and the page heading shows the issue details. If the search page remains visible, continue searching rather than reporting completion.
skills.when_to_apply: When locating a GitLab issue through global search, especially when results include multiple issue matches and an “Issues” scope link alongside individual issue-title links.

skills.title: Use GitLab Merge Requests Navigation
skills.principle:
1. If the starting GitLab URL shows “Page Not Found,” navigate to the Home or Dashboard link.
2. In the dashboard navigation, select the “Merge requests” entry rather than the “Issues” entry.
3. Confirm completion when “Merge requests” is focused or expanded and its menu shows options such as “Assigned to you” or “Review requests for you.”
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to switch GitLab’s task scope from Issues to Merge requests, especially when the initial page is invalid and the dashboard navigation is available.

skills.title: Use Valid BrowserGym Action Syntax
skills.principle: Issue a syntactically valid action using only the required element reference, such as clicking the observed link bid without appending its label or malformed arguments. If execution returns an empty-action error, stop repeating the same malformed command; re-read the observation and use the link’s observed destination directly or another valid control. Confirm completion by checking the URL or visible page state changed to the requested scope.
skills.when_to_apply: When a GitLab navigation link is visible but BrowserGym reports an empty action or the page remains unchanged after a click attempt. Reinspect the current accessibility tree before retrying or switching to direct navigation.

skills.title: Recover From GitLab 404 Pages
skills.principle:
1. Treat a 404 as evidence that the guessed route is invalid; do not keep retrying URL variants.
2. Return to a confirmed accessible page, such as Home, and inspect the fresh accessibility tree before acting.
3. Locate the current project-search control by its observed role or label, then search for the target project and open the result.
4. Verify the project page loaded before searching its merge requests.
skills.when_to_apply: When GitLab shows “Page Not Found” after navigation, especially when subsequent actions report stale or missing element IDs. A confirmed page reload and fresh element inspection are prerequisites.

skills.title: Recover Repository Navigation Through Search
skills.principle:
1. If a direct repository URL shows 404, search the target project name using GitLab’s global search.
2. If project results are empty but related merge requests appear, open a related result to enter the project context.
3. Use the project navigation link or breadcrumb labeled with the project name to reach the repository root.
4. Verify the URL and page show repository contents, then stop; treat navigation-completion timeouts as successful when state confirms arrival.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when a GitLab repository URL is invalid or project search returns no direct project result, but related issues or merge requests identify the target project.

skills.title: Filter GitLab Merge Requests by Status
skills.principle:
1. If the starting project URL shows 404, return to the GitLab dashboard.
2. Open the dashboard’s “Merge requests” navigation entry.
3. Select the “Merged” status tab, or navigate to the merge-request view with its merged-state filter.
4. Confirm the page URL and visible “Merged” option reflect the selected status; an empty-results message still indicates the filter is applied.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to show GitLab merge requests with a specific status and the initial page may be invalid or lacks visible merge-request content.

skills.title: Verify Merge Requests Page Before Filtering
skills.principle: Do not infer filter availability from the Projects dashboard. After activating the Merge requests navigation entry, confirm that the URL and main heading change to a merge-request listing. If it only expands a submenu, select the relevant destination link or open a project’s merge-request list, then inspect its status controls for “Merged” and verify the resulting list updates.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to filter merge requests but the current accessibility tree still shows Projects, or when clicking “Merge requests” expands navigation without changing the page.

skills.title: Use the Sign-Out Account-Switch Link
skills.principle: On GitLab, select the visible “Sign out and sign in with a different account” link, even if the current page is an error page. Confirm completion when GitLab navigates to the sign-in page showing “Username or email,” “Password,” and a “Sign in” button; then stop unless credentials are provided.
skills.when_to_apply: When the task is to switch GitLab accounts and the current page exposes the account-switch link, including on a 404 page. Credentials are required to complete the subsequent sign-in.

skills.title: Use Fresh Labels for Account Switching
skills.principle:
1. Open the signed-in user menu and select the visible “Sign out” link, not the avatar image or profile link.
2. Confirm sign-out by checking that GitLab shows the “Sign in” form.
3. Re-read the current accessibility tree before every action; element IDs from earlier pages may now target different controls.
4. Fill the new account credentials and submit “Sign in,” verifying the resulting signed-in state.
skills.when_to_apply: When switching GitLab accounts, especially after navigation or redirects. Prerequisite: the current page exposes a signed-in user menu and a visible “Sign out” control.

skills.title: Use Visible Help Navigation
skills.principle: When the requested GitLab page is not the current page, inspect the accessibility tree for a semantically labeled navigation link matching the destination and activate it. Confirm completion by checking the resulting page title, URL, or heading; if already on the requested page, report completion without navigating further.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab navigation tasks when the current page may be a 404 or unrelated page but exposes global navigation, or when the requested destination is already visibly confirmed.

skills.title: Use GitLab Global Search
skills.principle:
1. Locate the “Search for projects, issues, etc.” searchbox, even if the current page appears unavailable.
2. Enter the requested query and activate “Search.”
3. Confirm the GitLab Search page loads and inspect result-scope tabs such as Projects, Issues, or Merge requests.
4. Report completion only after matching results and counts are visible.
skills.when_to_apply: When searching GitLab for a project or issue and a global searchbox is available, including on an unexpected or 404-looking page.

skills.title: Clarify Missing Search Targets
skills.principle: When the request lacks the project or issue name, ask for the exact search term instead of guessing. Once provided, use the textbox explicitly labeled “Search GitLab” for global searches, or “Filter by name” for the project list, verifying the observed role before filling it. Confirm results match the requested target before opening an item.
skills.when_to_apply: Apply to GitLab project or issue searches when the requested target name, issue title, or other distinguishing detail is absent or when multiple search controls appear in the accessibility tree.

skills.title: Filter GitLab Projects to Personal
skills.principle:
1. If the initial project URL is unavailable or shows an error, return to the GitLab dashboard using the visible Home or Dashboard link.
2. In the Projects view, select the visible “Personal” filter rather than “All” or “Starred.”
3. Confirm completion when the Personal view is active and the page displays the user’s owned project list.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view personal projects in GitLab and the dashboard or project page is accessible, especially when the starting URL is invalid or displays a 404 error.

skills.title: Verify Filtered State Before Acting
skills.principle: After applying a GitLab project filter, re-observe the page and verify the URL and visible project list. If the requested view is already active, report completion and stop. Never reuse accessibility bids from a prior page state; locate the current control again before clicking.
skills.when_to_apply: When viewing GitLab projects after navigation, filtering, or sorting, especially when the accessibility tree has changed or the requested filter URL and matching project list already appear.

skills.title: Terminate After Confirming Completion
skills.principle: Once the target page is visibly loaded and its contents satisfy the request, report completion and terminate immediately. Do not repeat no-op actions or continue interacting after the goal is confirmed.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for navigation or viewing tasks when the current page title, URL, and visible content clearly match the requested destination and no additional modification or selection is required.

skills.title: Stop After Confirmed Project Exploration
skills.principle: For an open-ended GitLab exploration task, open the Explore projects view, inspect a representative project’s summary and repository or README, then report completion once those details are visible. Do not keep switching between Topics, Most stars, Trending, and unrelated pages after sufficient exploration is confirmed.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when the task broadly asks to explore GitLab projects without specifying a target. After reaching Explore and viewing at least one project’s details, README, or repository contents, conclude instead of continuing navigation.

skills.title: Clear Tooltips Before Clicking
skills.principle: When a tooltip intercepts the intended repository link, move the pointer to a neutral area or dismiss the tooltip, then retry the original target. Verify navigation by checking that the breadcrumb or URL reflects the requested directory before choosing another file or section.
skills.when_to_apply: When browsing GitLab repository trees, a click timeout reports that a visible tooltip or overlay intercepts pointer events and the intended directory remains available.

skills.title: Recover Navigation After a 404
skills.principle: When the requested GitLab page returns “Page Not Found,” use the visible “Home” or “Dashboard” link to reach the project dashboard. Locate the relevant navigation entry, such as “Topics,” open it, and verify the resulting page state. Report the page’s explicit empty-state message when no items are available.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab browsing tasks when the initial destination is missing or invalid, but the 404 page provides a working Home link and the dashboard exposes the requested resource.

skills.title: Recover and Open Assigned Merge Requests
skills.principle:
1. If the current GitLab URL shows “Page Not Found,” navigate to the dashboard using the visible Home or Dashboard link.
2. Select the navigation entry labeled “Merge requests,” then choose the assignment-specific option such as “Assigned to you.”
3. Confirm completion when the page heading reads “Merge requests” and categorized tabs or counts with the request list are visible; report completion and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: Use when asked to view the current user’s GitLab merge requests, especially when starting from an invalid project URL or a dashboard showing the Merge requests navigation entry.

skills.title: Open Assigned Merge Requests
skills.principle:
1. Expand the GitLab sidebar’s “Merge requests” entry if needed.
2. Select the nested “Assigned to you” link for the user’s merge requests, rather than stopping at the expanded parent menu.
3. Verify navigation by checking the URL contains the merge-requests path and the main content lists merge requests.
skills.when_to_apply: When asked to view personal merge requests and the sidebar parent is expandable, especially if the current URL or main heading still shows the Projects dashboard.

skills.title: Use Dashboard Navigation After 404
skills.principle: When a guessed GitLab URL shows a 404, return to the dashboard rather than retrying path guesses. Locate the navigation entry labeled "To-Do List" and open it. Confirm completion by checking the page heading and visible pending/done counts, then report the state and stop.
skills.when_to_apply: Use for GitLab tasks involving the to-do list when a direct or guessed URL fails, but the dashboard is reachable and its accessibility tree exposes the relevant navigation entry.

skills.title: Navigate to Project Issues
